Breaking: Cold Plunges Are Finding a Newly introduced Place in Residential Design

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Once relegated to backyards and home gyms, cold plunges are finding a newly introduced place in residential design.
  • In a recent development, the interest goes beyond athletic recovery.
  • According to recent reports, in the Heber, Utah, residence by Berg Design Studio, Hydro Systems’ Marquis bathtub demonstrates how traditional freestanding tubs can accommodate emerging wellness technologies, including cold plunging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once relegated to backyards and home gyms, cold plunges are finding a newly introduced place in residential design. As the wellness practice grows in popularity, homeowners are increasingly looking to incorporate cold therapy directly into their bathrooms, transforming what was once a standalone piece of fitness equipment into an integrated feature of the home.

In a recent development, the interest goes beyond athletic recovery. Cold-water immersion has been associated with potential benefits ranging from reduced muscle soreness to improved sleep and stress management, although research into its broader health effects remains limited. Still, the appeal is evident. According to Houzz’s 2024 Summer Trends Report, searches for “cold plunge” increased 74% year over year, while searches for “indoor sauna” rose 69%.

According to recent reports, in the Heber, Utah, residence by Berg Design Studio, Hydro Systems’ Marquis bathtub demonstrates how traditional freestanding tubs can accommodate emerging wellness technologies, including cold plunging. Photography by Steve C. Wilson.

That interest reflects a larger shift toward wellness-focused residential spaces. The organization’s 2026 report found that searches for “wellness room” had increased 164%, suggesting that homeowners are thinking more intentionally about how their environments can support relaxation and well-being.

For interior designers, these changing priorities are introducing fresh considerations into residential projects. Arizona-based designer Stephanie Larsen, who incorporates cold plunges, infrared saunas, and integrated aromatherapy systems into her work, has seen clients place greater emphasis on these features. “Today’s clients are craving homes that heal and inspire,” she told Luxe Interiors + Design. “They want spaces infused with wellness technology.”.

Accommodating those requests means thinking beyond individual fixtures to how different wellness experiences function together. Cold plunges, for instance, are often paired with saunas for contrast therapy, which alternates between hot and cold exposure. Bringing both into a residential setting requires careful consideration of available space, plumbing, and the relationship between the different elements. Manufacturers, meanwhile, are developing more integrated systems that offer greater flexibility.

Industry observers note that hydro Systems integrates cold-plunge technology into freestanding bathtubs, bringing cold therapy into residential bathrooms without the need for separate equipment. Photography courtesy of Hydro Systems.

“We’re seeing wellness become a more intentional part of residential design, with dedicated spaces that bring together multiple hydrotherapy experiences in a single tub, from cold plunging and whirlpool to oxygenated microbubble therapy,” says Ashley Steinhardt, VP of Sales at Hydro Systems.

The California-based bath manufacturer has developed its Hydro Chill technology to incorporate cold plunging into customizable bathtubs, eliminating the need for a separate fixture. Its latest iteration also introduces smart-home functionality, allowing owners to adjust water temperatures and schedule plunges remotely.

According to recent reports, hydro Systems is also exploring how multiple hydrotherapy experiences can share the same footprint. Its upcoming Hydro Chill Ultra delivers both hot and cold water through a self-contained system that generates its own hot water. Because it doesn’t require a traditional hot-water connection, the technology offers additional flexibility for installations in pool houses and dedicated wellness rooms.

Featured in an Atlanta Homes Showhouse, Hydro Systems’ Slate bathtub features a custom color and polished finish, with integrated Hydro Chill cold-plunge technology. Paired with a wood-paneled sauna, the tub demonstrates how cold therapy can become part of a thoughtfully designed residential wellness space. Photography courtesy of Hydro Systems.

It has been revealed that while expansive home spas provide room for separate saunas, plunge tubs, and other amenities, integrating hydrotherapy into an existing bathroom requires a different approach. Multifunctional fixtures can help reduce the space needed for these experiences, making them easier to accommodate within conventional residential layouts.

“Wellness doesn’t have to be confined to a dedicated room,” Steinhardt indicates. “Hydrotherapy can also be incorporated into smaller bathroom footprints, bringing wellness into everyday routines.”.

Hydro Systems’ Hydro Chill cold-plunge system is incorporated into a home gym alongside weight-training equipment, bringing cold-water immersion into a dedicated fitness and recovery space. Photography courtesy of Hydro Systems.

It has been revealed that cold plunges may still be a relatively niche residential amenity, but their growing visibility is prompting designers to reconsider what a bathroom can accommodate. As more wellness features make their way into the home, the challenge will be integrating them without compromising the functionality, comfort, and aesthetics of the spaces around them.

Industry News: Friday Five With Shaina Tabak: Art, Architecture, and the Spaces Between

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, though she’s still pursuing her MFA in Visual Arts at Columbia University, artist Shaina Tabak is hardly a newcomer to the art world.
  • Tabak’s own work is equally expansive.
  • ‘On Certainties (streetlight)’ (2026) by Anthony Discenza and ‘Arbor Armor’ (2015–2026) by Yasue Maetake on display at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, though she’s still pursuing her MFA in Visual Arts at Columbia University, artist Shaina Tabak is hardly a newcomer to the art world. The RISD graduate, who earned her BFA in furniture design, already has more than 20 exhibitions under her belt. Now she’s adding curator to her résumé with 260 Madison, an artist-run exhibition bringing together more than 50 artists across a former Duane Reade storefront and a 23,000-square-foot office floor above it in Midtown Manhattan.

Tabak’s own work is equally expansive. Drawing on history, technology, and materiality, she explores the relationship between the digital and physical worlds, often starting with digitally modeled forms that she translates into sculptures through hands-on processes such as cutting, perforation, lamination, and extrusion.

‘On Certainties (streetlight)’ (2026) by Anthony Discenza and ‘Arbor Armor’ (2015–2026) by Yasue Maetake on display at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

In a recent development, but her interest in materials extends beyond their physical properties. She also sees them as records of labor, manufacturing, extraction, and use. Her work examines contemporary material culture through a historical lens, imagining how the things made and valued today might be understood generations from now. As she puts it, her sculptures are “less concerned with imagining the future than with creating historical distance from the present.”.

It has been revealed that that perspective comes through in her recent work, which examines the increasingly blurred line between looking and shopping. In her Brooklyn studio, the Queens-born artist has been embedding collected industrial objects in three-ply cardboard, referencing the packaging and shipping systems that support consumer culture. She’s also exploring the influence of visual search and algorithmic commerce, where objects spotted in an image can lead to an endless stream of purchasable alternatives. It’s a commentary on a culture in which images don’t just inspire desire; they generate transactions.

‘First Water (deer)’ and ‘First Water (banner)’ (2026) by Dexter Barker-Glenn on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

For today’s Friday Five, we spent five minutes with Shaina Tabak to explore the ideas behind her curatorial debut at 260 Madison and the influences shaping her own work in the exhibition.

‘Ghosts’ (2025) by Alisa Berger and ‘Impaler Shield’ (2026) by Kari Cholnoky on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

For her curatorial debut, Tabak drew on Columbia University’s MFA community and her own network of artists, bringing together emerging talents and established names. Co-curated by artistic duo Dayana Matasheva and Edson Niebla Rodríguez of Demon Lovers, Inc., 260 Madison includes artists such as Simon Denny, Jon Kessler, and Eva and Franco Mattes. The exhibition was organized in collaboration with the building’s owner, AmTrustRE, which gave the curators full creative control.

‘Longcat’ (2026) by Eva & Franco Mattes on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

On view through Nov. 22, 2026, the expansive exhibition brings together familiar materials, objects, and technologies that are dismantled, reconstructed, or made strange. Exposed HVAC, ripped-out toilets, and corporate-logo wallpaper create the backdrop for works spanning sculpture, fresh media, and video. Tabak’s goal for 260 Madison is to “examine the systems organizing contemporary life—from control, surveillance, AI, and extraction to the material and architectural structures that shape how we work, move, and live.”.

Below, in her own words, Tabak shares the influences that shaped her approach to 260 Madison, from artist-run exhibitions that challenged traditional institutions to architectural theories and sculptures that informed her own work.

Shaina Tabak’s works ‘Localized Collapse / Frozen Zone’ (2026) and ‘Sweep Towards Skylight’ (2026) on view at ‘260 Madison.’ Photography courtesy of the artist.

Sources indicate that “The first one, Damien Hirst’s Freeze (1988), was suggested to me by my professor Jon Kessler. Freeze was particularly compelling because it took place amid the redevelopment of London’s Docklands and was itself supported by real-estate developers, revealing the uneasy relationship between artistic independence and the production of urban capital. That history made me particularly conscious of a contradiction in our own project: While 260 Madison temporarily interrupts the building’s commercial function, the exhibition also generates cultural value for a property undergoing modernization.”.

In a recent development, “A more recent exhibition, Christopher Wool’s See Stop Run (2024), took place in New York City’s Financial District and demonstrated how artists could operate outside established institutions by appropriating vacant commercial spaces. Wool’s exhibition was also installed on a gutted office floor and offered a more immediate architectural reference, allowing the building’s exposed infrastructure and traces of demolition to enter into dialogue with the work. With 260 Madison, we wanted to push these precedents even further, treating the vacant corporate office as a material record of changing relationships between labor, capital, and the built environment.”.

Photography courtesy of Shaina Tabak.

“Rem Koolhaas’ book Delirious New York and his essay “Junkspace” were really helpful in connecting the architecture of the space to the exhibition. My partner has worked on the 17th floor of 260 Madison for the past three years—a complete coincidence—and his 9-to-5 job as a paralegal brought to mind Koolhaas’ concepts of the vertical schism, architectural lobotomy, and definitive instability as I considered the exhibition’s function.”.

“All three of Koolhaas’ concepts, in their own ways, describe the Manhattan skyscraper as a structure in which the exterior remains independent of the interior, allowing different floors to accommodate radically different and constantly changing activities without altering the building’s outward appearance.”.

Industry observers note that “I was thinking about House, a temporary public sculpture by Rachel Whiteread, when creating my sculpture Swept Towards Skylight (2026) for 260 Madison. I embedded an earlier work in insulation foam and coated it with cement to give the illusion that the negative space around it had been cast solid. Whiteread’s work transformed the interior of a house slated for demolition into a concrete monument to its former inhabitants and the lives that had occupied it.”.

“I kept returning to this idea while curating 260 Madison, where the vacant office floor still bears physical traces of the labor and routines that once animated it. I wanted the building to function not simply as a container for artworks, but as an artifact in its own right, with its exposed infrastructure and signs of abandonment becoming part of the exhibition. What interests me about House, and what I hoped to capture at 260 Madison, was how architecture outlives its function and becomes a monument to the systems that once gave it meaning.”.

Industry observers note that 260 Madison is on view through Nov. 22, 2026, at 260 Madison Avenue in New York City.

In a recent development, A 25-plus-year veteran of the interior design industry, Danine Alati began her career at commercial design publication Contract, where she spent 11 years before moving into luxury lifestyle media and working on titles including Hamptons and Art Basel. Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

The Peralta D Supercar Is Literally Sculpted From Copper

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that but what if you didn’t have to worry about such concerns?
  • In a recent development, “It was a proposal I made to the client, Carlos Peralta,” Giugiaro claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the last century or so, ever since wood fell out of style, the bodies of most automobiles have been made from a few tried-and-true materials: carbon fiber, fiberglass, aluminum, and steel, with the metals proving most popular. The choices are a balancing act, forcing carmakers to weigh price, safety, convenience, and appearance to determine which substance makes the most sense for the masses.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

Industry observers note that but what if you didn’t have to worry about such concerns? What if cost was no object, practicality a formality, and there was no need to cater to the wants of more than one owner? Well, that was the lucky circumstance designer Fabrizio Giugiaro, founder and CEO of GFG Style, found himself in when creating the Peralta D, a gran turismo with a body made of hand-hammered copper.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

In a recent development, “It was a proposal I made to the client, Carlos Peralta,” Giugiaro claims. The duo had worked together before on the design house’s first one-off automobile, the spitshine-polished 1980s-esque Peralta S. For the follow-up, Giugiaro wanted to draw a deeper connection to the owner. As an industrialist, Peralta has business interests involving copper, so Giugiaro suggested it as the material.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

Giugiaro’s name is well known in the automotive world. His father, Giorgetto Giugiaro, is a master of clean-line designs—he penned the DeLorean DMC-12, the BMW M1, the original Lotus Esprit, and the first Volkswagen Golf. The senior Giugiaro’s career has included work for Ferrari, Lamborghini, Bugatti, and many more of the world’s most notable automotive brands. The father-and-son duo founded GFG Style together over a decade ago, but it’s only been in recent years that they’ve been dedicating their talents to bespoke coachbuilt cars for individual collectors, as with the Peralta D.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

Recent findings suggest that and while using copper for a car’s bodywork may be unorthodox, the designer indicates it wasn’t as difficult as it may seem. “It really surprised us that copper proved to be much more malleable than the aluminum we had worked with previously; it is also considerably easier to weld and polish,” Fabrizio says. “Of course, it does come with the disadvantage of greater weight, but since it was combined with a supporting structure made entirely of carbon fiber, the overall balance between the materials ultimately worked out well.”.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

It has been revealed that beneath all that copper lies the chassis of a 2025 Maserati GranTurismo Trofeo—itself a stylish design, but one far removed from the almost brutalist simplicity of the Peralta D’s angles. Instead of traditional doors, the car features a dramatic opening system inspired by the Peralta S’s single-motion dome, with independently opening side windows and gullwing-style openings at the rear to access the back seats.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

Industry observers note that inside, copper-colored leather adorns most surfaces, broken up (almost) only by the infotainment and dashboard screens, which offer some of the few hints of its Maserati roots. Meant to showcase the bond between its owner and his daughters, the car comes with a few (perhaps stereotypically) female-oriented features, such as a passenger-side makeup station with an illuminated mirror and dedicated cosmetic storage. And while the rear seats are tight, a retractable refrigerator designed to hold a bottle of champagne and four copper glasses means occupants can easily distract themselves.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

While the Peralta D might seem to push the boundaries—or at least the materials—of road-going automobile design to their limits, Fabrizio suggests even wilder builds may follow in its tire tracks.

“I have another alternative material in mind, one that has only ever been used once before,” he states, “so it will be another surprise…”.

Photography courtesy of GFG Style.

Will Sabel Courtney has been working in journalism since 2010, specializing primarily in automotive and men’s lifestyle writing. He has driven too many cars to count over the course of his career. A native of Vermont, he has lived in Latest York City for two decades, dividing his time between Manhattan and Brooklyn, where he now resides.

A Practical Guide To Naming Things

📅 2026-10-06 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1228 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • The language we use shapes the way we think about things, but also the conversation we have about it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Naming is hard. The language we use shapes the way we think about things, but also the conversation we have about it. That’s why we have so much confusion about colors, icons, UI components, features — and that’s why we struggle to name design tokens, HTML classes, and variables.

Sometimes, the names we choose are too generic, so it’s difficult to understand what exactly is meant. And sometimes they are too specific, leaving little room for flexibility and reuse. How do we choose the right names? And which naming conventions work best? Let’s take a closer look.

If you’re looking for some inspiration for naming HTML classes, CSS properties, or JavaScript functions, Classnames is a wonderful resource jam-packed with ideas that get you thinking outside the box.

The site provides thematically grouped lists of words perfect for naming. You’ll find terms to describe different kinds of behavior, likeness between things, order, grouping, and association, but also themed collections of words that wouldn’t instantly come to one’s mind when it comes to code, among them words from nature, art, theater, music, architecture, fashion, and publishing.

How would you choose the right name for a given color? Fortunately, David Aerne maintains a tremendous repository of color names, at the moment with 30355 unique color names, sourced from various references and 1000s of user contributions.

Of course, the repository comes with a color picker and name search and plenty of other color pickers as well. Tremendous work, which is also a fantastic reference to keep nearby.

According to recent reports, what makes a good name? Javier Cuello summarized a set of naming best practices that help you name your layers, groups, and components in a consistent and scalable way.

Sources indicate that as Javier points out, a good name has a logical structure, is short, meaningful, known by everyone, and not related to visual properties. He shares do’s and don’ts to illustrate how to achieve that and also takes a closer look at all the fine little details you need to consider when naming sizes, colors, groups, layers, and components.

In a recent development, how to build a flexible design token taxonomy that works across different products? That was the challenge that the team at Intuit faced. The parent tech giant of products such as Mailchimp, QuickBooks, TurboTax, and Mint developed a flexible token system that goes beyond the brand theme to serve as the foundational system for a wide array of products.

Industry observers note that nate Baldwin wrote a case study in which he shares valuable insights into the making of Intuit’s design token taxonomy. It dives deeper into the pain points of the old taxonomy system, the criteria they defined for the fresh system, and how it was created. Lots of takeaways for building your own robust and flexible token taxonomy are guaranteed.

In a recent development, looking at what other people call similar things is a great way to start when you’re struggling with naming. And what better source could there be than other design systems? Before you end up in the design system rabbit hole, Iain Bean did the research for you and created the Component Gallery.

It’s a collection that includes plenty of examples for more than 50 UI components — from accordion to visually hidden — and also lists other names that the UI components go by. A fantastic resource, and not only with regard to naming.

Recent findings suggest that features often have low adoption due to poor discoverability. Feature adoption needs time — first the feature must be discovered, then understood, then tried, learned, and eventually built into existing workflow. Erin Gannon has written a helpful practical guide on how to make sure all of it happens.

Good names are driven by user needs and problems. They should signal the value or outcome of a feature (the job-to-be-done), and — most importantly! — tap into the user’s own language. So ask people to explain a feature in their own words and then use the words they use.

According to recent reports, A wonderful example of naming guidelines for a complex multi-brand, multi-themed design system comes from the Vodafone UK Design System team. Their Variables Taxonomy Map breaks down the anatomy and categorization of a design token into a well-orchestrated system of collections.

Industry observers note that the map illustrates four collections required to support the system and connections between tokens — from brand and primitives to semantics and pages. It builds on top of Nathan Curtis’ work on naming design tokens and enables everyone to gather insight about where a token is used and what it represents, just from its name.

If you want to explore more approaches to naming design tokens, I’ve put together a list of useful Figma kits and resources that are worth checking out.

Romina Kavcic created a helpful little tool for naming design tokens — from learning how they work and how to name them well to configuring your own naming structure with components, categories, states, and roles.

If you are looking for the right name for your product or service, Onym is a fantastic open-source repository that organizes tools and resources for finding names for brainstorming, vetting, guides, sprints, etymologies — all the way to cautionary tales and agencies that name things, as well as useful books to take a look at.

A quick-reference list of tools and guides for naming just about… well, anything, in one place:.

The right name is the one that’s well-understood and used by the team and customers. So much time is wasted speaking about the very same thing but in different dialects — the designer’s dialect, the developer’s dialect, the product manager’s dialect, and the user’s dialect. That’s what often causes frustration and confusion.

Industry observers note that so if you see low adoption, it might be merely because of the name. And pay attention to potential naming conflicts and put them in a backlog of things to address later. It’s one of those fine little details that can reduce frustration and confusion and help teams work together better.

In a recent development, we hope you’ll find these wonderful projects useful — put together by wonderful creators. A friendly shout-out to everyone sharing their work with folks to use and learn from! That’s one of the reasons why we truly love the web and people building and designing it. 💚.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the National Gallery of Canada (NGC) and the Sobey Art Foundation named the artist Lotus L. Kang asthe winner of the 2026 Sobey Art Award during a ceremony on Saturday (14 November). The Toronto-born, Upcoming York-based photographer, sculptor and installation artist won the 23rd edition of the annual award, the most high-profile and lucrative prize devoted to Canadian contemporary artists, and will receive C$100,000 ($70,000).

The other five shortlisted artists—Melaw Nakehk'o (from the Circumpolar region), Samuel Roy-Bois (Pacific), Audie Murray (Prairies), Caroline Monnet (Québec) and Shane Perley-Dutcher (Atlantic)—will each receive C$25,000 ($17,500), while the 24 longlisted artists each received C$10,000 ($7,000), bringing the total value of the award to C$465,000 ($325,800).

Sources indicate that in a statement, Jonathan Shaughnessy, the chair of the jury for this year’s Sobey Art Award, praised Kang for “the commitment and rigour demonstrated in her practice for well over a decade”. He continued: “Through installations using unfixed photographic film, cast and found objects, and fabricated armatures, her practice resists the stabilising impulses traditionally associated with photography. Reoccurring motifs including lotus root, flowers, soju bottles, birds, anchovies, are not fixed objects, but repositories of place, longing and desire.”.

Recent findings suggest that partial view of Lotus L. Kang's installation In Cascades (2023-24) in Whitney Biennial 2024: Even Better Than the Real Thing at the Whitney Museum of American Art Photo: The Art Newspaper.

According to recent reports, kang, a recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2024 whose work was included in the 2024 Whitney Biennial and the 2025 Shanghai Biennale, works across sculpture, photography and site-responsive installation. Her materially dense, non-linear installations explore the liminal space between industrial and architectural forms, familial and social histories, as well as poetry and non-human figures. One of her celebrated installation works, Mother (2020), comprised dozens of metal mixing bowls filled with scattered abstract clay, rubber and stone sculptures as well as aluminium casts of fruit and anchovies. Her critically acclaimed solo exhibition at 52 Walker in New York last year featured several greenhouse installations as well as one made of strips of film extended around a spinning rotary dryer.

Sources indicate that “It is an honour to be recognised by this prize,” Kang remarked in a statement. “I am grateful to those I love, those who love me and those who have supported me; you keep me going. The recognition of this prize means that askew ideas are worth pursuing. Art is essential to life, progress and love.”.

During the ceremony, Kang told those assembled at the NGC and those watching via livestream: “I just want to congratulate the other artists. It’s an honour to be nominated alongside you. Shane, Melaw, Caroline, Audie, Samuel. It is really inspiring to be showing alongside you, and who knows what would have happened, and I’m just glad we’ll all keep making art, because it’s really the best thing. So, thank you so much.’’.

Lotus L. Kang, Receiver Transmitter (49 Echoes I), 2022-25 © Lotus Kang. Photo: Courtesy of the artist and 52 Walker gallery, Latest York.

Rob Sobey, the chair of the Sobey Art Foundation, offered his “heartfelt congratulations” to Kang and added: “We also celebrate tonight all 29 artists on this year’s longlist and shortlist for their creativity and vision. We are proud to champion their work and grateful to the National Gallery of Canada for helping bring these remarkable artistic voices to audiences at home and around the world.”.

Selected by an independent jury of curators and cultural leaders, Kang was chosen following a rigorous review process. The jury, who evaluated the artists’ practices, achievements, and contributions to contemporary art in Canada included Kimberly Phillips, the director of the Marianne and Edward Gibson Art Museum at Simon Fraser University, representing the Pacific region;Daisy Desrosiers, a curator at large for North America at Tate, representing the Quebec region;and Helen Nisbet, the director of Glasgow International, serving as international juror.

Works by all six shortlisted artists are right now featured in the 2026 Sobey Art Award Exhibition at the NGC in Ottawa (until 3 January 2027).

Sources indicate that the late Frank H. Sobey, an enthusiastic collector of Canadian art, established the Sobey Art Foundation in 1981 and the Sobey Art Award was launched in 2002. Five years ago, the award’s criteria were amended from a prize devoted to “emerging artists” under 40 to recognising artists of any age who are at a “critical juncture” in their careers. Past winners have included Brian Jungen (in 2002), Annie Pootoogook (2006), Abbas Akhavan (2015), Laakkuluk Williamson Bathory (2021) and Nico Williams (2024).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hybrid and remote work have changed what people expect from a modern workspace. No longer do people want fixed seating or single-purpose design. Instead, they are looking for modular, multi-use furniture that boosts productivity while maintaining comfort and style. When Chris and Jon Panichella set out to design their latest seating collection for Arcadia, they turned to everyday life for inspiration.

“The idea for Almeya began with a woman working from an inflatable raft at the beach,” the Panichellas explain. “She could recline and read in one position, then sit up and work in another—a simple moment that captured how much people now expect from their spaces: comfort, flexibility, and function. That observation became the very first concept sketch that eventually evolved into the Almeya offering we know today.”.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

With a full family of products—including modular, lounge, work-lounge, benches, and occasional tables—the Almeya Collection offers a fluid experience that adapts to these modern shifts in productivity and collaboration. Across the series, soft, organic forms invite comfort and ease, while integrated tables, flexible configurations, and strategic power stations allow for both focus and sociability.

Sources indicate that almeya began with a single lounge chair and an integrated two-tiered side table. The idea was simple: the combination could function as a self-contained work island, with two separate surfaces, power access, and an optional rotating tablet. With this concept in mind, the Panichellas developed a standalone lounge chair, love seat, and sofa with the same flexible spirit. (Case in point: The swivel-base lounge chair allows for adaptability and easy collaboration). Finally, the complete collection came together, designed to support the various—and often unpredictable—ways people work and gather.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

To inspire interaction, designers are encouraged to group lounge seating intermittently to foster spontaneous connections. To create pathways or natural flow within a space, they can explore Almeya’s modular capabilities. The organic curves of the lounge models also create an inviting warmth, blurring the line between contract and residential. And for healthcare and education settings, optional clean-outs are offered between the seat and back.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

In a recent development, completing the collection, occasional tables carry the same gentle, organic language for a cohesive experience. Available in multiple sizes and shapes, tables feature upholstered sides and are offered with ash or walnut veneer, laminate, Corian, and Fenix top surfaces.

See the full Almeya Series at arcadiacontract.com.

At 55,000 miles for a seat that costs $5,000 to $12,000 in cash — with zero fuel surcharges and a free stopover in Hong Kong — this redemption delivers 9 to 22 cents per point. It requires more planning and effort than a simple hotel booking, but the payoff is a genuine luxury travel experience that proves the asymmetric value the FI community builds its travel rewards strategy around.

It has been revealed that this sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

#22389. Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2064 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Industry observers note that the way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking. He has over 25 years experience working with clients such as Doctors … More about Paul ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that the way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy. If it were turned into a movie, reviewers would say it was unbelievable. Nobody could be that stupid.

Recent findings suggest that yet here we are. And what makes it all the more frustrating is that we have been here before.

Back in 2014, I wrote a book for Smashing Magazine called Digital Adaptation, looking at the mistakes being made in how organizations were approaching digital transformation and what they should be doing instead. The similarities between then and now are striking.

So in this post, I want to look back at Digital Adaptation and see how the lessons in that book apply to the AI era and what we can learn from the past to help us navigate the challenges of AI today.

The biggest mistake, both then and now, is approaching each as a technological challenge.

Sure, both digital transformation and AI are technological advances, and yes, some level of technological implementation is required. But that is the tip of a very large iceberg.

Recent findings suggest that back in the midst of the digital transformation era, IT departments were rolling out CMSs, CRM systems, intranets, and so on. Meanwhile, on the customer-facing side, organizations were rolling out websites, apps, and personalization. But they were putting almost no emphasis on how people were going to use these systems.

Internal systems were hard to use, and customers either didn’t care what was being built or wanted something else entirely.

Sources indicate that the same is happening with AI. Senior management are buying into the hype, and IT teams are rolling out Copilot Studio licenses organization-wide and considering the job done. Sure, there is a bit of organization-wide generic training, but that’s about it.

Just like before, staff are left wondering what to do with these upcoming systems and feeling under pressure to use them and deliver results.

After all, this time around, it is even worse, because this time, staff fear for their jobs. They have read the same headlines that you have, and no amount of promises from senior management is going to make them feel any better.

In a recent development, I mean, think about it from a staff member’s point of view. AI offers them very little personally, even setting aside the fact that management may be intending to use it to replace them.

The main reason senior management are excited about AI is that it provides additional productivity. People can do more in less time. But that does not benefit staff. They are still required to work 9 to 5, but now they are expected to do more in the same time. They don’t get any time back, and they don’t get paid more, so why would they embrace AI?

It has been revealed that one strategy is to help staff identify the parts of their job they hate and how AI can help them do those tasks more quickly and less painfully. People tend to be a lot more receptive to change when it is presented as an opportunity to improve their working lives.

Sources indicate that but, that should just be the beginning. Organizations may need to consider providing incentives for staff to adopt AI in terms of career progression, compensation, or shorter working hours.

Also, adopting AI is not a simple task. It involves challenging every working practice they have built up over (in some cases) decades. All of that procedural knowledge has to be rebuilt. That is a lot to ask of anybody in even the best of circumstances, and most employees do not find themselves in the best of circumstances.

It has been revealed that most are overworked and struggling to stay on top of their to-do lists. They don’t have time to sit down, learn a new tool, and figure out how it fits into their workflow.

Recent findings suggest that that doesn’t just take time. It also takes a lot of consideration and experimentation. It is not enough to just send a member of staff on a training course and expect them to be able to use AI to its full potential.

Industry observers note that at a minimum, staff need training specific to their roles, such as the AI training I provide to UX teams. But organizations should be going even further.

Recent findings suggest that they need to develop sophisticated training programs that help staff from different departments understand how to use AI in their specific roles. They need ongoing support and the time to experiment with AI to find the best ways to use it.

But formal training will only take you so far. In my experience, the most effective support comes from colleagues, which is why I would start with the enthusiasts rather than the resisters. Every organization has a handful of people who are already experimenting with AI, often without anybody asking them to. Bring those people together, give them the time and space to share what is working for them, and let their enthusiasm spread to everyone else.

It has been revealed that I saw this work during the digital transformation era too. In Digital Adaptation, I described an internal conference where staff indicated their colleagues what they had built, and it did more for adoption than any memo from the top ever could. People are far more likely to try something when they see a colleague in a similar role using it successfully than when they are told to by senior management.

Unfortunately, experimentation comes with a big downside… mistakes will be made.

Many organizations have, to be frank, a culture of fear where mistakes are seen as a sign of incompetence. However, by its very nature, learning a new tool like AI will involve making mistakes, and this can be a massive barrier to adoption.

According to recent reports, I saw this during the era of digital transformation. Senior management would demand digital transformation and were confused when it didn’t happen.

What they didn’t realize was that they were sending mixed messages to staff. Sure, they were asking for digital transformation, but they were still demanding that the same key performance indicators (KPIs) be met, and they still pointed out any mistakes in their annual reviews.

There was no space to fail, as the pressure to deliver was relentless.

In a recent development, this time around, it seems to be even worse. I hear horror stories of staff being reprimanded for using too many tokens just weeks after being told to adopt AI. Or staff being lectured so much about what they should or should not do with AI that they are afraid to try anything. It is safer to just do what they have always done.

Look, I get it. AI cannot be rolled out without some governance in place, but again, this is an area that organizations have typically handled poorly.

In the midst of digital transformation, governance would either be non-existent, or it would be so strict that it would stifle innovation, and unfortunately, I see the same pattern emerging with AI adoption.

Staff need some governance to help them know where they stand. It helps them understand what is expected of them and what they can and cannot do.

But too often organizations have been so strict that it is easier not to do anything at all. Pages of instructions about what people should and should not share with AI create that sense of fear that I mentioned earlier.

Of course, mistakes will get made, but that is the cost of change, and so organizations need to accept that and do what they can to mitigate that in how they roll out the technology.

It has been revealed that that noted, organizations will need to be careful in how they roll out AI from an IT perspective. Once again, it is easy to lock everything down and stifle the adoption of AI.

Again, this is something I highlighted back in 2014 with digital transformation. Overstretched IT teams would pick a set of technologies and roll them out organization-wide, often with little or no consultation with the individuals who would be using them. Anything outside of that set of technologies had to go through a complex approval process, normally involving a steering committee. The result was a glacial pace of change that was one of the major contributing factors to the failure rate of digital transformation projects.

Sources indicate that today we are seeing the same thing. IT teams are opting into a tool like Copilot and calling it a day, but that often falls massively short.

Sources indicate that take, for example, a UX team I am working with at the moment. Management is pushing hard for AI adoption, and the team is excited about the potential of creating an AI-powered research repository and even AI personas. It sounds like a wonderful case study in AI adoption, with enthusiastic management, an excited team, and innovative ideas.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, the reality is that nothing is happening because Copilot cannot deliver on the team’s vision, and so they are at the moment bogged down in bureaucracy as they try to persuade the AI steering group that they need to use a different toolset. Understandably, the team’s enthusiasm is waning. Why bother?

It has been revealed that and that team is one of the more patient ones. In many organizations, staff are not waiting for the steering group at all. Just as we saw shadow IT during the digital transformation era, with people signing up for Dropbox and Google Docs because the official tools could not do what they needed, we are now seeing shadow AI. When the in-house AI tool will not let people do their jobs, they open a personal ChatGPT or Claude account on their phone or home laptop and get on with it.

According to recent reports, that is far more dangerous than the problem the restrictions were meant to prevent. Tech giant data ends up in tools the organization has no control over, with no oversight and no record of what has been shared. In trying to lock everything down, organizations end up pushing the risk somewhere they cannot see it.

According to recent reports, the instinctive reaction is to clamp down with stricter policies, blocked websites, and warnings about disciplinary action. But that rarely works, and it drives the behavior further underground. Shadow AI is a symptom, and a useful one, because it shows exactly where the official tools are falling short.

Sources indicate that look, I understand the cost of a messy, out-of-control tech stack. It is not ideal. However, in the early days of adoption, we may have to live with a bit of chaos while people explore the edges of what is possible and work out common use cases.

Organizations need to allow staff to explore different uses of AI and even different AI apps to find what suits their specific needs in their specific roles. They can always start locking things down later as the real organizational needs become clearer.

I admit all of this feels dangerous to some organizations. They want to control the AI adoption process centrally and make sure nothing goes wrong. I understand that. But change comes with a degree of risk, and the risk of moving too slowly is greater than the risk of moving too fast.

However, a bigger danger still is when organizations see this as a technological challenge and overlook the human side of things. AI adoption is not simply about rolling out upcoming technology. Just like digital transformation, it is about people, culture, and change management. The sooner organizations realize the scope of what they are dealing with, the better.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the objects we carry often reveal more about us than we realize. From the jewelry we wear to the accessories we keep within reach, even the smallest possessions become expressions of personal style. Yet as technology plays an increasingly central role in our lives, the devices we interact with most remain largely defined by their utility. Bringing more personality to these everyday essentials is the idea behind Pocket Full of Joy—a new collaboration between ESR, a consumer tech accessories brand, and creative duo Craig & Karl—which transforms phone cases and wallets into colorful, functional accessories.

Known for their vibrant compositions and playful iconography, Craig & Karl bring their distinctive visual language to a collection of iPhone cases and magnetic wallets. The collaboration draws upon the duo’s affinity for bold colors and familiar imagery, translating their graphic sensibilities into objects designed to accompany their owners throughout the day. The result is a collection that explores how artistic expression can become part of everyday life.

Across the collection, sticker-like illustrations, saturated hues, and expressive typography lend a sense of character to otherwise utilitarian surfaces. A collage of playful symbols evokes the spontaneity of a personal scrapbook, while the graphic “OK” design introduces a lighthearted note of optimism. Elsewhere, the cheerful “HI” motif transforms a magnetic wallet into a small, portable greeting. Each composition reflects Craig & Karl’s recognizable aesthetic while giving everyday accessories a more personal character.

Recent findings suggest that behind the playful graphics are the practical features that define ESR’s accessories. The Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Flex Stand incorporates a built-in adjustable stand, MagSafe compatibility, and protective construction, allowing it to move between different activities without sacrificing its colorful design. Coordinating magnetic wallets hold cards and cash in compact silhouettes, while the Magnetic Wallet Stand with Grip adds an adjustable viewing stand and finger loop for greater versatility. Together, these features bring Craig & Karl’s expressive graphics to everyday accessories.

It has been revealed that the collection’s appeal also comes from the way it brings art into objects that have become nearly inseparable from modern life. Where traditional artworks invite observation, these designs encourage interaction, becoming more personal through repeated use. A phone placed on a café table, a wallet retrieved during a morning commute, or a device propped against a desk becomes a small, unexpected moment of visual interest.

According to recent reports, with Pocket Full of Joy, ESR and Craig & Karl make a case for bringing more creativity into the everyday. Sometimes, the most memorable design details are found in the things we carry without a second thought.

In a recent development, the ESR × Craig & Karl Pocket Full of Joy collection will be available Nov. 14, 2026, at esr.com and amazon.com, with iPhone cases starting at $49.99 and magnetic wallets starting at $25.99.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Studio Freight builds the Thesis brand identity from zine culture: an asterisk mark, dot-grid Harber type, and electric lime.

Sources indicate that the system starts from a position, not a logo. Thesis builds brands on Bitcoin, backing its conviction with capital and code, and Studio Freight answers with a visual language pulled from indie hacker zines and early computing: black and white, gritty textures, hand-drawn spheres and gears, and one electric lime doing all the shouting. The asterisk sits at the center, somewhere between a footnote and a flag, and the whole identity reads like a samizdat pamphlet that learned to behave on a screen. The voice matches, what the studio calls adult punk: spirited defiance tempered with wisdom, unafraid to make guesses about restoring autonomy in tech.

Two typefaces carry the system. Harber, a dot-gridded display face, holds the texture of a printout from a different internet, with dotted letterforms that spell the name at poster scale, in the site navigation, and ghosted behind the asterisk on the homepage. Antique Legacy Semibold does the clear work, setting plain statements in a voice that stays readable while the display type makes the noise.

It has been revealed that the grid is the dot grid itself. The asterisk mark, the dotted THESIS letterforms, and the dotted figures in the launch graphics all sit on the same dotted construction, so every panel reads as one argument. The studio coined a word for the position behind it, counterventure, naming a studio that creates ideas from the inside instead of waiting for them to walk in, operating against the extractive defaults of the venture model.

The material language is print, even on screen. Hand-drawn spheres and gears, gritty textures, and a black-and-white field give the system the feel of print passed hand to hand, and the electric lime cuts through it in exactly one place at a time: a poster, a headline, a hand-drawn illustration on a lime field. The stationery keeps the same discipline, a white card that carries the name and the counterventure label, and nothing else.

Recent findings suggest that the system stretches across the launch site, where the asterisk fills a monitor above the tagline, and into product work, where a phone screen for tBTC carries the dot-grid mark and a line about decentralized cryptography. A poster fills its frame with one word in flat lime, and a manifesto sheet sets the studio's own words in typewriter type over the dotted asterisk, including its line about making bitcoin accessible to all.

Industry News: Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that brecht De Ruyte is a self-taught front-end developer located in Belgium with a passion for UX and Design. After more than a decade of working in tech, he … More about Brecht ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Recent findings suggest that in design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment. But when I heard that the native CSS random() function landed in Safari and is rolling out in Chrome 156, I started wondering: where does randomness actually make sense on the web? Is it something we want in our design system? To find out, I did what I always do in doubt: I built a bunch of playful CodePen demos exploring organic typography, bouncing letters, splayed cards, and a punk fanzine.

As someone who loves building design systems and tinkering with CSS architecture, a significant part of my day job revolves around control. We set up spacing scales, lock down typography, set up color tokens, and make sure everything aligns on a grid. Consistency is usually our bread and butter as design engineers and a proud badge of skill when creating design systems. If a card suddenly jumps 20 pixels to the left on a refresh, it’s not creative expression; it’s a bug that the project manager will log.

So when I first heard that the native random() function from the CSS Values and Units Level 5 spec was shipped in Safari, and is presently rolling out in Chrome 156 (with positive signals from Mozilla on Firefox as well), my first reaction was: that’s pretty cool!

And my second reaction was: wait… where would I actually use this without making a mess? How can I convince designers that random might be a good idea for a design system?

Because let’s be honest: why on earth would we want randomness in our stylesheets when we’ve spent the last decade trying to make the web more predictable? Even when using flexbox or fluid typography, we’re still trying to make things as aligned and uniform as possible.

If you step away from the browser for a second and look at physical things around you, nothing is ever truly uniform.

It has been revealed that take an old letterpress print: the ink bleeds slightly into the paper grain, some letters have a microscopic tilt, and the baseline isn’t always that straight. Or think about a deck of Polaroid photos dropped on a coffee table; those photos aren’t perfect, probably not straight either. Or what about lights flickering in a street at night? That little bit of analog messiness is what makes things feel alive, organic, and human.

On the web, we’ve gotten so good at pixel perfection that sometimes our interfaces end up feeling a bit sterile. We notice this even more now with rapidly created designs by an unguided LLM; we usually end up with the same sort of design we had 10 years ago. Everything is squared off, aligned, neat. It works, but frankly, it does get a bit boring.

Recent findings suggest that randomness in CSS doesn’t have to mean throwing your design system out the window. It’s about little imperfections and playfulness. Maybe let’s even call it fun.

Industry observers note that to see what this actually looks like in practice, I spent a few hours tinkering in CodePen. The demos might feel a bit isolated, but I’m sure that many designers could make the best of this controlled chaos. But before we look at those demos, let’s take a look at the syntax.

According to recent reports, the random() function is specified in CSS Values and Units Module Level 5. It generates a pseudo-random value inside your CSS without needing JavaScript or a build-time Sass loop.

The formal specification looks like this:.

In practice, and across current browser implementations, you can just write comma-separated arguments:.

It won’t be a shocker for most people, but I thought I should at least mention that your minimum and maximum bounds must share the exact same unit type.

The CSS parser needs to know what dimension it’s dealing with. You can use lengths, angles, time, percentages, or plain unitless numbers:.

If you ever need to combine units, you’ll have to reach for calc() inside the arguments so each side resolves properly.

The optional third argument is the step size. If you don’t add it, the browser picks from a continuous range. But if you provide a step, it rounds the random value to discrete increments:.

This can be helpful in cases where you want things to jump around a bit, but you still want them to land on your pre-defined grid.

According to recent reports, normally, every time random() is evaluated on a property, it creates an independent random value. But there could be an example where you create a box that sets inline-size and block-size at random, but at the same time you need them to match so the element stays a perfect square.

That’s where the caching key comes in:.

In the latest spec, a bare dashed ident like --square-size shares its seed globally across every element in the document (which would make all cards identical). To keep width and height linked on a single element while giving each card its own independent size, the spec requires pairing it with the element-scoped keyword (e.g. --square-size element-scoped).

To see this in action, I created a little example. In the top row, the tiles have uncached dimensions, which distorts each tile into an unpredictable, mismatched rectangle. In the bottom row, both inline-size and block-size share --square-size, guaranteeing that each tile remains a pristine 1:1 square. Refresh the CodePen a couple of times and notice the bottom cards keeping the same randomness:.

See the Pen [Uncached vs cached random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e91-4bac-765e-b04e-a53636759163) by @utilitybend.

Because we’re still in the rollout phase, you’ll want to wrap your experiments in @supports:.

According to recent reports, there’s also another function in the spec called random-item(). While random() handles numerical ranges, random-item() lets you pick from a list of predefined tokens or keywords:.

This can be handy to randomise from a set of design tokens. This one does not have any browser support at the moment, but it certainly is something to look forward to.

And now for the practical part.

When I started playing with the feature, I was also doing some typography tricks with animations. So that’s where my first thought went: Typography! What if we just add a tiny bit of imperfection to a word?

In a recent development, think of vintage book covers. The letters aren’t misaligned by miles, but they have small imperfections.

See the Pen [Imperfection random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-157f-708d-a704-fa067114aaca) by @utilitybend.

Here is the CSS powering the letters:.

I also added a little hover effect. While you’re reading, the word feels playful. But the second you hover over it, every character snaps back.

One quick accessibility warning here: If you break a word into separate elements so you can style each letter, screen readers will often read it out as individual characters: “i - m - p - e - r - f - e - c - t - i - o - n”, or pause awkwardly between each one. That’s a terrible user experience.

Always hide the visual spans from assistive tech and provide the full word:.

Screen reader users get the clean text, and sighted users get the fun visual quirks.

Once I had those letters sitting there with their little tilts, I couldn’t resist: what if we animated it?

Industry observers note that I started tinkering with a bounce keyframe. I was just goofing around, but the end result gave me a little smile. If you animate every letter with the exact same timing, you get that clean sine wave we’ve all seen before. But if every letter gets its own jump height, its own duration, and its own landing squash, suddenly the word looks like a bunch of little characters jumping around on a trampoline.

See the Pen [Bouncy imperfection with CSS random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-c117-729f-9844-ddf19fc1fc96) by @utilitybend.

Here is how the bounce parameters are wired up:.

Notice the negative animation delay (--delay: random(-3s, 0s)).

Industry observers note that if you set a positive delay, the letters sit frozen on page load, waiting for their timers to expire before jumping. By using a negative delay, the browser pretends the animation has already been running for a few seconds. The moment the page loads, every letter is already bouncing at its own rhythm.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve built cards. Lots of cards. So many cards… Portfolio grids, blog summaries, feature lists. And most of the time, they sit in three or four neat, boring columns.

In a recent development, for dashboards, that’s exactly what you want. But if you’re building a lifestyle portfolio, a children’s website, or a collection of vacation photos, we can be a bit more playful. In the following example, I did just that:.

See the Pen [Random card tilt [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e93-849d-72a9-9254-3f4305e58a34) by @utilitybend.

Here’s how I put that together:.

In the example, playing around with the shadow was a fun experiment. I will probably try more effects with that in the future.

Industry observers note that here is where modern CSS features start getting really interesting. In the previous demo with tilting cards, we used pure randomness. But what if you have a stack of cards that needs to fan out across the screen as you scroll?

In this example, I decided to use math for the structure and randomness for the human imperfection.

See the Pen [Scroll drivin animations with random() tilted cards [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e94-79c6-70b1-97d4-66b7c2d736b0) by @utilitybend.

Look at how cleanly this works:.

If you’ve ever looked at brutalist or high-end fashion websites, you’ve probably seen horizontal marquee text drifting across the screen as you scroll down the page.

Usually, you see developers creating classes like .drift-slow, .drift-fast, .drift-reverse, or using a hefty JavaScript scroll listener to compute transforms.

With random() and a tiny bit of math, we can get procedural drift speeds in just a few lines:.

See the Pen [Random() velocity scroll animation [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-4cbe-77bd-9128-685d2c75cc56) by @utilitybend.

It has been revealed that calc(pow(-1, sibling-index())) gives us alternating directions (1, -1, 1, -1), and random(15%, 44%) decides how fast each row travels. As you scroll, each typographic line moves at its own tempo.

According to recent reports, I love photography, and one of my favorite things about prime lenses is shallow depth of field. When you shoot at a wide aperture like f/1.7, only whatever is right on your focal plane stays sharp. Everything else melts away into soft bokeh. Yep, photography is all about that bokeh!

By combining random() with filter: blur(), opacity, and scale, we can recreate that lens feel:.

See the Pen [All about that random() bokeh [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-fe50-76dc-943b-d75fcaf704e6) by @utilitybend.

In a recent development, some words land at blur(0px) with full opacity right in front of your eyes. Others blur out to 6px or 8px and fade into the background. And when you hover over any blurry item in the back, it rack-focuses right into sharpness. It’s a great little effect for decorative hero sections or tag clouds.

Now that we’ve played with the wild side, let’s talk about where this actually belongs in our daily work.

In a recent development, but! I am happy to be proven wrong here. I encourage you to challenge the status quo and experiment with this.

Any time you use animations, you have to respect user preferences for reduced motion:.

Industry observers note that if someone prefers reduced motion, it could also be a good idea to flatten the angles, not just the animations. I can imagine that a lot of random angles can also upset people while scrolling. Design should be fun, but never at the cost of accessibility.

Sources indicate that tinkering with random() over the last couple of days was a lot of fun. I’m still not sure if I’ll be able to convince my designer friends, but what I do know is that it brings a bit of joy.

Sources indicate that whenever we wanted a bit of organic randomness on the web, we had to make compromises: either pull in a JavaScript animation library, or write huge preprocessor loops that spit out hundreds of lines of static CSS. Having this built into the browser engine with zero JavaScript overhead is such a welcome addition.

According to recent reports, we spent the last decade mastering consistency, tokens, and design systems. Now that we have that foundation in place, maybe it’s time to let a little bit of playful messiness back onto the web.

I really believe that the web is supposed to be fun.

Never mind the defaults; here is CSS random().

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the UAE is home to a trove of Modernist building designs thanks to the country’s founding in 1971 and the ensuing construction boom. One such building is the decommissioned Terminal 1 of Zayed International Airport, which was designed by the French architect Paul Andreu and opened in 1982. Now a designated heritage site, it is the unique venue for the Abu Dhabi edition of the itinerant art and design fair Nomad (18-22 November), which returns to the city for a second time in partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism.

In a recent development, “Architecture has always been fundamental to Nomad,” notes the fair’s founder and director, Nicolas Bellavance‑Lecompte. “[Terminal 1] has a very particular architecture, but also a history as a place of movement and exchange. Rather than placing conventional booths inside it, we wanted to work with the building as we found it—its terminals, corridors, scale and different spatial conditions—and allow those qualities to become part of how the works are experienced.”.

Simone Crestani’s Forsythia (2026), on show with Lebanese art and design gallery PIK’D at Nomad Abu Dhabi Courtesy PIK’D and NOMAD Abu Dhabi 2026.

According to recent reports, this year, the fair is expanding that mission with ambitious site-specific takeovers of four of the airport’s private terminals by Nilufar gallery, Gallery Fumi, Galerie Gastou and the jewellery advisory firm A2Z. There are 50 exhibitors taking part this year (compared with 40 last year) including local returning participants such as Leila Heller Gallery and the A/P Room as well as international spaces like Paris-based Galerie BSL, Milan’s Galleria Rossana Orlandi and Carpenters Workshop Gallery from London.

Highlights at the fair will include Maison Intègre’s bronze objects made using the ancient technique of lost wax, cast from recycled metal at its foundry in Burkina Faso; Seoul-based gallery Vein’s pairing of contemporary Korean practices with traditions including ottchil lacquer and mother-of-pearl inlay; and Polish design from Craftica Gallery.

Bellavance‑Lecompte states that jewellery will also be in the spotlight—as well as the 450 sq. m exhibition by A2Z, there will be presentations from the designers Studio Renn, Mattar jewellers and the gallery and advisory Ars Belga/Matthu-Boghossian. The Belgian jewellers Levuma will collaborate with the London gallery JCRD Design to bring together fine jewellery, diamonds and Brazilian design.

Another key development for Nomad this year is its expanded roster of institutions and non-profit initiatives on show in the old airport’s departure hall. Joining Irthi Contemporary Crafts Council—a Sharjah-based organisation that works with female artisans from the UAE and the wider Middle East, North Africa, South and Southeast Asia regions—which returns for this edition, is the recently established Design Commission Abu Dhabi and a collaborative presentation from the Institut du Monde Arabe (IMA) in Paris and House of Artisans, a cultural centre in Abu Dhabi that preserves traditional Emirati crafts. The project will bring together the French Sudanese fashion designer Abdel El Tayeb, who won the Confirmed Talent category of IMA’s 2024 Design Prize, and Emirati artisans to create a site-specific installation. “[This project] speaks to an idea at the heart of this edition: craft is a living practice, and something new can emerge when makers from different places work together,” Bellavance‑Lecompte says.

For Nomad’s inaugural Abu Dhabi edition, galleries reported sales exceeding $20m and many are “returning this year with more ambitious projects”, Bellavance‑Lecompte claims. He expects that Abu Dhabi’s expanding cultural calendar and soon-to-open Guggenheim museum will bring more international collectors, curators and attention to the city and to Nomad. “Last year showed us that there is serious interest in collectable design, and this year we can build on those relationships,” he says.

• Nomad Abu Dhabi, Old Abu Dhabi Airport, 18-22 November.

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Sources indicate that so what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions? Is there really any noticeable difference between carets, chevrons, arrows, and triangles?

Recent findings suggest that well, research shows that there is some difference indeed. But what’s more interesting is that split menus are harmful, why it’s better to not have icons and text labels link to different actions, and why the caret is the safest icon choice. Let’s dive in!

In a recent development, the findings aren’t very surprising: without any icon in use, owners expect that tapping on the menu item would take them directly to a new page. Users often struggle with custom icons as they don’t clearly signal that they’ll open an accordion. And people tend to tap fairly equally on the icon and on the label for most icons.

Many designs (like the one below) tend to slightly overcomplicate things by adding arrows and carets pointing everywhere, depending on the state of the accordion. But typically we don’t need to use an arrow to indicate a link to the category.

The rule of thumb is very simple: if it’s a link, the easiest and most effective way is to simply underline it — without any arrow, caret, or other icon. Perhaps it’s not particularly exciting, but it works flawlessly every single time.

Using a right-facing arrow icon ▶ isn’t associated with an expectation of going directly to a new page. And having the same icon pointing down ▼ doesn’t necessarily imply that an accordion is going to open on tap/click.

In a recent development, it’s a good idea to avoid split buttons for accordions — where the text label links directly to a page, but the icon opens the accordion. Instead, it’s much more reliable to allow users to tap on a main category and expose the menu; and to access the category page, we add a link to it inside the menu.

For accordions, we typically use +/− or arrows ↓/↑ to signal expanded and collapsed states, and typically it works well. However, both have many different interpretations. Plus + can mean anything from saving for later to adding to cart to zooming in, and can be particularly confusing for multi-level navigation, with many levels open at the same time.

Arrows ↓/↑ can mean scrolling or sliding or finding the next match, but also a jump to a particular portion of a page. Both plus and arrows are well-understood and work, but depending on the design, can be confusing — mostly because they are overloaded.

Industry observers note that the safe choice is to use the caret/triangle pointing down ▼ by default, and change it to a caret pointing up or a caret pointing sideways ▶ on interaction. If you need an alternative, then +/- typically work well, too.

But we certainly don’t need any further icons or arrows to indicate where the links go. The same goes for split menus, which often produce more mistakes than help. Instead, we have one button or dropdown that does exactly one thing — reveals all options and allows users to drill down.

According to recent reports, and if you need a direct link, we link the title directly to the page and underline it. More often than not, simpler is better.

Latest Update: BOND Unveils Aleph Farms Brand Identity

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (450 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BOND builds the Aleph Farms brand identity from a single flipped letter for cultivated meat: the ancient aleph, turned over, becomes an ox.
  • Recent findings suggest that BOND calls it turning steak on its head.
  • Aleph Farms reads in a sturdy grotesque, white on a deep green field, with the flipped letter tucked into a circle as the mark, the ox reappearing as a small geometric head.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BOND builds the Aleph Farms brand identity from a single flipped letter for cultivated meat: the ancient aleph, turned over, becomes an ox.

Recent findings suggest that BOND calls it turning steak on its head. Cultivated meat is one of the most significant developments in food production in generations, and the studio treats it as a story about continuity, not the future. Aleph Farms grows meat directly from animal cells, without raising or slaughtering animals, and BOND was asked to build both the parent brand and its first consumer product brand, Aleph Cuts. The name comes from the first letter of one of humanity's oldest writing systems, first drawn as the pictogram of an ox, and the identity took Gold at the European Design Awards in 2024.

The wordmark does the talking. Aleph Farms reads in a sturdy grotesque, white on a deep green field, with the flipped letter tucked into a circle as the mark, the ox reappearing as a small geometric head. Aleph Cuts gets a different voice entirely: soft, rounded, almost liquid letterforms in dark green on coral, the same ox mark sitting beside it. The parent brand is the steady statement, the product brand is the appetite.

The flip is the organising principle of the whole system. BOND runs it through typography, motion, imagery, and communication, so every panel reads as one argument. The palette stays tight: deep green, coral, and pale blue against off-white, with the ox mark repeating at every scale, from card to plate. The parent brand and the product brand keep distinct roles while sharing the same idea and visual language.

Recent findings suggest that the material language is quiet and tactile. Business cards carry the mark blind debossed into dark green and white stock, the circle and the ox pressed into the paper rather than printed on it. The same mark is pressed into the center of a plate, a small stamped seal in the middle of an empty dish, waiting for the food. Nothing shouts. The identity holds its nerve and lets the mark do the work.

In a recent development, julia Stotz photographs the food the way the brand thinks. A skewer comes off a smoking grill against a dark green backdrop, sliced steak stacks on a white plate with mushrooms and peppers, and the meat stays the subject, never a prop. The photography keeps the palette of the system, green backdrops, pale cloth, so the product shots sit inside the identity, not next to it. The result is a brand for something that never existed before that still looks like it has always been at the table.

See more from BOND on their site.
