AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?

📅 2026-11-17 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • According to recent reports, this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms. Andrew leads the … More about Andrew ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

It has been revealed that lately, I’ve been thinking and writing a lot about what AI is doing to product development, and what that means for accessibility. The thing that has my wheels turning is a finding from Level Access’s 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. Basically: AI is helping us hit fast-forward on the build, but testing practices haven’t kept up.

In a recent development, we asked more than 2,500 professionals where they noticed AI was speeding up their work in the SDLC. Most said they noticed gains in planning (58%), design (61%), and development (51%). But QA and testing lagged behind: Only 30% said AI had sped up that stage.

These results point to a two-speed workflow. AI has turbocharged design, planning, and development, while checking and validation are still running at a very different pace. This means a lot of teams are likely racing through the build, then being forced to hit the brakes the moment someone has to answer a pretty fundamental question: Is this thing actually accessible?

Accessibility has historically been treated as a QA bottleneck, and AI is pushing far more work into it, faster. If your team has already shifted left on accessibility, you’re off to a good start. But AI has reshuffled the workflow, so even proactive teams need to work out where those early checks belong now.

Recent findings suggest that this matters because right now, the web is moving in the wrong direction. WebAIM’s latest scan of the top million home pages found that automatically detected errors per home page rose 10.1% in a year, from 51 to 56.1 per page. WebAIM cited AI-assisted coding as one possible contributing factor.

So how do we get validation out of first gear? How do we build human judgment into the workflow as AI keeps pushing the pace?

We looked at the organizations that are improving across every accessibility metric they track (a group we call the “improvers”) to find out what they’re doing differently.

Here’s what stood out: AI adoption made the smallest difference of anything we measured. Improvers use AI at a similar rate to everyone else we surveyed. Their edge highlights up in the maturity of their surrounding accessibility practices — things like training, communication, and a culture of accessibility.

Industry observers note that A quick caveat: This is survey data, so it only highlights correlation, and mature programs may simply be better at tracking and reporting their wins. Even so, this finding was hard to ignore.

And it got even more interesting. Professionals in mature accessibility programs were nearly six times as likely to say AI helps them prioritize complications. They were also nearly three times as likely to say it helps them tackle accessibility more proactively in development.

In other words, AI works best as an amplifier of a strong program. With context, testing, environments, and guardrails in place, agents can take on a large share of the work from drafting through to operations, and much of the time lost to waiting and handoffs goes away. People stay responsible for deciding what to build and for approving what ships.

So let me ask you: When it comes to accessibility, where does human judgment sit in your workflow today?

Not sure? Here’s a quick way to find out.

Sources indicate that pick a feature you shipped recently and trace it from the first Figma frame to production. Mark every moment a person decided whether it would work for someone using a keyboard, a screen reader, or their browser at 400% zoom.

How many marks did you get? If most of them cluster at the end of creation, you’re likely heading to one of two places: You’ll either ship accessibility barriers or spend the time you saved upstream fixing them later, when they’re harder and costlier to fix.

Here’s how to avoid both outcomes by building the right accessibility checks and judgment calls into the work your team is already doing.

Recent findings suggest that as AI takes on more work, people need to stay involved at three points: finding problems, fixing them, and documenting the evidence. Each one plugs into a step your team already takes, like a handoff, a pull request, or a review, so nothing latest gets added to the timeline, and accessibility keeps pace with the work that’s in motion.

Recent findings suggest that context fades fast. Put the first judgment checkpoints as close to the creation work as you can:.

Industry observers note that found the matter? Great. Fix it while it’s fresh. When complications end up as tickets, make sure the context travels with them. They should carry the element, the repro, the related WCAG criterion, a suggested fix, and the PR link, so context doesn’t leak.

The worst time to start gathering evidence is when somebody’s asking for it.

Every check, fix, and judgment call throughout the process described above should ideally leave a trail. A fix isn’t done until something fails if the glitch comes back. Ask your AI assistant to write the regression test with the fix and put the finding link and any judgment call in the PR description. That’s the receipt.

Sources indicate that A passing test shows a known issue hasn’t returned. It doesn’t show the experience works. For what automation can’t cover, add a short note to the PR: what you tested, with which assistive technology, and any judgment calls you made.

AI has given digital creation a speed boost, but broadly speaking, validating the work hasn’t kept pace. Closing that gap isn’t about adopting more AI in more places or abandoning the toolset that helped make your team faster.

According to our data, the opportunity in front of teams is to build the practice around that toolset, so that human judgment is flagged, embedded, and acted on earlier, and more often.

We’ve only scratched the surface of what our data tells us about AI and accessibility. If you’re curious about what else we found, check out the 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. There’s plenty more to unpack.

Manuscript filled with 16th-century apocalyptic visions could fetch £1 million at auction

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Giant comets blaze across dark skies, volcanoes rain down fire on hapless cities, floods rage and the moon turns blood red in a spectacular 16th-century manuscript coming up for auction at Christie’s in London, estimated between £700,000 and £1m.
  • The Book of Miracles, with 167 vivid watercolours illustrating natural phenomena—real and imagined—and scenes from the Old and New Testaments, was completed in Augsburg, Germany, around 1552.
  • Industry observers note that A page from the The Book of Miracles (around 1552) CHRISTIE'S IMAGES LTD.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Giant comets blaze across dark skies, volcanoes rain down fire on hapless cities, floods rage and the moon turns blood red in a spectacular 16th-century manuscript coming up for auction at Christie’s in London, estimated between £700,000 and £1m.

The Book of Miracles, with 167 vivid watercolours illustrating natural phenomena—real and imagined—and scenes from the Old and New Testaments, was completed in Augsburg, Germany, around 1552. It is attributed to Hans Burgkmair the Younger and Heinrich Vogtherr the Younger, painters, print makers and designers who had separate workshops but sometimes collaborated on notable commissions.

Industry observers note that A page from the The Book of Miracles (around 1552) CHRISTIE'S IMAGES LTD. 2026.

In a recent development, eugenio Donadoni, the director and international specialist in Medieval and Renaissance manuscripts at Christie’s, called the book an exquisite work, with its illustrations as vibrant after nearly 500 years as the day they were made. “Beyond their extraordinary beauty, these images offer us a glimpse into how people in the 16th century made sense of a world that could often seem mysterious and unpredictable. Today, we might understand a comet, an eclipse or an earthquake through science, but in the Renaissance these phenomena could be interpreted as signs of something greater, even as warnings of what was to come,” he says. “The manuscript brings together the remarkable visual imagination of the period, the events that captured people's attention and provoked their wonder and fear. Nearly 500 years later, these images remain as compelling as ever.”.

A page from the The Book of Miracles (around 1552) CHRISTIE'S IMAGES LTD. 2026.

The book is included in a series of sales of works from the Mickey Cartin collection. Cartin, who is based in Connecticut and built the electrical supply firm founded by his grandfather into a national company, began collecting in the 1980s across many categories, including books and manuscripts, old master paintings, furniture and contemporary art. Artnews included in him in its Top 200 Collectors list every year from 2007-13. He bought The Book of Miracles in 2010, three years after it was rediscovered in a private collection in Bavaria, and it acquired wider fame when the art publisher Taschen published a facsimile edition in 2013.

The manuscript, part of the sale An Alchemy of Ideas: Works from the Mickey Cartin Collection, will be on public view at Christie’s King Street sales room in London on 4-10 December, before the sale on 10 December.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Barkas builds the Kuda brand identity on More Life: a stacked wordmark, custom Kuda Modena type, and a deep Lagos purple.
  • The system starts from a sentence, not a logo.
  • It has been revealed that the type does the heavy lifting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Barkas builds the Kuda brand identity on More Life: a stacked wordmark, custom Kuda Modena type, and a deep Lagos purple.

The system starts from a sentence, not a logo. "If your bank isn't helping you live more, it's holding you back," Barkas writes, and the identity answers with the pulse of Lagos: a stacked KUDA wordmark in thick geometric capitals, deep purple owning every surface it touches, black as its sharper counterweight. Kuda began as "the bank of the free," challenging the friction and fees of traditional Nigerian banking, and the latest work keeps that challenger spirit, aimed at a generation that wants its money to fund a life rather than sit in an account.

It has been revealed that the type does the heavy lifting. Kuda Modena, a custom face drawn by Erkin Karamemet, sets the name at poster scale in heavy geometric capitals for the wordmark and the More Life lockups, with Suisse International alongside for support. The specimen demonstrates the full alphabet in lilac on deep purple, with the custom Naira sign sitting among the euro, dollar, pound, and yen, a small detail that roots the whole system in Nigerian money.

It has been revealed that the grid is the app itself. The home screen sorts everything into three plain groups, Essentials, Cardless Payments, and Lifestyle, each icon labeled in the same weight. The wordmark stacks KU over DA like a stamp, and the studio built four versions of the lockup so the mark stays legible from a billboard down to a card chip. Posters hold the same discipline: one line, one color field, the name at the foot.

It has been revealed that purple is the material here. Deep purple fields carry the type, the app, and the card, with lilac doing the bright work and black stepping in wherever the brand needs to sound serious, which is how Kuda Business reads against the personal product. Hand-drawn illustrations soften the geometry: a Lagos street scene in colored pencil, a woman in a pink robe on the SPEND card, loose doodles of everyday moments. Documentary photography from local photographers keeps the people real and unfiltered.

It has been revealed that the system stretches across every surface the bank touches. Three phone screens show the balance, the lilac card, and a PIN pad in one calm row. A billboard puts the stacked wordmark over a woman waving from a car window with the line "Less friction. More life." The stocks screen tracks a holding in dollars on the same purple field. Nothing in the system looks like a bank trying to look expensive; everything looks like a bank trying to keep up with Lagos.

See more from Barkas on their site.

#22352. Industry News: Has the couple in Jan van Eyck’s ‘Arnolfini Portrait’ been misidentified?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (995 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Has the couple in Jan van Eyck’s ‘Arnolfini Portrait’ been misidentified?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434) has been a signature work in London’s National Gallery since it arrived at the museum in 1842.
  • Now, on the occasion of the National Gallery’s exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits (21 November-11 April 2027), which brings together all nine of the artist’s surviving panel portraits, the Berlin-based curator Stephan Kemperdick, writing in a catalogue essay, has planted a possible bombshell by suggesting that the man in the Arnolfini Portrait is Van Eyck himself, and that the woman standing next to him is the artist’s wife Margaret, the sitter in another Van Eyck portrait from 1439, which is on loan to the show from Bruges.
  • Kemperdick’s theory, presented in recent talks but published now for the first time, is not an entirely upcoming one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434) has been a signature work in London’s National Gallery since it arrived at the museum in 1842. A few key facts about the dual portrait, showing a youngish man and his idealised wife, could be gleaned just by looking at the work’s prominent Latin inscription, which translates as “Jan van Eyck was here 1434”. Over the years, just about everything else associated with the painting, from its mysterious room to the obscure occasion, has been open to debate, other than the surname of the man—Arnolfini, connected to an extended family of wealthy merchants from Lucca active in 15th-century Bruges, where Van Eyck had his studio.

Now, on the occasion of the National Gallery’s exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits (21 November-11 April 2027), which brings together all nine of the artist’s surviving panel portraits, the Berlin-based curator Stephan Kemperdick, writing in a catalogue essay, has planted a possible bombshell by suggesting that the man in the Arnolfini Portrait is Van Eyck himself, and that the woman standing next to him is the artist’s wife Margaret, the sitter in another Van Eyck portrait from 1439, which is on loan to the show from Bruges.

Kemperdick’s theory, presented in recent talks but published now for the first time, is not an entirely upcoming one. In the late 1840s, the National Gallery’s future first director Charles Eastlake contended that the artist’s inscription, which he thought could be translated as “Jan van Eyck was this [one]”, meant that the painting was also a dual portrait of the artist and his wife. But in the early 1860s, the British art historian W. H. James Weale interpreted a reference in a 16th-century inventory to a certain “hernoul le fin” in the painting, which he regarded as the French version of the Italian surname Arnolfini. The connection between the couple and that family was thus set in stone, though scholars disagree, often vehemently, about which particular member of the Arnolfini clan is shown.

Kemperdick has revisited the inscription, which is unusually large and conspicuously places the artist’s name next to the male figure’s head. He argues this indicates a direct connection between Van Eyck and the man. He has also reconsidered the association between the “hernoul le fin” reference and the surname Arnolfini. Citing the early-modern categorisation of the late-medieval work as not a portrait at all, but rather a lewd genre painting, Kemperdick suggests that “hernoul le fin” is not the correct surname of the sitter, but a subsequent and mocking moniker used by later generations to misidentify the man as a “a deceived cheat”. Kemperdick also suggests that a reference to St Margaret in the bedstead statue near the woman’s head serves to identify her as Van Eyck’s wife.

In a recent development, kemperdick is the curator of German, Netherlandish and French Paintings before 1600 at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie, which is noted for its Early Netherlandish holdings and has in its own collection a Van Eyck portrait (around 1435-38) of the very same man who appears in the National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait. The two will be shown together in the London exhibition.

Nicholas Flory, the co-curator of Van Eyck: The Portraits along with Emma Capron, the National Gallery’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting, says that he and Capron find Kemperdick’s theory “interesting” but “speculative”, citing, among other reasons, that the woman in the Bruges portrait, whom we know to be Margaret based on the inscription, has greyish-blue eyes while the woman in the Arnolfini Portrait has brown eyes.

Other leading Van Eyck scholars also have their doubts. The German art historian Till-Holger Borchert—now the director of the Suermondt-Ludwig-Museum in Aachen and the former director of Musea Brugge in Bruges—is familiar with Kemperdick’s theory. “I’m not entirely sure I can concur,” he notes. He thinks the early-16th-century inventory reference—associated with the painting’s owner at the time, Margaret of Austria, the governor of the Habsburg Netherlands—is a near iron-clad reference to the Arnolfinis. The Ghent University art historian Maximiliaan Martens, who has been involved in the lengthy restoration of Van Eyck’s Ghent Altarpiece, also “doesn’t see any reason to doubt” that the inventory reference is to the Arnolfinis.

According to recent reports, the implications of Kemperdick’s theory are far-reaching. Another Van Eyck portrait at the National Gallery, from 1433, showing a much older man than the figure in the Arnolfini Portrait, is now tentatively identified by the London museum as a self-portrait. This, however, cannot be the case if Kemperdick’s theory is correct.

According to recent reports, the exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits will label the Berlin work with its previous and longstanding reference to the Arnolfinis, while the Gemäldegalerie, under Kemperick’s guidance, has recently renamed it Portrait of a Man with a Red Chaperon. And the debate about the couple promises to continue long after the show closes in April.

“I have thought for 30 years about this,” Martens claims of the figures in the Arnolfini Portrait. He says he is still not sure if the man is Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini (who was apparently not married at the time the painting was made) or his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini (whose wife had died before the painting was made).

Other aspects of the dual portrait that scholars continue to debate include whether the heavy-bellied woman is actually pregnant (Kemperdick and Martens think that may be possible, while Flory and Capron think she is just gathering up her heavy skirts), and whether the room itself is a real space or an imagined one (imagined, say Flory and Capron; real, notes Martens).

Beyond who made it and when, the Arnolfini Portrait remains a mystery, which is in keeping for an artist whose date and place of birth, among other foundational knowledge, is also speculation. Asked to comment on the enigma associated with the Arnolfini Portrait, Borchert says: “Can you tell me anything about Van Eyck that isn’t enigmatic?”.

#22351. British Airways Avios — Short Nonstop Domestic Flights

British Airways Avios — Short Nonstop Domestic Flights

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2484 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • Picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes.
  • The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from Latest York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

Most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA.

Here's the critical nuance that trips up fresh users: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

Industry observers note that avios are one of the most accessible award currencies in the ecosystem. You can transfer from four major transferable points programs at a 1:1 ratio:.

Sources indicate that marriott Bonvoy also transfers to Avios at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Avios), and Marriott throws in a 5,000 Avios bonus for every 60,000 Marriott points transferred. That's a less efficient path for this redemption, but worth knowing.

The 355-day booking window means you can transfer and book nearly a full year in advance — critical for holiday travel or high-demand routes.

Recent findings suggest that british Airways allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. That means you could theoretically fly into one city and out of a nearby city without paying for two separate awards — useful if you're exploring a region and want flexibility. For short domestic hops, this opens up creative itinerary options that pure point-to-point programs don't allow.

Before you touch your Avios balance, go to aa.com and run a standard flight search for your route. When the results load, look specifically for flights labeled 'Web Special' or filter by lowest MileSAAver awards. You're searching for American's own award inventory — the same inventory British Airways can see and book. If AA highlights saver-level availability (the lowest award tier), British Airways will almost certainly be able to book it too.

Sources indicate that this step saves you frustration. Don't transfer points until you've confirmed the flight you want is bookable at the saver level.

Double-check that your route qualifies for the 7,500 Avios tier by confirming it's under 650 miles. NYC to Boston is about 187 miles. LAX to SFO is about 337 miles. Both qualify easily. A quick Google search — '[City A] to [City B] flight distance miles' — gives you the straight-line distance. When in doubt, routes you'd describe as 'short regional hops' within the same metro corridor will almost always qualify.

Show of every Jan van Eyck portrait reveals many new sides to his works

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that but we stand to know a lot more about him this month, when London’s National Gallery brings together all nine of his surviving panel portraits along with his lone surviving drawing, also a portrait.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there is a lot we do not know for certain about Jan van Eyck, including where and when he was born. What we do know is that his career—from the early 1420s until his death in 1441—helped launch the Early Netherlandish school, influencing the use of oil paint far beyond his native Low Countries and instilling a new and arguably everlasting value of verisimilitude in Western art.

Sources indicate that but we stand to know a lot more about him this month, when London’s National Gallery brings together all nine of his surviving panel portraits along with his lone surviving drawing, also a portrait. The bijoux blockbuster show will give scholars a unique opportunity to compare scattered works of singular importance. Van Eyck: The Portraits—with a checklist that expands all the way to 13 through the addition of three works on paper by his followers—is built around some remarkable pairings.

Fresh from a conservation treatment completed in 2024, the National Gallery’s own Portrait of a Man (Self-Portrait?) (1433) will meet up with Portrait of Margaret van Eyck (1439), the artist’s wife, on loan from Bruges, where Van Eyck had his workshop when he was the court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.

The National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434), Van Eyck’s enigmatic view of an elegantly dressed couple in an impressive reception room, will be shown for the first time with its related work from the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin clearly showing the same man, Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) (around 1435-38).

Recent findings suggest that vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum is loaning Portrait of an Elderly Man (A Scholar?) (around 1438). It will be shown with the preparatory drawing from Dresden, in goldpoint and silverpoint on prepared paper, with its revealing notes on how to colour the painting itself.

Van Eyck’s devotional portraits, such as those in his groundbreaking Ghent Altarpiece and the Musée du Louvre’s recently treated Madonna of Chancellor Rolin (around 1435), are outside the scope of the National Gallery exhibition.

Recent findings suggest that some of the portraits have reverse imagery of fictive marble, and the museum is placing them in cases so visitors can view both sides. “We’re really excited to be able to show people how amazing the reverse is,” notes Nicholas Flory, who is curating the show along with Emma Capron, the museum’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting. Flory says the elaborate reverses suggest that “these objects were not designed for a single kind of specific space or to be flat against the wall”, but rather “to be interacted with”.

Newness abounds in the show. The Arnolfini Portrait had long had an ornate Gothic Revival frame until it was replaced in 2024 by a 15th-century gilded frame. Meanwhile, the Berlin work, showing its male figure in distinctive red chaperon headgear, completed a conservation treatment in 2023 that removed distorting yellow varnish. The result of that treatment, states Stephan Kemperdick, the curator of Netherlandish paintings before 1600 at the Gemäldegalerie, has been to “make the palette cooler”. Before, he says, the chaperon was “fire-engine red”, and the man’s face looked “suntanned”, whereas now, he says, the face is “pinkish or whiteish—a feature that distinguished people from the better classes in the 15th century”.

The London exhibition, which Kemperdick calls a “once-in-a-lifetime” event, is a culmination of sorts. Several Van Eyck works, including the Ghent Altarpiece, have undergone recent treatments, which Flory claims has been “an impetus in Van Eyck scholarship”, and the National Gallery show reflects new research into Van Eyck’s technique, his original frames and inscriptions. Recent analysis of the National Gallery’s self-portrait, examined during its recent treatment, revealed how Van Eyck modulated the blueness of the background in the lower-right corner to “throw the sitter’s shoulder forward”, Flory says, creating a 3D effect.

Recent findings suggest that just out of view of the show itself, lurking in Kemperdick’s catalogue essay, is a possible bombshell: that the couple shown in the Arnolfini Portrait are not the titular Italian merchant and his wife at all, but rather Van Eyck and his wife. This would also mean that the Gemäldegalerie’s Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) is also a self-portrait.

Sources indicate that the Arnolfini Portrait is among the gallery’s most popular works, and the minuscule size of the show is in marked contrast with the likely museumgoer interest. However, Flory states the diminutive roster is, in fact, the big attraction.

According to recent reports, “There was the possibility to expand it beyond Van Eyck and show his work in the context of his contemporaries,” Flory says. “But because he is such a monumental figure in the history of Western painting, and his portraits are so special, we really wanted to focus the exhibition on just Van Eyck himself.” Luckily, he adds, the remarkable loans, which have involved several museums sending some of their most precious works, mean “we got everything we were hoping for”.

• Jan van Eyck: The Portraits, National Gallery, London, 21 November-11 April 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cosina has confirmed the Voigtländer Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Aspherical lens for full-frame Sony and Nikon mirrorless cameras.

Slated to launch next month, the Voigtländer Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Aspherical is a newly introduced and improved version of Cosina’s Voigtländer VM-mount 35mm f/1.2 lens, which the manufacturer notes is prized for its “excellent performance and compact design.” The new version has been optimized for mirrorless cameras while maintaining the image quality and silky-smooth bokeh of its VM-mount inspiration.

Sources indicate that as is often the case with Voigtländer lenses, the E-mount and Z-mount versions sport slightly different designs but have the same internal components and optical formula. The E-mount lens has a relatively smooth barrel shape with diamond-knurled focus and aperture control rings. The Z-mount lens, on the other hand, has a scalloped focus ring with vertical ridges and simple ridges on its aperture ring. It also trades red accents for yellow ones, embracing Nikon’s classic color scheme.

Industry observers note that in both cases, the lens is compact. The E-mount lens is just over 60 millimeters (2.37 inches) long and weighs 380 grams (13.4 ounces). The Z-mount lens is 62.4 millimeters (2.46 inches) long and weighs 390 grams (13.8 ounces). Both versions accept 58mm filters.

Recent findings suggest that both manual-focus lenses can focus as close as 0.3 meters (0.98 feet), which results in a maximum magnification ratio of just 1:5.8. Macro lenses these are not. Cosina says that the manual focusing experience is top-notch thanks to a precise, full-metal helicoid unit and high-quality grease. The firm promises “appropriate torque.”.

Optically, the lens features nine elements arranged across seven groups in front of a 12-bladed aperture diaphragm. There are two aspherical elements, and Cosina promises high-resolution performance across the entire frame, even wide open at f/1.2. The company adds that “color shifts are well controlled,” meaning that the lens minimizes chromatic aberrations.

As for bokeh, a key selling point for an f/1.2 lens like this, Cosina claims that out-of-focus areas are “drawn naturally and point light sources, etc., are drawn as soft round bokeh rather than as polygonal shapes.” The aperture ring can also be de-clicked, which should bode well for video applications.

Industry observers note that the Cosina Voigtländer Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Aspherical lens will begin shipping next month. While global pricing has not yet been revealed, Asobinet notes that the Japanese price is 140,000 yen, which is around $880. Final global pricing may vary, of course. It is worth noting that the Nokton 35mm f/1.2 Aspherical IV for Leica M-mount is $999 right now thanks to a $150 holiday discount. There’s no word yet on a Canon RF-mount version, although Cosina does make a handful of Voigtländer lenses for Canon mirrorless cameras.

#22339. How to Film and Edit a High Energy Event Sizzle Reel

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1328 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

How to Film and Edit a High Energy Event Sizzle Reel

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1328 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that earlier this fall, I wound up at a music festival in Southern California called Same Same But Different.
  • Recent findings suggest that I used to regularly film festival sizzle reels and promos over a decade ago, and while I don’t do it much anymore, I still have the muscle memory to capture some good content.
  • It has been revealed that first, you have to actually get to the festival.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that earlier this fall, I wound up at a music festival in Southern California called Same Same But Different. I was there helping film a documentary with a friend and decided to actually document my whole process.

Recent findings suggest that I used to regularly film festival sizzle reels and promos over a decade ago, and while I don’t do it much anymore, I still have the muscle memory to capture some good content. Here’s a crash course on how I used to put together these festival sizzles and recap videos.

It has been revealed that first, you have to actually get to the festival. I’ve been to enough of these in the past that I know how to pack light, and thanks to Tucker, The Festival Guy, I had some extra backstage credentials. That mentioned, don’t put too much weight on that. Credentials don’t change how you film a festival; they get you a few extra cool angles, but most of what you’ll see here was captured from the GA section, since that’s where the real audience experience lies.

According to recent reports, because you’re capturing something so unpredictable, there are moments happening everywhere, so the first key thing is to always keep a lookout. Scan around you and find people dancing, action moments, anything that captivates and grabs your interest. The second thing I do for these high-energy reels is look for ways to match movement across the camera. If I pan left, I’ll pan left again into the next scene. If I tilt up on one shot, maybe I tilt down out of the next. I’m always editing in my head, picturing how these pieces will fit together.

It has been revealed that the last thing, and maybe the coolest part of festivals like this, is how much color and geometry surround you. I look for ways to build themes out of that. If there’s an umbrella spinning, I’ll find that shape and match it to another sphere or circle somewhere else. Match cuts are a huge part of this, and they add a lot of dynamic energy.

Recent findings suggest that it’s key to note something here about appearance and consent. These festivals often tend to have a very friendly, open, and vibrant crowd, and most people are actually excited to appear in front of the camera and show off their outfits and their moves. Almost all festivals now have a waiver along with your ticket binding the festivalgoer to consent to be filmed, so they can use it for their own sizzle reels. Having said that, you should always approach people with respect, and if you’re unable to ask for consent due to high volume or energy, always visually check in with your subject—if they appear to be uncomfortable, put a hand up, or turn away, then pivot your camera away, give a sign of apology, and don’t use that clip in your edit—always be kind, polite, and respectful.

Sources indicate that before I even touch the edit, I always like having music in the back of my mind, a playlist or a selection of some kind, because a piece like this is driven by the track. I pulled up Audiio, our partners, to find it. For this one, I wanted something upbeat. It was an electronic music festival, so I narrowed the genre to electronic, then the mood to energetic. Instrumental only is a good call here so vocals don’t step on the footage or change the tone.

According to recent reports, the way I listen is to click through very fast because I know within the first second or two whether the tone, style, rhythm, and pacing will work. I also tend to click into the sections with transitions to find out how the song’s energy moves and develops. There’s a ton to run through, so moving rapidly is how I get through it, and I already know the flavor I’m after.

Industry observers note that with the song picked, I drop it into the timeline. For the purpose of this sizzle, I trimmed it down to about a minute, landing on that first transition or breakdown before the second part of the song kicks in, which makes for a clean cut. A trick that helps me work faster: I find the different sections of the song and make cuts on the track itself. That helps me remember where each section starts and ends, and snapping to those cuts helps with timing. You can use markers or whatever tools your NLE offers; I like cuts because I can snap to them quickly.

Next are the selects. I run through each shot, set the in and out points, and look for what I was filming for: the transitions and the movements. I’d hold on a shot, whip pan out of it, find another, and whip pan into it, so I want to retain those moments and not trim into them. Then I categorize everything, which keeps me working fast. In this case, I’m using clip color as it’s swiftly recognizable. One category is crowd shots: attendees dancing and looking at the camera. Another is transitional elements. Beyond the whip pans and tilts, I was hunting for spherical elements while filming, and I caught a lot of them on the day: parasols, flow toys spinning in circles, staffs people were twirling. Those made great transitions, and it turned filming into a fun challenge, always looking for the next spherical thing to match cut.

Industry observers note that I also separated general B-roll, a walk-through category showing the different sections of the festival and its interactive experiences, a category just for flow toys and tools (poi, fire staff, hoops), stage elements, and stage close-ups. With everything categorized and color-coded, I can drop things in quickly and track where each element is going.

I start from my song cuts, and I like to place the transitional elements first—the movements and match cuts with the spherical elements—right on those cuts. Then I use the space in between to fill in as I go. For the opening, I listen to how the song starts slow and ramps up fast, so I want the energy to match that gradual build and sudden explosion into the beat. These will shift around as I work, but they’re bookmarks that tell me which sections are filled. I also had it in mind to move the piece from daytime to nighttime as it progresses.

Sources indicate that I like working in these small chunks first, then dialing in the timing so it matches the music. Keeping the music at the forefront as the driving element of these pieces is absolutely key. We cut to the beat, or at least make sure the actions on camera land on the beat. When a fan flies up, I cut on that motion and rise through the next shot with an intentional tilt up into the stage. A rapid zoom or pull-out works too; in one spot, we start on a painting and pull out promptly, right on the rhythm. Another jumps into an abstract shot just as the beat drops, then cuts in on one of those built-in movements—a rapid tilt up matched to the stage lights and lasers.

Industry observers note that with everything in place, the edit is almost done. The last thing I do is go through and add motion transitions where they help enhance the movement I built in. If a zoom or a whip pan isn’t as pronounced as I want, a motion transition can amplify it, really driving a powerful zoom in and out of the next shot. I’ll add just a few, but otherwise the piece is in a good spot.

It has been revealed that check out the final video above, and I’ll make sure to post more stuff like this when the opportunity presents itself. Until next time!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The British Museum and the V&A signed a loan agreement in 2024 with Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, the 16th Asantehene (King of the Asante), to return the gold regalia to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, the historic capital of what was then the Asante (Ashanti) empire.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Asante regalia gold objects on loan from the British Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) will remain on show in Kumasi, Ghana until 2030 following the extension of loan agreements by the two UK museums. The British Museum has loaned 15 objects while the V&A lent 17 pieces, almost all of which were looted during military operations in the late 19th century.

The British Museum and the V&A signed a loan agreement in 2024 with Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, the 16th Asantehene (King of the Asante), to return the gold regalia to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, the historic capital of what was then the Asante (Ashanti) empire. The loans will be renewed for a further three years at the end of the current term in April 2027. The two UK museums are legally unable to deaccession so the objects are being returned as long-term loans.

According to recent reports, “The rollover of the loan agreement was always likely and from both the British Museum’s and Manhyia Palace Museum’s point of view, this has been a successful partnership with increased visitors, training and expansion at Manhyia. There is nonetheless enduring frustration from many in Ghana, both in Asante and beyond, that this is only a loan,” indicates Barnaby Phillips, author of The African Kingdom of Gold: Britain and the Asante Treasure.

The loan renewal announcement followed a recent visit to Kumasi by Nicholas Cullinan, the director of the British Museum, following an invitation by the Asantehene.

According to recent reports, the gold regalia associated with the Asante royal court is on display in the Manhyia Palace Museum's Homecoming exhibition. Items shown include a small gold ornament in the form of a lute-harp (sankuo), one of the cast gold objects presented in 1817 to British diplomat Thomas Bowdich during his trip to Kumasi.

“The British Museum has about 220 pieces of Asante gold regalia and the Manhyia Palace Museum has been involved in the selection of objects [for loan]. There has been considerable input regarding what goes back to Ghana,” adds Phillips.

The idea of a loans deal, first discussed in the 1970s, was revived when the Asantehene visited London in May 2023 to attend the coronation of King Charles III.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A large-scale camera trap survey has revealed that the rarely seen flat-headed cat, traditionally thought to be nocturnal, also roams during the day.

Sources indicate that the flat-headed cat (Prionailurus planiceps), named for its flattened forehead and elongated skull, is one of the world’s rarest and least-studied wild felines. It lives in fragmented habitats across Brunei, Indonesia, and Malaysia. For years, the species has been traditionally considered strictly nocturnal.

Recent findings suggest that however, a newly introduced study published in Ecology and Evolution has challenged that understanding. Researchers used camera traps to monitor the proposed Lundu Mangrove Protected Forest in southwestern Sarawak, Malaysia, over a nearly three-year period between August 2021 and May 2024.

Sources indicate that during the survey, the researchers recorded the flat-headed cat 59 times, revealing an unexpected pattern of activity. According to a report by Mongabay, the camera traps highlighted that the cats were active during both nighttime and daytime hours. Although activity peaked around midnight among flat-headed cats, it also extended into the late morning and afternoon.

In a recent development, the findings revealed “considerable daytime activity,” suggesting that the species’ activity patterns may be more flexible than previously believed. The cameras also recorded an adult female accompanied by a kitten, providing evidence of the species’ presence and possible reproductive activity in the study area.

“This was particularly encouraging because it provides evidence of the species’ presence alongside potential reproductive activity in the study area,” Ahmad Ampeng, the study’s lead author and a research officer at the Forest Department Sarawak, tells Mongabay.

Industry observers note that the flat-headed cat is classified as endangered on the IUCN Red List. The species was also once considered possibly extinct in Thailand, until camera traps documented its presence last year, marking its first confirmed appearance there in nearly three decades.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mother Design rebuilds the MLB brand identity on Modernize Nostalgia: five custom typefaces, the 1968 batter mark, and the shapes of the game.
  • Mother Design calls it Modernize Nostalgia: take the most iconic pieces of baseball's visual past, refresh them, and put them back to work for a new generation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mother Design rebuilds the MLB brand identity on Modernize Nostalgia: five custom typefaces, the 1968 batter mark, and the shapes of the game.

The idea is a sentence, not a logo. Mother Design calls it Modernize Nostalgia: take the most iconic pieces of baseball's visual past, refresh them, and put them back to work for a new generation. The league wanted its brand to match the changes on the field, new rules and a new platform, Baseball Is Something Else. Nothing here is thrown away. The 1968 silhouetted batter logo, drawn by Jerry Dior, stays exactly as it is, and the wordmark beside it is redrawn for the wider system.

Type carries the whole system. Mother Design built five custom faces with five type designers, each one pulled from baseball history. Nick Sherman redrew Franklin Gothic as MLB Franklin. David Jonathan Ross and Bethany Heck derived MLB Clarendon from the 1845 slab serif. OH no Type Co. cut MLB Script from the script styles stitched across team jerseys. Skye Dillon drew MLB Block, the octagonal face found on old ballparks and uniform numerals. Tipotype made MLB Flare from hand-lettering. One poster sets all five in a single sentence.

It has been revealed that the grid comes from the game itself. Mother Design drew a set of shapes from the field: the rounded rectangle of the MLB logo, the pentagon of home plate, the base lines, the circle of the ball, the field seen from above. Color runs in three registers, Core, Extended, and Expressive, built from blues, reds, and creams taken from past and present MLB logos, then charged with club colors. A brand matrix plots every sub-brand by how close it sits to gameplay and what fans expect, so a ticket app stays plain and a social channel gets to play.

According to recent reports, the material is the uniform. Play Ball runs in red script across navy jersey fabric, the letters sitting on the weave. The 1969 World Series ticket, red paper dense with prices, rules, and the centenary logo, indicates how much of this history was printed, stamped, and torn at the gate. The batter logo keeps its red and blue halves and its white silhouette on deep navy, unchanged since 1968.

Industry observers note that the system stretches across the whole league. One grid holds twenty sub-brand lockups, Opening Day, Rickwood Field, the Tokyo Series, Spring Training, the Home Run Derby, the Draft, each built from the same shapes and type. The work rolled out over a two-and-a-half-year partnership, with events like Rickwood Field and MLB Together developed alongside the league's own design team.

Backlash Over ‘Robots’ Taking Photos at Christmas Lights Event

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A video of Christmas lights being switched on in Central London has provoked a debate about people’s picture-taking habits and the importance of living in the moment.
  • Industry observers note that the video was shared by BBC London on November 4.
  • The comments were flooded with people disgusted that no one appeared to be taking in the moment, instead watching a real event that was unfolding right in front of them through the small screen of their phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A video of Christmas lights being switched on in Central London has provoked a debate about people’s picture-taking habits and the importance of living in the moment.

Industry observers note that the video was shared by BBC London on November 4. It reveals a sea of people, seemingly every single one of them with their phones aloft, filming in anticipation of the elaborate lights on Carnaby Street turning on and the fireworks that followed.

A post shared by BBC London (@bbclondon).

The comments were flooded with people disgusted that no one appeared to be taking in the moment, instead watching a real event that was unfolding right in front of them through the small screen of their phone.

“I’ve stopped filming most things like fireworks and concerts when I realized I haven’t watched a single one of them back,” indicates Sufian Ahmed. “It’s so much about being in the moment. Experiencing it with the person you’re next to. You lose all that when watching it through a narrow screen.”.

Many compared it to an episode of the Black Mirror TV show, while others called out the people for being “robots.” Others pointed out the hypocrisy of social media customers complaining about the video while watching it on their phone.

Previous studies have found that taking a photo of an event affects human memory. A 2018 psychological study suggested that shooting photos or videos gives people a false sense that they preserved a moment, when in actual fact it’s the camera that did it for them.

Recent findings suggest that in 2013, researchers asked one group of people to tour an art museum without taking photos, while another group was assigned to take photos. Those who took photos were significantly worse at identifying items in the museum and recalled fewer details about the items they did remember than those who didn’t take photos.

In a recent development, dr. Kaitlyn Regehr of University College London and the University of Toronto notes public attitudes toward smartphones and technology are shifting.

“This is not the first year that people have attended events and watched those events through screens,” the smartphone academic tells the BBC.

“But what’s significant is that this year there’s a lot of critical public discourse happening. And that, I think, is really, really positive.

Dr. Regehr says the backlash could be down to “our discomfort with the amount of influence that substantial tech is playing on our lives.”.

Fans of the show will most certainly recognize Chris’s phrase, “Okeh, let’s talk about bokeh,” from many of his lens reviews, and now you can wear those words on your chest in two designs! This drop also debuts a newly introduced color option: natural! All of the t-shirts in this drop are available in this new color option.

Both bokeh-themed designs are also available as white hoodies.

We also worked with the team at Harper Finch to create a series of camera team designs! Canon, Nikon, Sony, and Fujifilm are some of the most popular camera manufacturers, and now you can rep your favorite team: red, yellow, orange, and green! Chris likes to rock Team Orange, while Jordan and I rep Team Yellow and Team Green.

All of these designs are available in either white or natural t-shirt colors and as white hoodies.

According to recent reports, breaking from our last drop, some of these options will remain as permanent fixtures in our shop and all of them will be available through the holiday season. They make great gifts for the photographer in your life (or if you like to stuff your own stockings). Make sure to check the handy size chart, but Harper Finch also has a great 30-day return policy and support if something doesn’t fit.

We are really excited about this drop, and we hope you like what we’ve created. But that’s not all: keep a close eye on the store during Black Friday weekend! While the merch already reflects the most discounted price we’ll ever offer it for, we do have some surprises in store for November 27 through 29.

#22328. Tech Report: All the Award-Winning Photos From Nature Photographer of the Year 2026

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1870 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: All the Award-Winning Photos From Nature Photographer of the Year 2026

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Nature Photographer of the Year 2026 winners have been unveiled, showcasing the world’s best nature, wildlife, and landscape photography.
  • This year’s competition received 27,108 entries from photographers in nearly 100 countries, a record-breaking number for the longtime photo contest.
  • Finnish photographer Hannu Ahonen bested stiff competition to earn the title of Nature Photographer of the Year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nature Photographer of the Year 2026 winners have been unveiled, showcasing the world’s best nature, wildlife, and landscape photography.

This year’s competition received 27,108 entries from photographers in nearly 100 countries, a record-breaking number for the longtime photo contest.

Finnish photographer Hannu Ahonen bested stiff competition to earn the title of Nature Photographer of the Year. Ahonen’s award-winning photo, “The One that Left and the One that Stayed,” is an extraordinary image of a water lily leaf positioned alongside its icy duplicate.

Recent findings suggest that “It is not often that a photograph of a plant is crowned the overall winner of a major photography competition, but the jury could not overlook this fascinating image by Hannu Ahonen,” says jury chair Theo Bosboom. “First and foremost, the photograph captures a unique situation: a water lily leaf with an almost perfect black-and-white replica of it lying next to it in the water.”.

Ahonen’s winning photo tells a compelling and unusual story. The living water lily leaf is positioned on the left, while the ice that formed on top of it and slipped off sits delicately to the side, blown away slightly by the breeze. Even the veins from the leaf are visible in the icy shell.

In a recent development, nature Photographer of the Year adds that the photo reveals the “marvelous beauty of nature” while embodying its transient character. The sheet of ice will soon melt away, joining the water that keeps the lily alive in the first place. It’s a symbolic photo at a time when climate change is impacting all life on Earth, especially its ice.

Recent findings suggest that “The winter ice had arrived, but it remained snowless for a long time. Some of the pond’s lily pad leaves began to crumble on top of the ice. The wind carried a few of them away, revealing delicate, frosty ornaments left behind. I eagerly captured this natural phenomenon, something I had never witnessed before,” Ahonen explains.

Ahonen has an inspiring story. He has ADHD and lives in a wilderness home in Finland with no carbon footprint. Rarely venturing more than a couple of miles from his home, he spends much of his time behind the camera in his yard, using photography as a spiritual escape and creative outlet.

Alongside the overall winner, Ahonen, the competition’s jury also selected winners across nearly a dozen categories. There are also special prizes for youth photographers and an accomplished portfolio. Ahonen took the top spot in the Plants and Fungi category, so that category is not included below.

French photographer Lucas Mugnier-Lavorel won this year’s Birds category for his environmental portrait of a Magellanic woodpecker in Patagonia.

“Environmental portraits of wildlife can make us feel closer to the animals despite being farther away from them, when done right. This image of a Magellanic woodpecker in its gorgeous habitat was a perfect example. It stood out from thousands of submissions because of its understated sense of place, beauty, simplicity, and timing,” notes judge Steffen Foerster.

“Overall, it was a very successful reminder of how the portrayal of nature in its literal state can still be the most powerful of photographic expressions,” Foerster concludes.

British photographer Paul Goldstein’s foggy photo of a giraffe earned the top prize in the Mammals category.

“Quiet images can be easy to overlook in the fiercely competitive mammal category, one of the largest in NPOTY. This ethereal image of a giraffe peeking out of the mist revealed its strengths gradually. Initially a little disorienting, it offered just enough of a visual puzzle to keep the viewer engaged until the image resolved,” Foerster explains.

Judges tapped Marcus Kuan’s macro photo of a surprisingly rich and diverse little ecosystem alongside a pitcher plant in the Other Animals category. The Singaporean photographer impressed the panel with his composition and lighting.

“The lighting, colors, and unexpected gathering of species immediately caught our attention. Kuan beautifully captured a world where crustaceans, amphibians, and carnivorous plants cross paths,” explains jury member Louis Guillot.

“As judges, we were drawn to the possibilities unfolding within this single frame. Could the pitchers be digesting invertebrates? Might the frog be exploring a potential egg-laying site, while the crab continues its daily search for food among the plants?” Guillot continues.

Photographer J Fritz Rumpf from the United States won this year’s Landscape category with a silhouetted photo of Iguazú Falls in Argentina.

In a recent development, “What immediately caught our attention was the incredible light and atmosphere in this photo. The longer we looked, the more fascinating it became. There is so much to discover: the last light of day illuminating the mist rising from Iguazú Falls, the silhouettes of trees and rocks, the birds circling above, the sunlight streaming through an opening in the rock at the center, and the subtle waterfall on the left,” says jury member Ilse Koks.

Another American photographer, Matt Pérez, won the Underwater category with a striking photo of a turtle beneath a collection of newt eggs.

According to recent reports, “Pérez’s photograph immediately drew us in. As a jury, we wanted to linger over it, exploring the details and wondering what we were seeing,” remarks Guillot. “Newt egg masses decorate the submerged branches like baubles on a Christmas tree, framing the scene and guiding our eyes towards the pond turtle with its piercing yellow eyes.”.

Guillot adds that the scene looks “otherworldly,” which is a very apt description.

Sources indicate that chinese photographer Xuzhong Liu’s abstract drone shot of a winding landscape ticks all the right boxes. It has interesting patterns, striking colors, and a very pleasing composition.

Liu captured the image in a wetland area in China and notes the scene strongly reminded him of peach blossoms he had previously photographed—hence the title, “Peach Blossoms in the Snow.”.

“This photograph has everything that can make a drone shot interesting and fascinating. First and foremost, there are beautiful shapes and subtle colours, but there is also a sense of alienation. What am I actually looking at, and what is the scale of the landscape in the photograph?” asks the chair of the judging panel, Theo Bosboom.

Czech photographer Petr Bambousek’s winning photo depicts a sobering scene of a Malayan sun bear resting inside a garbage incinerator.

“The winning image stood out for its striking depiction of the impact human activity has on local wildlife,” explains jury member Lana Tannir. “The sleeping Malayan sun bear inside a garbage incinerator creates a powerful visual contrast, showing how habitat loss and human waste increasingly force wild animals into close contact with human environments.”.

Tannir indicates Bambousek’s photo is “unexpected and unsettling.”.

Hungarian photographer László Tóth won the Black and White category for his striking, high-contrast, abstract photo.

In a recent development, “This photo really stood out to us. At first, we were not quite sure what we were looking at. It sparked some wonderful discussions among the jury and made us look even closer,” says Ilse Koks.

As for what the photo actually depicts, it’s a thin layer of snow on top of a frozen lake, shaped by the wind.

It has been revealed that this photo might be familiar to PetaPixel readers. Norwegian photographer Audun Rikardsen recently won an award for a similar underwater portrait of a polar bear peering down through a hole in the ice.

Recent findings suggest that “Just when we thought we had seen about every kind of polar bear image there is, along comes this shot taken from inside a hole in the ice looking up at the bear,” says Steffen Foerster. “Once you realize what is happening, you start thinking about how this shot could possibly have been taken. Then it dawns on you that it seems almost impossible, no matter how.”.

This special category, “De Lage Landen” (which translates to “The Low Countries”), celebrates photos captured in the low-lying region of northwestern Europe, including the Netherlands, where Nature Photographer of the Year is based. This year’s winning photo is by Hungarian photographer Enikő Kálovics.

In a recent development, “The winning image stood out for its ability to transform a familiar landscape into something dreamlike and unexpected,” says Lana Tannir. “The combination of the tiny lacewings, the autumn forest, and the purplish night sky creates a delicate, atmospheric interpretation of the nature of ‘De Lage Landen.'”.

American photographer Parham Pourahmad, who was also recently celebrated in the 2027 North American Nature Photography Association (NANPA) Showcase, won this year’s Youth category with a lovely monochromatic photo of a coyote beneath a large tree.

It has been revealed that “In ‘Tree of Life’, Pourahmad captured a striking scene that could comfortably hold its own in the adult categories,” claims Guillot. “Black and white was an excellent choice, defining the coyote’s silhouette and revealing the majestic oak’s intricate network of branches. Even within this wider scene, the coyote’s downward gaze is clear. Pourahmad explained that it was searching for rodent prey, a small detail that brings the photograph to life.”.

Pourahmad has also been named Youth Photographer of the Year.

The Fred Hazelhoff Award celebrates a portfolio of nature photos, rather than a single image. This year’s portfolio winner is German photographer Simone Baumeister.

In a recent development, “In the portfolio category, the bar is set considerably higher for participating photographers than in the individual categories. Whilst a single fantastic photograph is sufficient there, in the portfolio category you need a whole series of outstanding images that not only complement one another but also fit together well in terms of style and theme. Simone Baumeister has succeeded brilliantly in this with her portfolio on eagle owls in the city,” says jury chair Theo Bosboom.

Baumeister has been fascinated by owls for as long as she has been interested in nature photography. The eagle owl’s story is a positive one, in contrast to the plight of many species across the globe. The species, once on the brink of extinction in Germany, has made an incredible recovery. Its resurgence is thanks largely to major conservation efforts and extensive reintroduction programs.

“It was perched in twilight on a church, right below the street lamps, moving cars, and a string of people passing by, with music blaring from a pub right on the church square. Not a soul took notice of the impressive bird with a wingspan of 1.7 meters flying up the steeple, sitting enthroned right within everybody’s view,” the photographer claims of the first time she saw an eagle owl in a city.

Ever since then, she has been consistently excited by eagle owls and keen to photograph them in many different places. Observing and photographing them in various cities inevitably morphed into a dedicated project.

Alongside the category and special award winners above, the judges also selected runners-up and highly commended photos, all of which can be seen on the Nature Photographer of the Year website and below.

Entries for the Nature Photographer of the Year 2027 open on November 20, 2026.

According to recent reports, image creditsNature Photographer of the Year. Individual photographers are credited in the image captions.

Industry News: ‘It is an unusual model, but I am an unusual person’: Shafeena Yusuff Ali on her Abu Dhabi foundation and gallery

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (849 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali is attempting a one-woman band.
  • It was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art.
  • According to recent reports, vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali is attempting a one-woman band. Born in Abu Dhabi to the Keralan billionaire M.A. Yusuff Ali, whose Indian-Emirati conglomerate LuLu Group spans retail, hospitality and real estate, she considers among her roles: collector, dealer, art historian, writer, entrepreneur and adviser to corporate and private collections.

It was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art. A trio of successive master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact led her to establish Rizq Art Initiative in 2023, an Abu Dhabi-based organisation that includes a commercial gallery, an artist and curator residency, an education platform, an off-site exhibitions programme and an advisory. The organisation is presently in the process of separating into a for-profit commercial gallery and a non-profit foundation.

According to recent reports, vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014). Yusuff Ali has acquired a large number of works by the Indian artist Courtesy Rizq Art Initiative.

“It is an unusual model, but I think I am an unusual person,” she indicates. “Notmany gallerists have three postgraduate degrees, and carry both business and academic backgrounds. I understand how industries work and I have also written an art historical paper on each work in my collection”.

In a recent development, rizq, which in Arabic means “provision” or “sustenance”, was established to kickstart a nascent scene by plugging overlooked gaps in the local art ecosystem. “The biggest challenge facing the Abu Dhabi art scene is a lack of nuanced peripheral actors,” Yusuff Ali notes. “Critics, fabricators, experimental spaces, warehousing and storage. For an art ecosystem to work you need all these elements to work in coherence.”.

Industry observers note that informed by Yusuff Ali’s ties to both India and the UAE, Rizq focuses on artists from the Global South, including young Emiratis Shamsa Almansoori and Reem Al Mubarak, and the Keralan watercolourist Anupama Alias Ani. Of just five commercial galleries in Abu Dhabi “we are the only one focusing on artists from the global majority”, she notes.“This is crucial in a city where most inhabitants are from regions the art world doesn’t necessarily cater to.” During Frieze Abu Dhabi (18-22 November), the gallery is staging a solo show by Al Mubarak.

Beyond its Abu Dhabi gallery, Rizq also programmes offsite exhibitions, including a satellite show for the sixth edition of the Kochi Biennale in Kerala, contributing to a growing dialogue between the art worlds of South Asia and the Gulf.

According to recent reports, yussuf Ali's heritage also informs what she buys: areas of interest include lesser-known South Asian Modernists, such as the Keralan painter K.C.S. Paniker, as well as pioneering artists of the UAE like Hassan Sharif. Perhaps the artist whose work she has collected most widely is Vivek Vilasini, the only Indian member of the Flying House, a 2000s experimental art collective in Dubai that has hugely influenced today’s contemporary art scene in the UAE. “Vivek is a friend,” Yusuff Ali states. “It is remarkable that an Indian artist in the UAE has played such a central role in defining the nation’s art history.”.

As for Abu Dhabi, Yusuff Ali believes in the long term, and understands that the local market is “only just beginning to grow”. Presently her private funds keep Rizq’s gallery afloat, but she is quick to point out that she speaks the language of business alongside art. “I have established a proof of concept and spent the past three years demonstrating measurable impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “I am confident that the next time we speak, we will have brought enough patrons on board to become profitable.”.

The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you bought?

Industry observers note that shafeena Yusuff Ali: The first significant work was a Mona Saudi sculpture, Mother and Child (1981), before she passed away. I bought it when I was pregnant—and at a generationally different price. When I was buying it I fully realised it was special.

A painting by one of the forgotten masters of Kerala, N.K.P. Muthukoya.

If you could own any work from a museum what would it be?

I’d like to hang a work by Amrita Sher-Gil alongside one by Princess Fahrelnissa Zeid. My life bridges South Asia and the Middle East and these two women are strikingly similar in how they lived painful but luxurious lives.

Where do you like to eat in Abu Dhabi?

My favorite shawarma place is Al Akkawi.

What do you recommend doing outside the fair?

November is perfect biking weather. Walk around the city—don’t drive. And get a boat to one of the outer islands. They can be really magical.

What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?

Sometimes it gets too homogenous—the same seven galleries showing the same seven artists.

What should people know before coming to Frieze Abu Dhabi?

The culture here is quite shy, and highly relationship based. Newcomers might struggle if they lack patience.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is not a drill. The Sony FX5 really has launched.

Last month, after numerous delays, Sony said the highly anticipated FX5 cinema camera would finally launch on November 15. As Sony Alpha Rumors reports, Sony actually delivered, and preordered cameras have begun shipping to customers. Multiple Sony Alpha Rumors commenters confirmed they have received their orders from retailers including Adorama and B&H.

Video creator Brandon Washington took to Instagram to share that his preorder arrived, with numerous commenters chiming in that they have gotten their hands on the FX5 as well, including someone who walked into local stores without a preorder and picked up a unit.

According to recent reports, that stated, some who preordered have not yet received their cameras, so it’s unclear how many orders have been fulfilled versus how many customers are still waiting. It is, frankly, impossible to know because both Adorama and B&H are treating fresh FX5 orders as “preorders,” meaning the camera is not actively in stock yet. Meanwhile, the FX5 is not available to order directly through Sony in the U.S.

To say the FX5’s launch has been tumultuous would be an understatement. The camera was announced on July 22, and at the time, Sony mentioned it would begin shipping just a few weeks later in “mid-August.”.

Recent findings suggest that when the planned release date arrived in August, Sony said the FX5 was delayed by at least a month. One month became two and then three. In early October, PetaPixel reported that the delay may have been tied to an issue with the rear LCD. Sony itself has never officially explained the delay.

In any event, the Sony FX5 has finally arrived. While it may take some time before all preorders are fulfilled, this is undeniably great news for videographers and creators. The Sony FX5 has certainly impressed us at PetaPixel so far, and we’re looking forward to doing a comprehensive review of the camera as soon as possible.

As PetaPixel wrote in July, there’s reason to believe the FX5 is Sony’s most important cinema camera to date. And now, finally, it’s here. It sure seems like Sony has a winner on its hands.
