📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

It has been revealed that picture this: you're settled into your seat on a United flight out of LAX, the Pacific stretching endlessly outside your window, and you know — you genuinely know — that the person next to you paid $400 for this exact seat while you paid **7,500 miles**. That's the Hawaiian sweet spot, and it's one of the most quietly powerful redemptions available to anyone building a travel rewards strategy. Hawaii has always been the aspirational American vacation. It's the honeymoon destination, the bucket-list family trip, the anniversary getaway. And because of that demand, flights from the mainland — especially during spring break, summer, and the holidays — rarely go on sale. A round-trip economy ticket from Los Angeles to Honolulu will routinely run **$400–$700**, and during peak travel windows, prices can push past $1,000 for a family of four. That's real money. FI-community money. Now consider what Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles charges for that same seat: **7,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of cash pricing ($200 for a one-way), you're extracting **2.7 cents per point**. At the high end ($500 during peak season), that same 7,500 miles is worth **6.7 cents per point** — a figure that makes even seasoned travel rewards enthusiasts do a double-take. For context, most people in the points world consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. **Getting 6.7 cents per point is extraordinary.** It's not a fluke or a loophole — it's a structural pricing inefficiency baked into the Turkish award chart, which treats all short-haul domestic U.S. flights (including Hawaii, which is technically a domestic route) at the same rock-bottom rate. This is the fundamental insight behind every great travel rewards redemption: **loyalty programs price awards based on their own logic, not cash fares.** Turkish Miles & Smiles sees LAX→HNL as a short Star Alliance partner flight. The fact that cash fares on that route are elevated because of destination demand is irrelevant to their award chart. That gap — between what Turkish charges in miles and what the market charges in dollars — is exactly where you save. For a ChooseFI community member who already holds Citi ThankYou Points, this redemption is within reach right now. You don't need to fly Turkish. You don't need to connect through Istanbul. You just need availability on United, 7,500 miles, and about 20 minutes.

Sources indicate that the magic here comes down to one core concept: Star Alliance partner pricing on a domestic U.S. route.

Turkish Airlines is a Star Alliance member, and like most alliance programs, they allow their members to book award flights on partner airlines — including United. Where Turkish gets interesting (and generous) is in how they price those partner awards. Their award chart uses a fixed, distance-based or zone-based structure, and for short-haul U.S. domestic flights, the price bottoms out at 7,500 miles one-way in economy.

According to recent reports, here's the pricing inefficiency in plain language: Turkish Miles & Smiles doesn't care that Hawaii is an aspirational, high-demand destination. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Camera Intelligence, the company behind the controversial Caira camera, is leaning into the current trend of vibe-coded camera hacks by making it a dedicated feature of its smartphone-mounted Micro Four Thirds camera system.

Sources indicate that to call the Caira controversial is not a hot take: it’s one of the few cameras on PixelMeter that have an equal number of recommended, mixed, and panned reviews. The experience is highly subjective.

“I’ll give the Caira this: No one else is really making anything like it,” Chris Niccolls wrote in his review from earlier this year.

Sources indicate that “I’m left with a concern about who would actually enjoy using the Caira camera. Advanced photographers will not enjoy the problematic handling, the generative AI features, and the fiddly control scheme, but this camera was never intended for them anyway. I worry that casual crowds will not appreciate the benefits of buying, carrying, and learning about interchangeable lenses, and see much benefit in the purchase of this product over their smartphones. Content creators might want to dabble with the different optics and some manual controls, plus they will find the separate functionality of the phone apart from the camera useful, but they generally already have DJI Pocket Osmo or Sony ZV cameras with mobile apps.”.

From its inception, the Caira camera has been cozy with AI. In fact, it was one of the most panned features of the camera when it was in beta — Google’s Nano Banana image generator was built directly into the system, allowing users to generatively edit photos directly in the camera. Before the camera debuted, Camera Intelligence reined in the capabilities of the system in response to the blowback.

It has been revealed that “When we first announced the generative editing feature in October, it was an extremely raw, early, novel, and nebulous concept. We were not expecting to get everything perfectly right. But, it was being considered from a point of view that many people outside the camera industry find it challenging and overwhelming to navigate and maximize the benefits of editing tools like Lightroom and Photoshop,” Camera Intelligence’s CEO, Vishal Kumar, told PetaPixel.

Recent findings suggest that while AI was significantly pulled back, it’s clear that Camera Intelligence’s goals for Caira are heavily influenced by it. That is reinforced today as the company is fully embracing vibe-coding camera hacks, a trend that has gotten very popular over the last couple of months. Think Magic Lantern, but for any camera and at the whim of the photographer.

Sources indicate that “Something big is happening in the camera industry right now. Photographers are using AI tools like Claude Code and ChatGPT to hack their own cameras and add features the manufacturer never shipped. Many people are vibe coding these modifications without permission or a safety net, and some are bricking expensive cameras in the process,” Kumar states.

Sources indicate that “At Camera Intelligence, we’ve been waiting for a moment like this and want to embrace and encourage this development. We’ve always had ambitions to provide access to our operating system that runs on the Caira (did you know that ‘Caira”‘ stands for ‘computational artificial intelligence camera’?). We’re opening up Caira, our Micro Four Thirds camera that attaches to an iPhone, through our fresh ‘Creative Sandbox’. It’s a new, safe development environment inside Camera Intelligence OS where our customers can build their own features for the camera using their own AI coding tools.”.

Recent findings suggest that it’s hard to tell if this was something Camera Intelligence always envisioned as a possibility or if it’s just an example of the company jumping on the latest trend, but it is taking the capability seriously. It is hosting a Holiday Camera Hack in its London office in December, which is a one-day hackathon for up to 20 photographers, video creators, and engineers. Applications for that are open.

Image creditsCamera Intelligence.

Josh Puckett built Allo, a free open source typography family with three variable axes, true obliques, and a playful interactive specimen site.

Josh Puckett started Allo from Rasmus Anderssonâs Inter 4.1, then redrew every single glyph to give it a warmer, friendlier voice. Released under the SIL Open Font License at $0.00, it also nods to Seb McLauchlanâs Honk Sans. You can see that personality right away in the colorful sticker pile and the multi-language greeting wall on the homepage. It feels approachable without turning cartoonish.

Sources indicate that under the hood, Allo runs on three variable axes: Weight from 100 to 900, Roundness from 0 to 100, and an Optical Size axis from 14 to 32 that adjusts automatically between body text and display headlines. The family packs 606 glyphs, support for over 50 languages, and true obliques drawn from scratch rather than slanted mechanically. Practical touches show up across the specimen cards, including tabular figures, fractions, lifted punctuation beside capitals, and arrows that form as you type.

Stylistic sets make the system even more flexible for interface work. SS01 switches to a single-story lowercase a, while SS02 activates disambiguation for tricky characters like I, l, 1, O, and 0. Thereâs also a built-in grid of crisp UI icons and keyboard symbols like Command, arrows, and checkmarks.

It has been revealed that what makes the release memorable is how fun the website is to explore. Puckett pairs Kenneyâs CC0 interface sound effects with interactive UI cards covering everything from CO2 readings to boarding passes and pizza polls. The best part sits in the variable axes canvas, shown in the video below. Dragging the vertical bar across ABC123 splits the screen between the solid "As set" type on the left and the "As drawn" Bezier outlines with red control handles on the right, updating weight and roundness live as you move.

How iPhone Duo’s Unlock With Front Camera Works (and How It’s Different Than Face ID)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The newest iOS 27 developer beta partially addresses one of the iPhone Duo’s biggest shortcomings: its lack of Face ID.
  • Industry observers note that when PetaPixel reviewed the iPhone Duo, scoring it a 7.5, Jaron Schneider knocked Apple’s debut foldable for its reliance on relatively slow, inconsistent Touch ID.
  • Sources indicate that “I have found that Touch ID is slower than Face ID for unlocking the phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The newest iOS 27 developer beta partially addresses one of the iPhone Duo’s biggest shortcomings: its lack of Face ID.

Industry observers note that when PetaPixel reviewed the iPhone Duo, scoring it a 7.5, Jaron Schneider knocked Apple’s debut foldable for its reliance on relatively slow, inconsistent Touch ID. While Apple’s recent smartphones have all used Face ID to unlock promptly, the iPhone Duo sticks with Touch ID. It’s finicky, and consumers must hold the phone in just the right way to unlock it. Even when it works as expected, it’s not quite as swift as Face ID.

Sources indicate that “I have found that Touch ID is slower than Face ID for unlocking the phone. It got to the point where I was so grateful that I have an Apple Watch because I could set it to automatically unlock it when it sensed I was wearing the watch. Unlock with Watch is also, somehow, faster than using Touch ID. It removed a lot of the friction I was butting up against with Touch ID, but it requires a Watch,” Schneider wrote of his Apple Watch-powered workaround.

However, with today’s launch of the iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple has begun testing a new feature: Unlock with Front Camera.

In a recent development, to be clear, this is not Face ID. The iPhone Duo still lacks the necessary hardware to offer the iPhone’s typical unlocking method. However, Unlock with Front Camera is set up in a similar way, requiring users to look at the front camera and turn their head from side to side. Like Face ID, it is also fast and works at off-angles.

I have been using an iPhone Duo review unit for the past few weeks as part of a long-term follow-up review and have been forced to rely on Touch ID on numerous occasions, often finding it frustrating. I installed the upcoming developer beta on the Duo, set up Unlock with Front Camera, and am very much on board with it.

In a recent development, again, it’s not a perfect Face ID replacement. It requires the user to use Touch ID every so often, for starters, about every 45 minutes. Just as other iPhone users occasionally need to enter their passcode for certain tasks or after a restart, iPhone Duo users will still need Touch ID even with this latest feature.

Unlock with Front Camera does seem to work in poor lighting conditions, although I have not been able to test it yet in total darkness. Given the front camera’s lack of an infrared sensor, I expect some challenges.

Face ID relies on the iPhone’s TrueDepth sensor to quickly and securely confirm the user’s identity against existing robust data. Without Face ID and TrueDepth, the iPhone Duo doesn’t promise the same level of security or performance. Even so, Apple is clearly confident that Unlock with Front Camera is sufficiently secure, at the very least.

According to recent reports, unlock with Front Camera promises at least some of Face ID’s convenience, which is ultimately more key to most users than Apple’s absolute top-notch security. The iPhone Duo still stores facial data privately and securely to confirm (or deny) a match between the user attempting to unlock the phone and the initial setup imagery.

The Duo can definitely tell the difference between me and a picture of me. When I attempted to fool the Duo, it not only didn’t fall for my cleverly laid trap, but it also locked the device and required me to use Touch ID again. This is also its response when someone else tries to unlock my phone. If something doesn’t jibe, owners must either use Touch ID again or enter their passcode.

Recent findings suggest that it also works only with the front-facing camera, not the under-display one on the inner screen. That’s not a huge glitch, but it’s worth noting.

So no, the iPhone Duo doesn’t suddenly have Face ID thanks to a software upgrade, but it does have something that is at least better than what we had and addresses a very common complaint lodged against Apple’s latest phone.

I will continue my long-term testing of the iPhone Duo, using it as my only smartphone. It has not been without its shortcomings, but Apple stated today that there are now more than 200,000 apps that natively support the Duo. Between that and Unlock with Front Camera, the Duo genuinely keeps getting better.

#22318. Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section to reflect the 'turbulence and violence of our times'

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1031 w)
📖 Baca

Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section to reflect the 'turbulence and violence of our times'

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.
  • Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.
  • Industry observers note that curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.

Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.

Industry observers note that curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds. In some ways, the section builds upon conversations from other parts of the fair. Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi, for instance, will investigate historic routes of migration, trade and cultural exchange across the Indian Ocean. Global Futures appears to attempt this within a contemporary context.

“The process of putting together Global Futures actually came together quite beautifully and organically,” Malik notes. “We started with a number of proposals, looking at projects that felt so apt to this moment. We thought about what it means to have a fair, what it means to have this international constellation of galleries at this moment in Abu Dhabi. What are the conversations happening within the cultural sphere that are prevalent to this moment?”.

With Taymour Grahne Projects, the Kuwaiti artist Ala Younis will present 11 works from her Climate Conditions series. The mosaic panels, crafted out of hand-cut stones and mounted on metal frames, depict old office buildings, municipal structures and other places in Abu Dhabi that are often overlooked. Younis first unveiled the series in her 2025 solo exhibition at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery. The project materialised after a three-year stay in the Emirati capital. Knowing the city’s propensity for rapid change, she sought to document and commemorate the structures as she saw them. In rendering their likeness in mosaics, Younis alludes to the Roman tiles that have outlasted the structures they once decorated. The title of the project refers to how the structures interact with the environment—their wood and metal bits expanding and contracting to changes in humidity and temperature.

Sources indicate that the Mexican artist Tania Candiani, on the other hand, looks underground for a more sprawling and rhizomatic type of structure. Her Root Systems, presented by Galeria Vermelho, charts networks of plant roots in embroidery, unearthing a subterranean language with its own systems of exchange and communication.

“These projects established two very different but sort of complementary points of departure,” Malik indicates. “They look at these ideas of migration, of ecology, of transformation—shared across different temporalities and across different structures.”.

These themes, Malik claims, resonate across the other presentations in Global Futures.

Through his Naked Sweet Potato series, Abdullah Al Saadi transcribes his personal engagement with the landscape of his native Khor Fakkan. Studying the different shapes and textures of sweet potatoes, the Emirati artist renders a language from the vegetable. He makes jewellery from it and he uses it to revisit his childhood, to transcribe his excursions to the UAE countryside. Where Candiani lays bare the universal language of roots, Al Saadi’s Naked Sweet Potato introduces an idiosyncratic and deeply personal lexicon to the conversation. The series includes drawings, paintings, sculptures and engravings, as well as collected materials. First shown at the UAE National Pavilion during the 2011 edition of the Venice Biennale, Naked Sweet Potato will be presented at Global Futures by Aisha Alabbar Gallery.

With Zawyeh Gallery, the Palestinian artist Mohammed Joha will exhibit No Shelter, building upon the series he is presenting at this year’s Venice Biennale (until 22 November). His canvases feature stratified layers of discarded textiles, paper and cardboard that come together as vibrant, abstracted landscapes.

The artist, who is based in France, began the series as he watched the destruction of his native Gaza from afar. His work comes as a poignant expression of heartache, the shredded materials evoking the devastation of Gaza and the forced displacement of its population. The way they come together in colourful compositions, however, simultaneously stands up against the violence, insisting on reconstruction in the face of ruin.

“I looked at projects that reflected the turbulence of our times, the violence of our times,” Malik says. “Things can feel unsettled and art opens up a dialogue for us to understand one another.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Indian-born artist Arshi Irshad Ahmadzai, showing at Global Futures with the Mumbai-based gallery Chatterjee & Lal, will be showing her series Azal se Abad tak, which includes drawings and paintings on cloth. The works investigate how different cultures have articulated the concept of eternity.

The Ghanaian artist Godfried Donkor will present paintings, collages and embroidery with Gallery 1957. He draws from an eclectic range of inspirations for his works, including comic book superheroes, boxing athletes as well as mythological figures.

Finally, Marfa’ Projects will exhibit works by the Lebanese artist Seta Manoukian. A celebrated figure of the late 1960s Beirut art scene, Manoukian’s paintings are a stunning, often otherwordly depiction of life during the Lebanese Civil War. The works Manoukian produced after emigrating to Los Angeles in the late 1980s can be regarded as attempts at establishing stability and certainty in the aftermath of the conflict. These include works from her T-Shape series, which will be exhibited at the fair.

“We have work from her Rose series to her Rock series, as well as one of her early more figurative paintings,” Malik notes. “In a constellation of around five or six works, we’re trying to build something that feels like a journey through the life of a really iconic artist.”.

All in all, the Global Futures section, Malik says, seeks to draw connections between the exhibiting artists in a way that does not reduce the “specificity of where these artists are from and what they’re talking about”.

Sources indicate that “I think we’ve chosen works together that really represent [a given] body of work by that artist in the best way possible,” Malik indicates. “It was really about building shared connections […] while also thinking about how they intersect in the UAE and in this rapidly transforming city.”.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

Astronaut Loads 35mm Film Into Analog Camera While in Space

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (446 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • German astronaut Rabea Rogge flew on the Fram2 spaceflight mission in April 2025, bringing her trusty second-hand analog camera.
  • In a recent development, rogge is an Arctic roboticist, at the moment studying for a PhD at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology in the Department of Marine Technology.
  • Last week, Rogge shared a video on Instagram as she loaded up a roll of 35mm film while onboard the SpaceX Crew Dragon Resilience spacecraft.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

German astronaut Rabea Rogge flew on the Fram2 spaceflight mission in April 2025, bringing her trusty second-hand analog camera.

In a recent development, rogge is an Arctic roboticist, at the moment studying for a PhD at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology in the Department of Marine Technology. She is also Germany’s first-ever female astronaut.

Last week, Rogge shared a video on Instagram as she loaded up a roll of 35mm film while onboard the SpaceX Crew Dragon Resilience spacecraft.

While many celluloid shooters have encountered difficulties loading film on terra firma, Rogge deftly loaded a roll of Kodak Portra 160 into the camera that she calls a “sturdy companion.”.

A post shared by Rabea Rogge (@rabearogge).

It has been revealed that “Analog pictures from space,” Rogge captions the post. “My old second-hand analog camera has been a sturdy companion on all my expeditions from under -20°C [-4°F] in the high Arctic to the humid climate at sea around the equator. On Fram2 it got to launch on a rocket as well – and it still lives on so far!”.

In a recent development, petaPixel identified Rogge’s camera as a Minolta X-700 with a 45mm lens attached. The X-700 was the flagship SLR for the now-defunct Japanese company for the best part of 20 years. In 1982, it won the European “Camera of the Year” award, and it is still popular in the second-hand market today.

Recent findings suggest that with the film loaded in the camera, Rogge was afforded stunning views of Earth thanks to the Crew Dragon’s 360-degree cupola. At 2,000 square inches, it was the largest single window ever flown to space. Rogge, along with her crewmates Chun Wang, Jannicke Mikkelsen, and Eric Philips, were also the first people to ever orbit over Earth’s north and south poles.

“Can’t imagine the face of the people from the film lab when they scanned your roll,” comments Thibaut Everaerts on Instagram.

Rogge’s camera is far from the first Minolta to ever fly from space; in fact, the first American to ever orbit the Earth, John Glenn, took a Minolta Hi-Matic (repackaged as an Ansco Autoset) with him into space.

Despite buying the automatic camera for just $40 from a drugstore in Cocoa Beach, Florida, NASA engineers modified the camera with a pistol grip so that Glenn could use the camera while wearing his bulky astronaut gloves.

The photos that Glenn took in 1962 and their resulting popularity are credited with helping NASA realize how key it was to document Earth from space.

How AdHoc made Dispatch feel like an animated TV series

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dispatch looks, sounds, and plays like an animated TV show, and that was deliberate: AdHoc wanted it to be a no-barrier entry point for people who don't usually play games.
  • The game stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as Robert Robertson, a former hero turned dispatcher for a team of reformed supervillains, alongside Jeffrey Wright, Laura Bailey, and members of the Critical Role cast.
  • You can read how four video tracks and a doughnut shop gave Dispatch its start, but here I ask co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO, and both co-creative directors, how they nailed down the premium animation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dispatch looks, sounds, and plays like an animated TV show, and that was deliberate: AdHoc wanted it to be a no-barrier entry point for people who don't usually play games. A year after its launch on 22 October 2025, the episodic superhero workplace comedy has more than five million players, and the upcoming Dispatch Deluxe Edition offers new ways to play, including replacing its graphics with storyboard art.

The game stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as Robert Robertson, a former hero turned dispatcher for a team of reformed supervillains, alongside Jeffrey Wright, Laura Bailey, and members of the Critical Role cast. Getting that cast to feel like they're in the same room, and getting the player to feel part of the story, took a lot of invisible work.

You can read how four video tracks and a doughnut shop gave Dispatch its start, but here I ask co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO, and both co-creative directors, how they nailed down the premium animation.

Industry observers note that how do you keep dialogue, facial expressions and performances consistent when the player can send a scene in different directions? While it was made using Unreal Engine 5, it starts on the page. "Everything is written with choice in mind," notes Herman.

AdHoc built its own tools to ingest scripts, including a playable script you can read and click through. That produces the recording script actors use in the booth, which Herman says is "a little bit crazy to read on a linear page". Do it long enough, though, and it starts to make sense. Each scene has a spine, and every time a choice appears, different options eventually trunk back into the main flow.

The studio also uses recordings as a directing tool. AdHoc ingests every performance as it’s captured, so when an actor records opposite someone already in the booth, the team can play those existing lines back for them to react to. In Herman’s example, with Aaron Paul already recorded, the team can bring in Erin as Blonde Blazer, play Paul’s lines for her to read off, then play him again after her response. It’s a clever bit of craft: AdHoc builds each conversation around real delivery. The effect, Herman claims, is to simulate the actors being in the same room, which helps performances feel grounded and integrated. It also gives a scene its flow, because the actors know where they’re coming in from, and it makes testing branches easy.

In a recent development, it's clever craft. Rather than recording actors in isolation and hoping the performances fit together later, AdHoc builds the conversation around real delivery. The effect, Herman says, is to simulate the actors being in the same room, which helps performances feel grounded and integrated. It also gives a scene its flow, because the actors know where they're coming in from, and it makes testing branches easy.

Recent findings suggest that by the time animation begins, the voice work is trusted, and the team is happy with it. The facial animation then comes down to knowing every character. "Not everyone laughs the same. When they cry, they look different," Herman says. "Every character is their own person. Like they are on the page, they are in animation." Getting there takes "a lot of review, a lot of ref", and the team shoots plenty of reference footage for its animators.

For AdHoc, the problem was the seam: the point where a cutscene ends and gameplay begins. “The goal was always to make it feel integrated,” Lenart notes. Part of the studio’s philosophy is that gameplay and story should feel like a seamless handoff rather than two different experiences. He and Herman had worked on plenty of games with clear story sections and clear gameplay sections, “and you could feel that break every single time”. That, he says, “always kind of drove us crazy”.

When they dreamed of starting their own studio, one mandate was to choose mechanics that feel like an integrated part of a character's life, not scenes contrived for interactivity. If someone has to break into a room and pick a lock, it shouldn't be something the character would never do.

For Dispatch, that meant the shift mechanic. Robert sends heroes out on calls because it's his job. "It's the thing he does every day," notes Lenart. "So, when he sits down at his computer to do it, it feels natural.".

In a recent development, the team also made sure the Z-Team keep talking to the player throughout each shift, so the dialogue and relationships keep flowing, and the story never stops for gameplay. At times, a shift cuts out to a cinematic and back in again, and Lenart says that only feels organic because "we spent a lot of time and effort to make it that way".

Herman and Lenart both spent years at Telltale Games, the studio behind The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, and Tales from the Borderlands, and Dispatch forced them to drop much of their old way of working.

At Telltale, Lenart notes, cinematics were "fast and loose". Episodes were made in what the studio called live development: they would release one episode, then spend the next six weeks on the following. Things "could change at any time". Player feedback from the previous episode could feed straight back in, with tweaks to cinematics and character intentions right up until the day before shipping.

In a recent development, dispatch had a different goal. AdHoc wanted the visuals and style to feel like "a premium animated television show" that wasn't a barrier for people who might enjoy a story like this but aren't typically into games. That meant a more traditional animation pipeline, with decisions made much earlier and, in some cases, locked down a year in advance.

Industry observers note that "That was a really significant learning curve for us since we were used to being able to make small adjustments all the way up until the last minute," Lenart claims. But he now thinks the discipline made the game better. It "forced many detailed conversations way earlier in the process, which only better informed how each piece of the story was going to play out". His verdict: "Oh, this is actually the way to make the best quality product.".

The Dispatch Deluxe Edition is out now on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and Nintendo Switch / Switch 2, and $10.99 digital upgrade path for existing owners.

These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian released Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Head of Instagram Adam Mosseri has declared that, judging by the look of the iPhone Duo, “it’s going to be pretty challenging” to design the app for the unusual format.

Apple released the Duo last month, the company’s first-ever folding phone. The first-generation device has come under criticism for not being optimized for apps like Instagram.

Taking to Threads yesterday, Mosseri notes, “Having spent about a year with a foldable as my daily driver, I’m actually excited about trying the Duo once I can get my hands on one. That mentioned, the more I look at the details of the device, the more I think it’s going to be pretty challenging to design Instagram in a way that feels great for this format.”.

In a recent development, replying to a comment on the post, Mosseri agreed with one user who remarked the best experience presently comes when the phone is unfolded and rotated vertically into portrait orientation. But Mosseri adds that the company wants to “make the experience in other orientations better.”.

Replying to another comment, Mosseri elaborated further on the challenges posed by the Duo.

In a recent development, “I’m not criticizing the format,” he says. “It’s just very different than today’s format and so much about Instagram has been designed for the tall vertical screen.”.

Since the Duo’s release, Instagram owners have complained that the app simply doesn’t look very good on the foldable device, pointing specifically to what Mosseri calls a “double stack of buttons” on the right-hand side of the screen.

“It makes total sense to me that the nav goes on the right-hand side of the Duo when it’s closed because it’s ergonomically effective, but that’s where the like, comment, and share buttons go in the Reels viewer,” he points out.

Instagram has rolled out a more optimized version of the app, saying in a blog post that it is “continuing to adapt the Instagram experience for Apple’s first foldable iPhone.”.

It took Instagram a very long time to release a version of the app that’s native to the Apple iPad.

We find Logitech's officially endorsed options are sleek and well built, and this is a very good saving.

Recent findings suggest that apple hiked the price of all of its current iPad models around the middle of 2026 because of the increase in the cost of components, particularly memory (RAM) and internal storage (SSDs). The whole consumer tech sector has been impacted by these price rises, which have been caused by a shortage of component due to the demand from companies building AI data centres.

This means that this year's iPad Black Friday deals will inevitably be more expensive than last year's. There's no sign that starting prices will fall again any time soon.

It has been revealed that keeping in mind the size of discounts seen during previous iPad Black Friday sales is a good way to gauge whether it's the right time to buy or if prices could fall further. The pattern we've seen is that the best deals on the latest generation of iPads tend to be up to $70 off the standard iPad and $100 off the iPad Air and up to $200 off higher-spec iPad Pros.

It has been revealed that in 14 years of tracking prices, our experience is that there is rarely any difference between Black Friday and Cyber Monday iPad prices. They are usually the same deals under a different name. On a very few occasions, we have seen new discounts appear on Cyber Monday.

The best iPad for you will depend on what you want to use it for. For browsing, watching movies, social media and just occasional note taking and sketching, this year's standard 11-inch iPad with the A16 chip will do just fine, and it doesn't make sense to spend more. Aim to spend no more than $399 on this,.

If you're an artist and want a more efficient drawing experience, I'd recommend stepping up to the iPad Air. A new M4-chipped generation of this tablet was released in March, and Amazon's already slashed the price by $100 in a Black Friday deal. This tablet comes in two choices of size: 11 inches or 13 inches.

Recent findings suggest that if you're a professional artist and you have the budget for it, the iPad Pro is the top-of-the-range option. Also coming in 11- and 13-inch models, it has a superior screen with a bright OLED panel for improved contrast along along with a faster 120Hz refresh rate for a seamless drawing experience.

Coming with the M5 chip, this is the iPad to choose if you want to replace you're laptop when working on the go, and it's cut out to handle more demanding creative software, including video editing.

Recent findings suggest that remember that all iPads come in various configurations, with the option of WiFi and cellular connectivity or just WiFi alone, plus two size options for the Pro and Air and at least two choices of internal storage capacity. When quoting prices above, we've generally quoted the price of the base model with WiFi and the smallest SSD. This might not necessarily be the option that meets your needs, but retailers will usually list other configurations under the same product listing.

Recent findings suggest that if you use a tablet for work and want to store large files on the device, you may need a higher capacity. The iPad Pro, for example, is available with 256GB, 512GB, 1TB or 2TB. the price rises notably, but the higher-spec models sometimes come in for bigger discounts.

Sources indicate that we'll be linking directly to the best Black Friday iPad deals across all four models here on this page. The best thing you can do to prepare to choose the best deal for you is to think ahead about which iPad you want and in which configuration.

It has been revealed that once you've decided which iPad you want (the Pro, Air, mini or standard iPad), choose the size (there's a choice of 11in or 13in with the iPad Pro and iPad Air), whether you want cellular connectivity or WiFi alone and which storage capacity you'll think you need. Whether you can make do with the starting capacity or you need to hike it up to 512GB, or even 1TB or 2TB on the iPad Pro will depend on how you expect to use the device and whether you'll also be using cloud storage or will want to store large design or video files on the tablet itself.

Apple is unlikely to run any direct iPad Black Friday discounts itself. Instead, it's likely yo offer gift vouchers worth up to $100/£80 with the purchase of certain iPads. This might be appealing if you know that you're going to want to buy another Apple product in the future, but most people would be better off going for deals at third-party sites.

In previous years, we have seen good Black Friday iPad deals at most of the major retailers in the US and UK. In the US, Amazon and B&H Photo tend to have the best prices, while Walmart and Target can also be worth checking.

In the UK, Amazon and Very tend to have the biggest discounts, while Laptops Direct is worth checking for discounts on older models. We track prices at all of these retailers and more.

Traditionally, Black Friday was the Friday after Thanksgiving in the US. It's since extended to cover almost all of November at some retailers. As for when Black Friday ends, many retailers continue it until the Monday after Black Friday itself, which some call Cyber Monday. This year, that falls on 30 November 2026.

Photographer Sets World Record With Tiny Film Camera

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An art teacher and photographer has been given a Guinness World Record for creating the world’s smallest working film camera.
  • Measuring just 2.48 × 2.41 × 2.48 centimeters (0.97 x 0.94 x 0.97 inches), the design of the Pocket Obscura is based on one of the best-selling cameras of all time, the Kodak Brownie.
  • “The project took almost a year from the initial idea to the finished camera and official record attempt,” the camera’s creator, Luke Fazekas, tells PetaPixel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An art teacher and photographer has been given a Guinness World Record for creating the world’s smallest working film camera.

Measuring just 2.48 × 2.41 × 2.48 centimeters (0.97 x 0.94 x 0.97 inches), the design of the Pocket Obscura is based on one of the best-selling cameras of all time, the Kodak Brownie.

“The project took almost a year from the initial idea to the finished camera and official record attempt,” the camera’s creator, Luke Fazekas, tells PetaPixel. “There were plenty of hours spent designing, printing, testing, refining, and starting again.”.

Fazekas, who is based in Melbourne, Australia, says that one of the biggest challenges was getting the minuscule camera to actually function and take recognizable photographs.

“The camera uses a tiny pinhole aperture rather than a conventional lens. I tried different pinhole aperture sizes, focal lengths, and camera dimensions to achieve the desired results,” he explains.

It has been revealed that “Another challenge was getting the exposure right. The camera has a manually operated shutter, which I lift for a predetermined amount of time depending on the available light. With such a small aperture and no conventional lens, getting a consistent and well-exposed image requires plenty of testing and fine-tuning.”.

Fazekas claims he’s always been fascinated by analog cameras and the mechanics of how they work.

“The camera itself takes inspiration from the Kodak Brownie, particularly its simple box-camera design,” Fazekas says.

“The Brownie helped popularize photography by making cameras affordable and accessible to everyday people. I have always been interested in its influence and how such a simple design could have such a significant impact.”.

A post shared by Luke Fazekas (@doctordarkroom).

Fazekas has previously 3D printed components and adapters for old film cameras that have long been discontinued. From that, he began wondering what the world’s smallest analog camera was.

“I began researching and was surprised to discover that, according to Guinness World Records, no such record existed. When I enquired, they sent me a measurement as a benchmark. The idea of being the first to attempt it was tempting, and what started as a bit of fun soon developed into a much bigger project,” he notes.

“I really enjoy combining different creative disciplines, and this project brought together photography, design, technical exploration, and problem-solving.”.

According to Australian Photography, Fazekas had to find a qualified metrologist — someone who specializes in the study of measurement — so that his Pocket Obscura could be measured to the nearest 0.01 centimeter.

“It is great to have the record officially recognized, but I do not think this is necessarily the end of the project,” Fazekas adds.

In a recent development, “To achieve the record, the focus was on the camera itself. Now that I can consistently produce recognizable images, I want to spend more time refining and improving the photographic results.

“I still feel that I have not quite achieved the perfect exposure, and perhaps that is something I will be chasing for a long time. That is part of the appeal of analog photography; there is always something to discover and improve.”.

For many photographers, their first taste of film was via a pinhole camera, and Fazekas sees his creation as a potential educational tool.

In a recent development, “Coming from a visual arts teaching background, I love the idea that something like this can introduce students to photography through a combination of art, science, mathematics, and technology,” he says. “It demonstrates that you do not necessarily need sophisticated equipment to create something interesting.”.

Image creditsCourtesy Luke Fazekas.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nako Baev built THE OBJECT 01, a modular 3D-printed chair in recycled PETG that weighs 20 kg and pairs brutalist mass with Japanese restraint.
  • It has been revealed that at 1.320 meters long and 0.875 meters tall, the lounge chair looks like poured concrete at first glance.
  • Every joint follows a strict rectilinear block logic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nako Baev built THE OBJECT 01, a modular 3D-printed chair in recycled PETG that weighs 20 kg and pairs brutalist mass with Japanese restraint.

It has been revealed that at 1.320 meters long and 0.875 meters tall, the lounge chair looks like poured concrete at first glance. Look closer at the studio shots and the surprise is its weight. Baev printed the entire structure from recycled PETG using a modular block system that keeps the frame down to 20 kg. It's heavy in presence, yet light enough to move across a room.

Every joint follows a strict rectilinear block logic. In the wide studio view against the raw plastered wall, you can trace how four thick boxy volumes interlock to form the base, seat slab, cantilevered armrests, and tall backrest. Baev finished the 3D-printed chair in a cold grey tone he calls "Kyoto Fog." A close-up of his hand resting on the armrest reveals a smooth matte surface with crisp 90-degree edges, completely free of ornament or surface decoration.

The piece started as a few decisive lines on paper. Baev cites the quiet emptiness of raw architectural spaces, along with the lonely atmosphere of video games like Silent Hill and Half-Life, as key emotional references. An open monograph on the Bauhaus Building in Dessau sits beside him in the studio photos, echoing that interest in pure structural volume. To compress development time on this 3D-printed chair, he paired optimized printing workflows with AI tools for early form studies, technical testing, and final refinement.

Seen in use with Baev seated inside its deep frame, THE OBJECT 01 reads less like a prototype and more like usable architecture. It doesn't hide its geometry or its recycled material. Each modular block earns its place by cutting waste and holding the silhouette together.

See the full project by Nako Baev on Behance.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, just months after her death, a work by Yayoi Kusama set a fresh auction record at Sotheby’s in New York, as the auction house kicked off the marquee November sales on Monday night with back-to-back auctions that brought in $378.7m (with fees).
  • It has been revealed that kusama’s No.
  • The 53-lot sale, which carried a pre-sale estimate of $226.2m to $323.1m—the highest since May 2024, according to Sotheby’s—saw two works withdrawn and five unsold, including works by Ellsworth Kelly, Kerry James Marshall, Roy Lichtenstein and Keith Haring, as well as Ayrton Senna's Formula 1 car inexplicably included in the sale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, just months after her death, a work by Yayoi Kusama set a fresh auction record at Sotheby’s in New York, as the auction house kicked off the marquee November sales on Monday night with back-to-back auctions that brought in $378.7m (with fees). The evening also saw records for Sam Francis, Jonas Wood, Firelei Báez and Tomma Abts. Not a bad start to a week in which auction houses expect to sell as much as $2.4bn in art.

It has been revealed that kusama’s No. 3P.B. (1960) fetched $12.5m ($15m with fees), against an estimate of $10m to $15m, setting a newly introduced auction record for the Japanese artist who died in August. One of Kusama's earliest landmark Infinity Nets series, the painting was included in a 1961 exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art, among the artist's earliest inclusions in an American institutional show. The work was the fifth most expensive lot in Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening auction, which brought in $224.78m ($268.7m with fees).

No. 3P.B. (1960) by Yayoi Kusuma. Courtesy Sotheby's.

The 53-lot sale, which carried a pre-sale estimate of $226.2m to $323.1m—the highest since May 2024, according to Sotheby’s—saw two works withdrawn and five unsold, including works by Ellsworth Kelly, Kerry James Marshall, Roy Lichtenstein and Keith Haring, as well as Ayrton Senna's Formula 1 car inexplicably included in the sale. While around 45% of lots hammered within their estimates, bidding was uneven.

In a recent development, roy Lichtenstein’s Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990) led the sale in terms of value, hammering for $22m ($24.6m with fees) against an estimate of $20m to $30m. It was followed by Willem de Kooning’s Water...Soft Banks and a Window (Untitled VIII) (1975), which fell short of its $20m low estimate, hammering for $17.1m ($20.3m with fees). Andy Warhol’s Flowers (1964) fetched $15.2m ($18.2m with fees), just above its $15m high estimate.

According to recent reports, sam Francis’s Towards Disappearance I (1958) sold for $15m ($17.1m with fees), at the low end of its $15m to $20m estimate, setting a new auction record for the artist. It was a case of déjà vu: the same painting had previously set Francis’s auction record when it sold in 1999.

One of the most exciting moments of the evening came when five bidders battled for six minutes over Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991), a depiction of an Old English Sheepdog. The work ultimately hammered for $9m to a roar of applause.

Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991) Courtesy Sotheby's.

Another standout result was Salman Toor’s Lavender Boy (2019), which went for $340,000 ($435,200 with fees), more than four times its $80,000 high estimate even without buyer's premium being factored in.

The evening kicked off with the single-owner sale of the collection of cable television magnate Theodore Baum and his wife Ruth. The 24-lot auction generated $90.8m ($109.9m with fees), comfortably within its $74.4m to $109m pre-sale estimate, with a 100% sell-through rate. However, one-third of the lots hammered below their low estimates, while just one-quarter exceeded their high estimates.

According to recent reports, the top lot was Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest (1965-68), which hammered for $16.2m ($19.3m with fees), among the highest results for the artist at auction, against an estimate of $12m to $18m. The Baums acquired the work in 1986 for just $65,000; including Sotheby’s fees, the winning bidder paid almost 300 times that amount.

Roy Lichtenstein's Two Paintings Sleeping Muse (Study) (1983) Courtesy Sotheby's.

It has been revealed that it was followed by an untitled 1998 Mark Rothko painting, which fetched $15.5m ($17.7m with fees), surpassing its $10m to $15m estimate. The Baums purchased the work for $115,000 in 1983, according to Sotheby’s, meaning Monday’s buyer paid more than 150 times that amount, including fees. The third most valuable lot was Andy Warhol’s The Scream (After Munch) (1984), sold for $6.8m ($7.9m with fees) against an estimate of $4m to $6m. Together, the three works accounted for around 42% of the sale’s $91.4m hammer total.

Not every work met expectations. Franz Kline’s Figure (1955) recorded the largest shortfall in dollar terms, hammering for $1.8m ($2.3m with fees), against an estimate of $4m to $6m—55% below its low estimate.

After the sale, Sotheby’s remarked works from single-owner collections achieved $239m (with fees), making up almost 60% of the evening’s total earnings.

“When your sale is the opener for a major season like this, there’s always a sense of heightened anticipation," Lucius Elliott, Sotheby's head of contemporary art marquee sales, remarked following the auction. "I think this evening’s sale did what everyone hoped it would—signaled that the market is in a great place and demand is strong. We saw real competition for coveted works, with a keen focus both on works from admired collections and for the works we specifically sought out for this sale to meet the demand we knew was there. The evening’s final tally—double that of the equivalent evening last season—says it all.”.

On Tuesday night, the New York art world's eyes will turn toward rival auction house Christie's for the 20th century auction, led by paintings with eight-figure estimates by Wassily Kandinsky, Gustav Klimt and Pablo Picasso.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Companies are offering people fake fine art photography portfolios, along with fabricated exhibitions and media coverage, to help them pose as professional photographers and secure U.K.
  • government launched the Global Talent visa in 2020 to attract the “brightest and best” creative artists — as well as scientists and researchers — from around the world.
  • Sources indicate that however, a BBC investigation found that companies have been increasingly exploiting the scheme to help wealthy applicants secure visas through fraudulent means.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Companies are offering people fake fine art photography portfolios, along with fabricated exhibitions and media coverage, to help them pose as professional photographers and secure U.K. talent visas.

The U.K. government launched the Global Talent visa in 2020 to attract the “brightest and best” creative artists — as well as scientists and researchers — from around the world.

Sources indicate that however, a BBC investigation found that companies have been increasingly exploiting the scheme to help wealthy applicants secure visas through fraudulent means. They say that these firms are offering people fabricated photography portfolios, exhibitions, as well as press reviews to help them present themselves as established artists and qualify for U.K. talent visas.

Sources indicate that following the BBC’s investigation, the U.K. Home Office is now revoking visas issued to two Nigerian men who claimed to be fine art photographers, because it believes they were obtained by deception. Nigerian art critic Molara Wood tells the news outlet that she had found her name attached to fake online reviews praising the works of these two fake fine art photographers.

“There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists,”Wood states.

A BBC reporter went undercover to investigate companies offering services to people applying for the Global Talent visa. One London-based firm told the reporter it could provide artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage, and letters of recommendation to support an application. The organization offered a “fully inclusive” package costing $132,000 (£100,000), which its representative claimed had never resulted in a rejected visa application.

Sources indicate that the package included up to 15 original works of art, with an additional $1,500 (10,000 yuan) charge to ship them from Beijing to London. The tech giant claims it could supply a range of photography, adding that commissioning artists in China was cheaper than in the U.K.

Industry observers note that the representative says the company would also arrange exhibitions and media coverage reviewing the reporter’s work to strengthen her application. Some of the material would be backdated to give the impression that she had been working as an artist for several years. For an additional $37,000 (£28,000), the company also offered to arrange for the reporter to receive a Chinese art award sponsored by Forbes magazine.

The U.K. Home Office tells the BBC that the company the reporter had dug out was already under investigation and it “will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh York has been sued by an internet trade group, which includes YouTube, Facebook and Instagram, over its plans to require social media platforms to put warning labels for users.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed the warning label law in November last year. The legislation — which is scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2027. — will require social media platforms that offer addictive features, such as algorithmic feeds, autoplay, infinite scrolling, like counts and push notifications, to display warning labels.

The law requires platforms to display a warning from the US Surgeon General stating that, while social media may benefit some young owners, “excessive use may be associated with significant mental health harms.” It also directs the commissioner of mental health to design warning labels for users that are approved by the state.

However, internet trade group NetChoice has filed a lawsuit against New York over the state’s upcoming law, according to a report by Reuters. NetChoice represents 30 groups, including YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, Instagram, SnapChat, and TikTok.

In a complaint filed in federal court, NetChoice indicates the warning label law violates the free speech protections of the US Constitution’s First Amendment by compelling its members to ​convey the state’s “preferred message” about online safety.

NetChoice notes New York’s law is “designed to block, burden, and browbeat social media people” by ​subjecting them to ​the warning when they sign on and after multiple hours of use, with no way to bypass it.”.

“Unlike a static warning on ​a product label, these warnings repeatedly interrupt users and ​block access to protected speech,” NetChoice says, according to Reuters.

NetChoice reportedly filed a similar lawsuit against California last month over a state law which is also slated to take effect on January 1, that will require social media platforms to caution children and teens that: “The Surgeon General has warned that while social media may have benefits for some young owners, social media is associated with significant mental health harms and has not been proven safe for young users.” In its lawsuit, the internet trade group argued that the legislation violated both the First Amendment and the federal Communications Decency Act (which protects online platforms from being sued over third-party content).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Panasonic has unveiled the Lumix SHX1, the first compact cinema camera to bear the Lumix branding. Previously, Panasonic separated its cinema and consumer imaging divisions between the two brands, but the SHX1 is the unification of the two under one roof.

In a recent development, “For decades, Panasonic has supported the video industry from broadcast to cinema, and its Varicam cinema cameras have been used to make films, dramas and documentaries worldwide. This expertise has also been carried into Lumix, and it led to the Lumix S1H, introduced in 2019 as a cinema-quality professional video model,” Panasonic says.

According to recent reports, “In 2024, Panasonic took this further by integrating its professional AV and consumer imaging businesses, which share a commitment to supporting customers’ creativity. The newly introduced Lumix SHX1 brings together the expertise of both businesses in a compact cinema camera.”.

The combination of the two Panasonic camera divisions and the existence of the SHX1 effectively means the end of the Varicam brand, but should result in a more cohesive overall camera line.

The SHX1 is, effectively, the S1 II packed into a box-style cinema body, with a couple of exceptions. Firstly, Lumix included an anti-aliasing filter to reduce moire at the cost of some sharpness while the camera also offers the ability to shoot BRAW, albeit with a caveat: it can’t capture it to the CFexpress or SD card slot and must instead use an external SSD.

Sources indicate that beyond that, the camera is capable of capturing basically what the S1 II already does. It features a 6K full-frame partially stacked CMOS image sensor with Dual Native ISO and Dynamic Range Boost, giving the camera effectively 15 stops of dynamic range when in V-log. The SHX1 comes with ARRI LogC3 pre-installed as well, allowing users to choose between V-Log and ARRI LogC3.

Sources indicate that in standard recording formats, the camera supports 6Kp30 and 5.1Kp60 in 4:2:0 10-bit, as well as in 3.8Kp48 4:2:2 10-bit, which is a new option compared to the S1 II. It also, of course, supports open gate recording and in-camera anamorphic de-squeeze.

According to recent reports, the sensor is equipped with a Phase Hybrid autofocus system with 779 points and the SHX1 has the same AI technology as found in the S1 II which enables eye and face detection. Also on-board is Panasonic Lumix's excellent five-axis in-body image stabilization system along with support for Dual IS 2 when combined with a lens that supports OIS and the feature.

In a recent development, professional interfaces include 12G-SDI and HDMI output, timecode input/output, and internal 32-bit float audio recording through the 3.5mm microphone input. The thermal design supports unlimited recording time in up to 4Kp120 and the design of the box camera means it supports micro V-mount batteries, too. Of note, there is no in-camera ND filter, which is an odd exclusion given the target market.

Panasonic also confirmed two optional accessories: the XLR Handle Unit AU-XHU1 and the Control Grip AU-GRP1.

Sources indicate that the Panasonic Lumix SHX1 is slated to become available in January 2027 for $4,699.99. A kit that includes both the handle and the control grip will be avaialble for $5,499.99.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shure is entering the increasingly crowded spatial audio market with its newly introduced MV360 microphones.
  • Recent findings suggest that just last week, Blackmagic Design unveiled the Ambisonic Microphone, a high-end studio solution.
  • Shure says its new MV360 “makes immersive audio more accessible to creators at every level.” To achieve this, the plug-and-play mic features ready-to-use Capture Modes, including immersive binaural, stereo, mono, and auto-tracking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shure is entering the increasingly crowded spatial audio market with its newly introduced MV360 microphones.

Recent findings suggest that just last week, Blackmagic Design unveiled the Ambisonic Microphone, a high-end studio solution. Last month, Sony arrived on the scene with its ECM-AX10, a $250 spatial audio mic for content creators. Built with creators in mind, Shure’s new $349 USB-C MV360 is much closer to Sony’s offering in both price and functionality.

Shure says its new MV360 “makes immersive audio more accessible to creators at every level.” To achieve this, the plug-and-play mic features ready-to-use Capture Modes, including immersive binaural, stereo, mono, and auto-tracking.

The mono and stereo modes are self-explanatory, working just as they would on a traditional mic. Immersive binaural promises a broader, more lifelike soundstage, which Shure states is ideal for headphone playback. Meanwhile, auto-tracking mode focuses the virtual microphone toward the loudest sound source, such as a speaker in an interview or podcast.

According to recent reports, each Capture Mode records a ready-to-use two-channel file that requires no post-production. However, creators who opt for full 360-degree recording gain significantly more flexibility, as they can edit the Ambisonic B-format (Ambix) file in Shure’s Motiv software or compatible third-party apps.

As Shure explains, the MV360 captures a stronger sense of place than a traditional microphone.

“Listeners can feel closer to a podcast conversation, more immersed in an ASMR scene, or transported into the middle of a bustling market or quiet forest,” Shure claims.

The MV360 is a relatively compact spatial microphone housed in an all-metal body. It records and draws power over a single USB-C cable, ensuring compatibility with a wide range of devices, including smartphones and many cameras. Alongside Shure’s Motiv apps, the MV360 supports various third-party applications, allowing customers to record 360-degree audio directly to Motiv or a DAW of their choice.

“Sound can make the difference between watching a moment and feeling part of it,” states Eduardo Valdes, Associate Vice President of Global Marketing and Product Management at Shure.

Industry observers note that “Until now, capturing that sense of presence has required expensive equipment, technical expertise and time that many creators simply don’t have. The MV360 changes that. It gives creators an easy way to bring listeners closer to the conversation, the performance or the world around them, while giving experienced professionals the control they need to shape every detail,” Valdes continues.

The Shure MV360 is available now for $349 and includes the USB-C mic, a small tripod, cold shoe mic clip, phone clamp, extra cables, carrying case, and windscreen.

Sources indicate that alongside the standard model, Shure also unveiled the MV360+ today, slated to arrive in early 2027. Designed for field recordists, videographers, and VR storytellers, the MV360+ works with mirrorless cameras, DSLRs, action cameras, 360-degree cameras, and more. It also adds onboard 32-bit float and internal recording capabilities, a rechargeable battery, and wireless control functionality.

The Shure MV360+ will retail for $449 when it arrives early next year.

Sources indicate that just days after we were passing our last respects to the Cybertruck, the Tesla Cybercab is finally available to order. Alas, like with the "flying Roadster", there's some important small print.

Industry observers note that the Cybercab will initially only be usable in the same locations where Tesla's Robotaxi ride-hailing service operates, which means it will be geofenced to specific parts of Texas and Florida. If you thought Adobe's subscription model was bad, at least there's the Creative Cloud Black Friday sale.

Recent findings suggest that cybercab sales aren't opening to the public at large. Like with the flight-mode Roadster, you'll need a personal invite from Tesla. Nevertheless, the company says it expects to make the first deliveries in Austin, Texas, as soon as December.

Recent findings suggest that those who get an invite will have to pay $29,990 for the car itself. If they want the vehicle to actually drive, they'll have to also commit to a Tesla Autonomy Subscription at $299 per month.

Recent findings suggest that people generally don't like subscriptions. Companies do since recurring payments usually provide higher margins and more stable long-term revenue than a one-off sale. People willingly accept that approach for phone data, streaming services and software, but it stings a but more when it comes with a physical product that also has an up-front cost.

Other carmakers have been roasted for this. BMW wanted people to pay $18 a month for heated seats. Mercedes-EQ decided to cap performance and ransom it back to customers in the form of an Acceleration Increase costing $100 a month. Other cash graps have included paywalled key fobs and garage door opening.

Recent findings suggest that admittedly, the Tesla Cybercab is different beast. You could argue that its autonomous driving capability is the real product and that the vehicle is just the shell for it. That service entails plenty of real ongoing costs for cloud infrastructure, remote monitoring systems, maps and safety updates.

Recent findings suggest that the controversial part is that the vehicle's usability will depend on the Autonomy Subscription because it has no manual controls. Cancelling won't downgrade it to a normal car – it makes it unusable. It's a piece of hardware whose usability depends entirely on an ongoing software service controlled by Tesla.

For comparison, an extra $10,000 would get you a Tesla Model Y with manual controls and an optional full-self driving (FSD) subscription at $100 per month.

Even Tesla CEO Elon Musk thinks the Cybercab monthly fee that his tech giant is quoting is "too high". Writing on X in response to a post by YouTuber Marques Brownlee, he suggested that it "should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.".

That might give Cybercab customers hope that the price will come down in the future. But it could also go up. The Tesla Autonomy Subscription Agreement states that the company reserves the right to adjust the monthly fee with just a month's notice. If it hikes the cost beyond a price you're prepared to pay, you lose the use of your car.

@MKBHD It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.November 14, 2026.

The agreement also allows Tesla to retain a lot of control over the product you just bought. It can modify service areas, update operating conditions, and control access to autonomous operation remotely. At least initially, those buying the car for personal-use will not be allowed to put it to work on ride-hailing networks. The car also films you during the entire ride and will pull over if the camera detects that you're infringing Tesla's rules.

These are unusual limitations compared with traditional car ownership, making it feel more like a temporary lease of a product whose branding Tesla hasn't yet managed to trademark.

A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

#22303. Do art fairs care about non-VIP visitors?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1424 w)
