Do art fairs care about non-VIP visitors?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1424 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that october’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans.
  • Industry observers note that “It’s important to be in Paris,” mentioned Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October.
  • According to recent reports, the previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that october’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans. No other city could match the range and quality of the French capital’s art fairs and exhibitions, both at public museums and private foundations. And what about all those charming restaurants, cafes and shops?

Industry observers note that “It’s important to be in Paris,” mentioned Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October. “Paris is the undisputed capital of the art world—once a year,” Sharp added, speaking at Post-Fair’s preview on 19 October, in the chic Marais district. Nearby, someone had sprayed “mort aux riches” across the window of a bank.

According to recent reports, the previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting. Further demonstrations, highlighting the neglected state of France’s secondary schools, the ever-rising cost of living and other grievances, had been planned in Paris and other French cities on the afternoon of Saturday 24 October. Unemployment in France for those aged 15 to 24 at the moment stands at 21.5%, almost three times the rate in neighbouring Germany.

On Tuesday 20 October, the day of the ultra-exclusive Avant-Première pre-preview of Art Basel Paris in the Grand Palais, the French activist collective Pillage de Classe (class plunder) posted a message on Instagram exhorting protesters to “take back” the famous Belle Époque exhibition hall on Saturday, the penultimate day of the week’s flagship fair.

Art Basel Paris has been held in the historic Grand Palais since 2024.

According to recent reports, of course, the Grand Palais was not stormed, Bastille-style. In the highly unlikely event of protesters managing to “take back” the building, they would have been disappointed, just as revolutionaries had been in 1789, when they discovered the prison they had liberated contained just seven detainees. Art Basel Paris, taking no risks, had closed the event two days early on Friday evening (after an excoriating letter from France's gallery association to fair director Karim Crippa, Art Basel recompensed exhibitors 20% of their stand fees).

The mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth took even fewer risks, emptying its stand the day before, leaving three paintings by the local artist Hélène Delprat. The fair had been shortened to three VIP preview days plus just one day for the general public. Satellite fairs, like Paris Internationale and Post-Fair, closed at lunchtime on Saturday.

That Saturday afternoon, more than 100,000 people duly turned out to demonstrate. However, these proved predominantly peaceful and were confined by the police to the outskirts of the city.

It has been revealed that the disruption in Paris had surely been a momentary blip. And Art Basel’s ultra-wealthy invitees, which the top end of the international art trade likes to call the “right kind of people”, had already been and gone. But what about the reputational impact?

“The collateral damage is substantial considering the whole point of being in Paris is to let yourself surrender to its myriad charms,” said Andrew Terner, a New York-based private dealer and collector, speaking in the immediate aftermath of the early closure.

In a recent development, the French authorities blamed “ultra-left radical groups” for the violence that had marred weeks of otherwise peaceful protests, begun in September by discontented teenage lycée students. Pillage de Classe is certainly a left-wing radical group; it views Art Basel Paris as a luxury playground in which art is used by the ultra-wealthy to protect their capital from taxation.

It has been revealed that but maybe (leaving aside its desire to take the Grand Palais by storm) Pillage de Classe has a point, at least with regard to the fair’s top French clients. In France, the net worth of the country’s 500 wealthiest individuals has ballooned from 6% of the country’s GDP in 1996 to 42% in 2024, according to a much-cited article in the French business magazine Challenges. Tax reforms introduced by President Macron in 2017 excluded stocks, financial assets (including art) and corporate investments from wealth tax calculations.

Moreover, in 2003 the French government had granted tax breaks of up to 75% for private individuals and 60% for corporations that supported the arts. This encouraged investment in glitzy private foundations, such as the Fondation Louis Vuitton, François Pinault’s Bourse de Commerce, the Fondation Cartier and the newly opened Île Seguin luxury hotel and Large art centre, which have become such an alluring feature of the Paris art scene for international visitors. According to research by Apollo magazine, Bernard Arnault’s LVMH luxury group received an aggregate tax break of €518.1m between 2007 and 2017 to set against the €790m the corporation spent building the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton.

Industry observers note that the ultra-wealthy have also grown a lot wealthier in the US in recent years. The share of the nation’s wealth held by the richest 0.0001% (around 200 individuals) is now more than seven times what it was in 1980, according to a November Substack posted by the Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman.

In a recent development, today’s art market is dominated by the world’s wealthiest people buying the world’s most expensive art. Most of these people are pretty old. This is not a good look now that the Democrats have won a landslide victory in the US midterm elections, driven by a massive turnout of young voters. Authoritarian rulers like Viktor Orbán in Hungary and Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia have been voted out of office. Young people have been protesting en masse about their diminished life chances in France and more than a dozen other countries across the world.

Suddenly, ordinary people matter again. The young matter. But do they matter at art fairs?

Take ticket-pricing. In October, the general public were charged £48 each to attend Frieze London, with students being asked to pay £32. Does Frieze, which is owned by the billionaire Ari Emanuel, the former chief executive of the US entertainment conglomerate Endeavor, want to actively discourage young people from visiting? Or is that ticket price an acknowledgement that pretty much the only students who can now afford to attend the UK’s art colleges come from more affluent backgrounds?

It has been revealed that the following week, Art Basel Paris, part of James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems investment portfolio, was charging €47 for a standard day pass and €30 for a student ticket. “The galleries pay for the fair. Visitors are a side business,” says Magnus Resch, a Newly introduced York-based author and art market entrepreneur. According to Resch’s back-of-an-envelope calculations, stand fees generate at least €15m, while tickets bring in less than €3m. “Charging the public €47 isn’t about the money. It’s about keeping the fair exclusive.” (Art Basel does not reveal detailed breakdowns of its revenue streams.).

It has been revealed that “It is key for the public to visit an art fair,” notes Guillaume Sultana, whose contemporary art gallery exhibited on the upper level of Art Basel Paris, where footfall is slower than down on the ground floor among the mega-galleries. “But a lot of general visitors on the weekend are a bit frustrated because public tickets are very expensive.”.

Sources indicate that sultana acknowledges that “the main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always”. Despite the fair being truncated, Sultana describes the experience as “very good”, having sold a painting by the young Syrian artist Osama Al Rayyan during the preview for €15,000, among other works.

In the funfair-mirror optics of the international art market, €15,000 might appear a relatively “affordable” price point. But traditionally, sensible collectors have been advised to spend no more than 5% of their available wealth on art. So, whoever bought that Al Rayan painting, should, theoretically, have had €300,000 of spare cash available. For would-be younger collectors in today’s tough economic conditions, these are intimidating figures, unless they can call on the bank of mum and dad.

Collecting art is in serious danger of being perceived as something that old, rich people do. With so many established collectors ageing and selling, rather than buying, and a democratic wave pushing back against oligarchical wealth, this might be a good moment for the art market to think more about inclusivity than exclusivity, to take a broader view of who might be the “right kind” of people.

After all, who wants “death to the rich” sprayed across their gallery window?

Latest Update: Panasonic Lumix SHX1 Review: The S1 II in Boxy Clothes

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1418 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when the Panasonic S1 II was announced, one of my first thoughts was, “How are they going to top this with an S1H II?” The answer was, they didn’t.
  • Sources indicate that if the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best.
  • It has been revealed that note that throughout this review I will be referring to this camera in comparison to the Panasonic S1 II.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when the Panasonic S1 II was announced, one of my first thoughts was, “How are they going to top this with an S1H II?” The answer was, they didn’t. Instead, Panasonic is bringing the internals of the S1 II to a latest form factor, a cinema box camera, and calling it the SHX1 ($4,699).If the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best. However, for content creators, it offers only minor upgrades over the less expensive and still incredibly capable S1 II. ProsClass leading image stabilization never seen in this style of cameraFantastic image quality with minimal rolling shutterExtremely modifiable designConsNo internal BRAW (requires an SSD)Some buttons feel mushy and are difficult to pressNo internal ND filter This is definitely not the FX5 competitor many were waiting for, but it still might make a lot of cinematographers and videographers very happy.

Sources indicate that if the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best. However, for content creators, it offers only minor upgrades over the less expensive and still incredibly capable S1 II.

It has been revealed that note that throughout this review I will be referring to this camera in comparison to the Panasonic S1 II. If you are unfamiliar with that camera, you can check out our review here. As well, as the SHX1 does not offer any stills capture, this review will be entirely focused on video capture.

The SHX1 is quite compact for a cinema camera, similar to a RED Komodo and weighing only 948 grams (33.4 ounces). In a departure from Panasonic’s previous BG-Series box cameras, this SHX1 includes a top-mounted LCD monitor, with extensive 4-axis articulation and 1.84M dots of resolution.

According to recent reports, the articulation is extremely useful, as you can shoot above your eye-line, something usually prohibited with top-mounted displays. There are dedicated exposure buttons on the body, as well as Menu, Back and AF-On. These buttons have a pretty unresponsive feel to them, with little haptic feedback to let you know you’ve actually pushed the button. These can be customized, something I recommend to avoid excessive menu diving.

As expected for a cinema camera, the top, right side and bottom of the camera have plentiful 1/4-inch mounting points for rigs and accessories. The camera is powered by Mini V-Mount batteries, most of which are the same height as the camera. There is an active fan system in the body, which allows even 4K/120p footage to be captured indefinitely.

It has been revealed that it’s worth pointing out that you can also purchase the SHX1 with an accessory kit ($5,499), which includes a top handle, XLR adapter and a side grip. The grip feels fantastic but is quite large. I consider it almost a necessary accessory, and the extra controls give operators several more options for custom buttons and a joystick for selecting the autofocus point. The top handle is very sturdy, and the removable XLR adapter gives you easily accessed gain controls. Unlike previous S-Series bodies, which relied on an XLR adapter to capture 32-bit float audio, the SHX1 can record 32-bit audio through the 3.5mm jacks and internal mic as well.

Industry observers note that footage can be stored on a UHS-II SD card, CFexpress Type B card, or external SSD. As expected with a cinema camera, there are locking ports for SDI video, timecode, and a full-size HDMI port. For further external control, a Live Production Unit called the AU-LPU1 will be released in early 2027.

The lack of built-in ND filters is a disappointment, but that was the compromise Panasonic was forced into when keeping the body so small. Screw-in filters or a matte box will be required for controlling light levels.

The sensor is the same full-frame 24.5MP partially stacked unit we saw in the S1 II, which is capable of outstanding results and well-controlled rolling shutter. The only difference is an anti-aliasing filter has been added to minimize incidents of moiré in finely detailed textures.

In my testing, though, I found very similar results to the S1 II, with neither camera giving me moiré even when shooting fabrics at moderate distance.

Industry observers note that like the S1 II, the SHX1 has a massive number of recording resolutions, frame shapes and frame rates. The headline feature is 6K Open Gate recording up to 30P, and 5.1K Open Gate using the full sensor up to 60P. For slow motion, the camera can capture 4K at up to 120P with sound. There is also the option to expand the dynamic range by reducing the readout speed. This does produce appreciably cleaner shadows, but with a corresponding increase in rolling shutter artifacts.

Sources indicate that video can be recorded with MP4, MOV and ProRes codecs for standard 10-bit video. There is also the option to capture 12-bit RAW video in either ProRes RAW or BRAW flavours. Bafflingly, though only ProRes RAW can be recorded to the CFexpress card, BRAW requires an external SSD. This is particularly odd as BRAW offers extremely efficient 12:1 compression rates, which could be easily written to a card. Adding insult to injury, the camera’s startup time is dramatically increased with an SSD attached, taking nearly 10 seconds and often leading to me missing shots.

The video quality itself from the camera is outstanding, with impressive detail and expansive dynamic range even when Dynamic Range Boost is not active. Log video can be captured in either Panasonic V-Log gamma or ARRI’s LogC3. The Panasonic V-Log gamma remains my favourite log curve to work with, but ARRI’s gamma is very flexible and the industry standard in the filmmaking world.

Recent findings suggest that what sets the video quality from the SHX1 apart from any other box camera is the inclusion of incredibly effective in-body image stabilization, based on the S1 II system. This works great in its default mode, but even better when Panasonic lenses are attached and the “Cropless” stabilization is engaged. The camera’s autofocus abilities are also quite reliable, though perhaps not quite as rock-solid as Sony’s and Canon’s more recent implementations. Humans and animals can be automatically detected, and there is a good degree of “stickiness” when following moving subjects.

Sources indicate that if you don’t require the box-camera form factor, then the SHX1 can be a confusing proposition. The S1 II features nearly all of the video capabilities with excellent photography specs and an EVF in a considerably more affordable package.

However, many professional videographers and cinematographers require the box-camera design to make it easy to build rigs or mount the camera in a variety of locations. The forthcoming Live Production Unit will add further versatility for using the SHX1 as a remote camera, something the S1 II cannot offer.

According to recent reports, as well, if absolute reliability is key, the more robust cooling system in the SHX1 means overheating will not be a concern even when recording demanding footage in hot areas. The S1 II has very good thermals for a hybrid mirrorless camera, but in professional situations absolute reliability is imperative.

Compact cinema cameras like the RED Komodo-X 6K ($4,995) and Blackmagic Pyxis 6K ($2,249) offer similar form factors and outstanding image quality. Unlike the SHX1, these can record extremely compressed RAW video internally. However, the autofocus performance is vastly behind the SHX1, and neither offers IBIS. RED and Blackmagic may offer more bang for the buck for filmmakers, but the SHX1 is the clear choice for handheld documentary work.

RED Komodo-X 6KBuy newly introduced on B&HRED Komodo-X 6KBuy used on KEH.comBlackmagic Pyxis 6KBuy new on B&HBlackmagic Pyxis 6KBuy used on KEH.com.

The Sony FX5 is also a compact full-frame cinema camera with great autofocus and IBIS. The FX5 can accept an optional EVF, has more reliable autofocus and records compressed X-OCN RAW video internally. However, the SHX1 features much more effective stabilization and industry-standard connections. For event work, the Sony makes more sense, whereas the Panasonic will find itself more at home in commercial environments.

It has been revealed that maybe. If the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best. However, for content creators, it offers only minor upgrades over the less expensive and still incredibly capable S1 II.

Xiaomi’s Eye-Catching Pro Series Phones Go Global for the First Time

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that xiaomi officially released its 18 Pro Series phones, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, at a launch event in Paris, marking the first time it’s pushing its Pro models outside of China.
  • Recent findings suggest that both will hit select markets — not North America — in the coming weeks and months and carry on Xiaomi’s existing partnership with Leica as camera-centric devices.
  • According to recent reports, xiaomi already foreshadowed this launch when unveiling the devices at Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit in September 2026, so specs, especially on the camera side, weren’t entirely a mystery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that xiaomi officially released its 18 Pro Series phones, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, at a launch event in Paris, marking the first time it’s pushing its Pro models outside of China. That also makes them outliers in another respect: they are rare slab smartphones with two displays.

Recent findings suggest that both will hit select markets — not North America — in the coming weeks and months and carry on Xiaomi’s existing partnership with Leica as camera-centric devices. They also feature a rear LTPO AMOLED screen positioned as a creative tool for those who like selfies but want more variety.

According to recent reports, xiaomi already foreshadowed this launch when unveiling the devices at Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit in September 2026, so specs, especially on the camera side, weren’t entirely a mystery. Once they released in China shortly afterward, the cat was pretty much out of the bag.

Industry observers note that we know the main differences between the two phones have to do with screen size, image sensors, the Snapdragon chip, and battery capacity. The 18 Pro Max gets a larger 6.9-inch LTPO AMOLED display (2624 x 1208) with Xiaomi’s own Shield Glass protection, a 1-120Hz variable refresh rate, 4,000 nits of peak brightness, and BT.2020 support. It also runs on the more powerful Snapdragon 8 Gen 6 Elite Extreme chipset and packs a 7,050mAh battery.

According to recent reports, otherwise, the Pro has a smaller 6.4-inch panel (2436 x 1120) with the same display specs as its Max sibling. It also steps down a bit, running on the Snapdragon 8 Gen 6 Elite chip, and, given its smaller size, has a 6,000mAh battery.

Xiaomi first showcased its Privacy Display feature for the main screen on both phones when it debuted these devices in China, and it works the same on either model. When activated through the settings, it recommends eight applicable apps, including Notes, Gallery, Messages, Google Photos, Gmail, Phone, and Contacts. Consumers can also enable it for any installed app via the Privacy Display settings, or choose to leave the feature on at all times, regardless of what’s onscreen.

There are slight differences in the rear display size, as the 18 Pro Max features a larger 2.9-inch panel compared to the 2.7-inch screen on the 18 Pro. Both will come with 12GB of RAM and 256GB or 512GB storage configurations, though the Pro Max also offers a 16GB RAM and 1TB storage variant.

It has been revealed that interestingly, Xiaomi equips both phones with almost the exact same camera specs. The three Leica-branded rear cameras are largely identical on both models, with one key exception: the 18 Pro Max uses the LOFIC-equipped Light Fusion 960L sensor, whereas the 18 Pro uses the standard Light Fusion 960.

It has been revealed that the 200-megapixel main camera (23mm equivalent) uses a Type 1/1.28 Light Fusion 960L image sensor and an f/1.67 aperture. Thanks to LOFIC technology, it delivers better dynamic range than both a standard sensor and the 18 Pro’s main camera. You can tell just by pointing both phones at any subject before even snapping the shutter. There’s also optical image stabilization with a CIPA-rated seven stops of shake correction. The Leica Summilux-designed lenses combine precision glass and plastic elements with what appears to be a glare-resistant coating.

According to recent reports, the 200-megapixel periscope telephoto camera (75mm equivalent) uses a Type 1/1.56 image sensor, an f/2.4 aperture, and 3.2x optical zoom. Finally, there’s the 50-megapixel ultra-wide camera, whose sensor size remains a mystery. It is somewhat of an outlier in that it’s a 17mm equivalent with a 102° field of view, which is noticeably narrower than most ultra-wide cameras on other phones.

In a recent development, on the software side, Xiaomi adds a new mode called Essential Moment that marries Leica color science with AI-driven image processing to emulate classic film and camera looks. Names like “B&W Film,” “Modern Vintage,” and “Iconic CCD” don’t specify exactly what stock they’re based on, but the new styles add a distinctly Xiaomi-infused element to the camera interface.

Recent findings suggest that this is how Xiaomi frames it: “B&W Film captures the depth and tonal range of classic monochrome photography, Iconic CCD recreates the vivid, saturated colors of CCD-era digital cameras, and Modern Vintage offers refined tones with natural detail for a timeless look. Consumers can also replicate the optical characteristics of two classic lenses — a 35mm Documentary lens and a 75mm Portrait lens with soft bokeh.”.

It has been revealed that there are some unusual limitations, however. Pro mode doesn’t allow owners to shoot in RAW at 50 megapixels, and there is still no 24fps option for video, including in Pro Video. None of the Leica styles and filters introduced in the Leitzphone by Xiaomi have migrated over to these devices, so you retain the same choices offered in other Xiaomi models.

The Back Display offers a fairly high degree of access to the overall camera interface, including modes, settings, customizations, and more. Xiaomi limits zoom to 0.7x and 1x, meaning there is no way to activate the telephoto camera, though the settings still let you hold up a palm to trigger the shutter hands-free.

While the live preview occupies a sizable portion of the display, Xiaomi configured it to light up in bright white elsewhere to help illuminate subjects in dimmer conditions. It limits available modes to Photo, Video, Portrait, and a retro-style option called Photo Booth, and strangely omits Leica filters from the equation (though you can still choose between Leica Authentic and Vibrant as the overarching style).

In a recent development, you also get the choice to shoot pixel-binned 12.5-megapixel or 50-megapixel stills, with video resolution options ranging from 720p all the way to 8K at either 30 or 60fps. Dolby Vision and a Teleprompter are also available as optional features.

Industry observers note that it’s a fully functional display in that it works with swipes and gestures just as the main display does. Tap-to-focus works, as does focus tracking when double-tapping on yourself or another subject in the frame. You can preview shots you’ve taken and either press the onscreen shutter or use the volume buttons to capture a photo or video.

Since the screen uses the rear cameras, the dynamic range advantages apply equally; Xiaomi doesn’t appear to neuter the experience by dialing things back, particularly with the LOFIC sensor on the 18 Pro Max.

It has been revealed that an added benefit of the Back Display is that it also works with notifications and real-time information, like calls, maps, ride-hailing, food delivery, audio recording, and more. Pin to Back Display allows you to pin text and images to it for quick reference, such as a boarding pass or QR code. There’s also the option to apply a different wallpaper to it, if you want.

Neither Xiaomi nor Leica made any mention of a photography or teleconverter lens kit for either phone, even as Xiaomi’s Chinese competitors continue to release more of them. There are possibilities there, but you would need a third-party setup to make it work. Thus far, Xiaomi has only made photography kits for its Ultra line, which it maintains is still the company’s flagship with a more specialized photography slant.

You won’t find the Xiaomi 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max in Canada or the U.S. unless you import them yourself. They’re both compatible with North American cellular networks, so there isn’t a hardware limitation in that regard. Warranty challenges aside, Xiaomi is offering five years of Android updates and six years of security updates.

Both models will come in the same four color variants: Black, White, Velvet Red, and Cosmic Blue. As for pricing, the Xiaomi 18 Pro starts at €1,399, while the 18 Pro Max starts at €1,599.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The earliest known photograph of Bogotá, the capital of Colombia, taken in 1842, has sold for $331,600 at auction.
  • According to recent reports, the daguerreotype, titled Rue de l’Observatoire, was sold by Christie’s this week as part of an auction of 350 photographs from the Roger Therond Collection: A French Passion.
  • This image, captured by French diplomat Jean-Baptiste Louis Gros, is not only one of the earliest known photographs of Colombia, but also one of the very first urban daguerreotypes made outside Europe and the United States.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The earliest known photograph of Bogotá, the capital of Colombia, taken in 1842, has sold for $331,600 at auction.

According to recent reports, the daguerreotype, titled Rue de l’Observatoire, was sold by Christie’s this week as part of an auction of 350 photographs from the Roger Therond Collection: A French Passion. Roger Therond, was a journalist who served as editor of Paris Match for half a century and spent decades building a collection that brings together major works from the history of French photography.

This image, captured by French diplomat Jean-Baptiste Louis Gros, is not only one of the earliest known photographs of Colombia, but also one of the very first urban daguerreotypes made outside Europe and the United States.

It had been initially listed by Christie’s with an estimated value of up to $89,000, but the photograph far exceeded expectations, selling for nearly four times its estimated value.

The historic daguerreotype reveals a nearly deserted street in the Colombian capital with the Andes mountains in the background.

Appointed chargé d’affaires in Newly introduced Granada (present-day Colombia) in 1838, French diplomat Baron Gros was also a painter and draftsman. Shortly after the daguerreotype was publicly announced in 1839, he began experimenting with the new photographic process in the country. France had made the invention publicly available to encourage its spread around the world. News of the invention was published in the local newspaper El Observador on September 22, 1839. Gros was among the early travelers who recognized the potential of photography as a way to document places, record information, and represent the world around them.

It has been revealed that “Photography in those days was, after all, the preserve of an elite; not everyone could afford the equipment,” Élodie Morel-Bazin, the European Head of Photography at Christie’s, tells Reuters. “He was a diplomat; he travelled a great deal; he probably came from a very distinguished family and had the means to devote himself to it. That was his hobby.”.

Christie’s claims the photograph is particularly remarkable for its 47-second exposure time. Its subject, a view of a city street, was also unusual for the period, when most photographs were portraits. The long exposure meant that people moving through the street were unlikely to appear in the image, leaving the city looking almost empty. The level of detail captured on the metal plate is remarkable, with the Andes mountains visible in the background. The auction house notes that photographing such distant features was technically challenging because haze and diffused light often obscured them.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.
  • The philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces.
  • Sources indicate that grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.

The philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces. Grynsztejn got the selection down to 65, then hit a wall. Paring it down to 60, as originally intended, became an excruciating process. The Guthmans, champions of the MCA for decades, did not force the museum to choose just 60.

Sources indicate that grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment. To date, the Guthmans have donated 130 works to the MCA—the largest donor gift in the museum’s history.

For Grynsztejn, building a great museum collection takes not only visionary leadership but visionary philanthropy. “The Guthmans have invested in Chicago artists, making their gift one that also has a civic impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. Included in the gift is work by Amanda Williams, Dawoud Bey and Rashid Johnson.

The Guthmans have spent decades supporting Chicago’s civic and cultural institutions. As a real estate lawyer, Jack started out by providing pro bono services. Meanwhile, Sandy directed her family’s foundation Polk Bros. Jack was elected as a trustee of the MCA in 1989 and currently serves on its board. For the MCA’s 50th anniversary, the couple donated 50 photographs by women artists.

Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995–96) Photo: Nathan Keay, © MCA Chicago.

According to recent reports, the current gift includes 23 pieces by artists of colour and 19 by women. Thirteen artists are new to the MCA’s collection, including Mohamed Bourouissa, James Casebere, Julia Fish, Christian Marclay, Adrian Paci, Elle Perez and Shinique Smith. Other gifts, like photographs by Bey, deepen the MCA’s holdings.

“In some cases, we are adding an entirely new collection,” Grynsztejn indicates, referring to Bey’s early photography in Harlem, “and in some cases, we are gaining an icon, as in Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995-96).”.

The MCA began as a kunsthalle in 1967. It started receiving gifts, so in 1974 it formalised its collection. Despite the fact that the very first piece to enter the MCA’s collection was by Marisol, it eventually began to reflect the usual gender and racial biases.

During her tenure, Grynsztejn has sought to change that by establishing the Women Artists Initiative, inspired by the experience of many colleagues who have found it more challenging to fundraise for exhibitions by women artists. The museum’s proof-of-concept came with the success of exhibitions by Faith Ringgold, followed by a traveling Yoko Ono retrospective. The MCA has added women artists to the collection at four times the national average. Recently, the initiative has been renamed the Madeleine Fund for Women Artists and now has a $5m endowment.

Since Grynsztejn’s arrival at the museum in 2008, the MCA’s collection has grown from approximately 1,300 to 3,800 works. At least half of the acquisitions under her leadership have been by women and artists of colour. “This is not woke or [diversity, equity and inclusion],” she indicates. “It’s good business and good culture. Because if you are a public trust, you are in service to your public.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Florian Lamm of Lamm & Kirch pairs OT Scholar type with Attila Hartwigâs photos in the Best Book Design 2026 Leipzig prize catalog.

There isnât a horizontal cover title anywhere on the front board. Designed by Florian Lamm of Leipzig studio Lamm & Kirch for Stiftung Buchkunst, the catalog for Best Book Design from All over the World 2026 shifts its name onto a narrow white fore-edge step along the right margin. Single upright capitals stack cleanly from top to bottom, ending in the year 2026 at the foot. On page 1, photographer Attila Hartwig curls a dark softcover volume into a tight loop so its fanned leaves catch an upward flare of studio light. Nothing sits flat on a white seamless sweep. Turn to pages 4 and 5 and a pinched black binding angled like a boat prow faces the hazy shadow silhouette of Anthology for Listening Vol. II, while page 14 captures an open wire-stitched gutter throwing a candle-like reflection straight up the grey sheet.

According to recent reports, opposite page 14, Omnitypeâs OT Scholar takes command of the directory. Three narrow columns sort national prize winners submitted from more than thirty countries, building a competition archive that traces its Leipzig roots back to 1963 without needing a single ruled divider line. Winners get solid black numbered dots. Fourteen awardees, led by Dutch Goldene Letter recipient Ouroboros Wings, French Gold Medal winner Picalso, and Silver Medal titles Odes and Sophie Thun: Zwischen Licht und Wand, carry white numerals inside black discs â while shortlisted books below wear hollow hairline rings.

That three-column grid holds steady across every country section, from Belgium and Canada to China, Austria, and Hungary. Inside each narrow column, left-aligned roman labels for Title, Author/Editor, Publisher, Design, Illustration/Photography, Printer, and ISBN hang clean beside italic book titles and thirteen-digit numbers. Dense Hungarian, Czech, and German diacritics stay sharp even at compact catalog sizes. Whenever a listed book wins a medal, its numbered black dot and jury commentary drop right inline above paired monochrome object photos anchored at the lower margin. Faint show-through across the thin uncoated pages gives this book design catalog the quiet utility of a working Leipzig Book Fair reference.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Framed by their car’s windshield, and then again by my rearview mirror, a man and a woman who seem to be a couple look like they'd rather be anywhere but together. He’s behind the wheel, doing all the talking; she’s looking straight ahead, motionless like a marble statue. Gradually, her face wears a desperate expression that only grows more hopeless as he continues talking and gesticulating.

Recent findings suggest that in the supermarket checkout line, I pick up a copy of TIME magazine for the first time in God knows how long, drawn to a painting of Jesus Christ on the cover. It’s a special edition promising to tell us “Who he was. Who he is. His miracles, his mission, his love.” I expect to see a lot of biblical sheep inside, but I don’t find any. I buy the issue as an artifact. I stopped believing in TIME magazine a long time ago.

Down the street, a place that pretended to be a legitimate art gallery for a couple of months, showing the worst possible commercial art, has finally given up, and now it’s selling fur coats. A man in a cowboy hat walks past two girls dancing for a social media video. The air is chilly, and I think of buying myself a leather jacket.

She looks at me with the most loving eyes as she holds a stack of perfectly folded laundry. She comforts me with her wide, auspicious smile, her jet-black hair, and her wrinkle-free, porcelain skin. I feel safe, accepted, and not judged. “Fast service, same day,” she promises because she’s just a model in an ad for a laundromat.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief.

“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Parthenon’s east pediment, ‘the most famous image of antiquity’, recreated in Frankfurt exhibition

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.
  • In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.
  • “Nothing came of that,” notes Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.

In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.

“Nothing came of that,” notes Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.

But now, Brinkmann notes his team has solved a riddle akin to “putting together a jigsaw puzzle without having all the pieces”. The results of decades of research will go on show in an exhibition, Athena, the Stage is Yours: the Parthenon Puzzle, opening at the Liebieghaus on 18 November.

In a recent development, long a flashpoint in Greek-British relations, the politics of the Parthenon surfaced in the run-up to the opening. The exhibition was to include marble fragments from both the British Museum in London and the Acropolis Museum in Athens. But, as The Art Newspaper reported last month, the Greek government withdrew its loan of nine fragments: according to Greek media reports, the request was rejected by Greece’s Central Archaeological Council on the grounds that they would be shown alongside British Museum pieces removed from the Acropolis by Lord Elgin. The Greek ministry of culture’s press office did not respond to emailed requests for comment and confirmation.

Greece has for decades demanded the return of the Parthenon Marbles taken by Elgin, which have been housed in the British Museum since 1817. The Liebieghaus has, however, secured a rare loan of two fragments from the British Museum. After the Greek government’s withdrawal, a British Museum spokesperson confirmed that the museum “will still be loaning”.

“The cancellation of the loans from Greece does not detract from the exhibition’s concept, or its scholarly significance,” declares Elisabeth Pallentin, a spokesperson for the Liebieghaus. “The exhibition is based primarily on fresh findings resulting from many years of research at the Liebieghaus.”.

Recent findings suggest that the east pediment is probably “the most famous image of antiquity”, Brinkmann indicates, with the centre of the sculpted ensemble composed of 3.5m-tall figures. The pediment was destroyed at some point between the fifth century AD and 1670—it is not known when or why, though there are plenty of theories—and 80% of it is still missing.

Recent findings suggest that the rest is in fragments in museums around the world. Until now, no one had succeeded in fully reconstructing the central figures, Brinkmann says. “In the last 200 years, there have been a lot of proposals, but we saw that there were always gaps.”.

A reconstruction of the figures in the east pediment of the Parthenon (detail).

Vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, 2026. Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung, Frankfurt am Main.

The most serious work on the east pediment had been undertaken more than a century ago by a British Museum curator, Arthur Hamilton Smith, Brinkmann notes. Smith partially recreated the east pediment using plaster casts from the British Museum and cooperated with colleagues in Athens to obtain more casts; his reconstruction went on display in the museum in 1908.

Sources indicate that “He did a fantastic job in preparing the way,” Brinkmann says. “That was our basis.”.

Recent findings suggest that although the Liebieghaus team recreated these fragments using scans and a 3D printer, the majority of the pediment was still missing. A breakthrough came when the team began investigating reliefs from the lids of Roman sarcophagi, which proved the key to unlocking the mystery.

Recent findings suggest that “It was really a chance discovery,” Brinkmann states. “During a visit to the Hermitage in St Petersburg in 2014, we noticed a figural relief on the lid of a sarcophagus that was clearly closely related to the composition of the east pediment. It refers to the few surviving figures from the corners of the pediment, such as Helios and Selene with their chariots, but also to figures that have repeatedly been proposed as having belonged to the east pediment, such as the Horae/Moirai.”.

Recent findings suggest that they discovered nine sarcophagi in total with relevant reliefs. Most were in the Vatican Museums and elsewhere in Rome. “They had been overlooked,” Brinkmann says. “But the Romans copied everything the Greeks did.”.

Jaques Carrey, drawing of the east pediment (left-hand side), Temple of Minerva, Athens (1674).

Bibliothèque nationale de France, ref.: FOL-FC-3.

It has been revealed that none of these reliefs demonstrated the entire east pediment ensemble; each depicted a different subset of the 39 figures. But with the aid of computer technology, the team established that the remaining fragments of the east pediment and the depictions on the reliefs were a 100% match.

Industry observers note that the team’s research has yielded some surprises. It was not previously known, for instance, that the Dioscuri, the twin horsemen known as Castor and Pollux to the Romans, were portrayed on the pediment. The figures served as models for the giant figures on the Quirinale in Rome, which are almost identical and date from antiquity, Brinkmann says. The twins are portrayed standing next to their bucking horses with anxious expressions, straining at the reins in an effort to control them.

This portrayal of the Dioscuri makes sense only in the context of the birth of the goddess, Brinkmann indicates. In mythology, Athena burst forth from her father Zeus’s forehead after he had swallowed her mother. Her birth is described in the Homeric hymns as causing Mount Olympus to shake, the earth to shriek, and the sea to swell and rage.

“The Dioscuri are heroic horsemen in mythology,” Brinkmann indicates. “They don’t lose control of their horses. But the birth of Athena was a primordial cosmic event that unleashed a natural disaster. What we see are the consequences.” Other figures in the recreated ensemble are also responding to the cataclysm: Hermes, for instance, is depicted holding onto his hat.

Recent findings suggest that brinkmann is known internationally for his research into polychromy in ancient Greek and Roman sculpture. An exhibition he curated, Gods in Color—Painted Sculpture of Classical Antiquity, has travelled the world, having been shown in several US locations, Athens, Oxford, Istanbul, the Vatican Museums and elsewhere.

In a recent development, it is possible that the new Liebieghaus exhibition will travel too, Brinkmann claims. But not, it seems, with marbles from the Athens collections, with recent developments giving little room to hope that a lasting settlement between Greece and the British Museum is on the horizon.

• Athena, the Stage is Yours, Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection, Frankfurt, 18 November-25 July 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “The Amiga was my first school.” For pixel artist Klas Benjaminsson, that’s less nostalgia than a CV. The Swedish creator of the Masters of Pixel Art book series learned his craft on Commodore’s 16-bit wonder, and three decades later, he’s gone back to class, creating a brand-new artwork entirely on an original Amiga 1200 (the Amiga ranks in our best retro consoles guide).

It has been revealed that the result is Beyond the Screen: wildlife, lush vegetation and ocean life bursting out of a glowing monitor. It’s built from just 640 x 512 pixels and 32 colours, a canvas that would make a modern phone wallpaper blush. Benjaminsson first sketched in pencil, then brought it to life in Deluxe Paint 4. He calls the Amiga’s limits a “sweet spot”: tight enough to push against, generous enough to make something great.

It’s also a nod to Jim Sachs’ Amiga Lagoon, the picture that revealed a generation what these machines could do, and a love letter to an era when your imagination really was the only limit.

Recent findings suggest that the timing is no accident. Retro Games’ full-size Amiga 1200 replica, THEA1200, lands on 4 December. Unlike the A500 Mini we reviewed in 2022, it comes with a working keyboard and Workbench desktop, so it’s built for creating as well as playing.

Artists can join in too, with PosterSpy inviting its community to reimagine Benjaminsson’s piece in their own style. Need a pixel fix first? Dive into our 31 amazing pixel art examples or learn how to break into pixel art. Then read on as Benjaminsson explains why limits still make for better art, and which retro tools you should try first.

Industry observers note that the upcoming THEA1200 arrives on 4 December. See more of Klas Benjaminsson's poster art at PosterSpy x THEA1200.

Klas Benjaminsson: One key point in the initiative of THEA1200 is to recreate the Amiga 1200 in modern shape, so it made sense to honor the original platform.

Recent findings suggest that KB: To be honest, the work "Amiga Lagoon" by Jim Sachs was a very key piece from the beginning. It visualised the power and creativity of the Amiga, and we agreed that an indirect homage to this masterpiece would be suitable for this occasion.There was an idea to create a “flow” coming out from the screen, showing waves of animals, nature and wildlife - flowing and growing out from this creative computer. I wanted a feeling that communicated “only your imagination sets the limits”.From sketch to finish, animals changed and shifted positions. But I felt the core idea was good and continued the work until the end.

KB: For me personally, growing up with the Amiga 500 and 1200 graphic standards, these limitations became something of a sweet spot for me. Limited enough to make it interesting to push the borders on what could be done, but also good enough to make it possible to create some great designs.

Recent findings suggest that KB: Deluxe Paint 4 on the Amiga was where bulk of work was done. Photoshop and GrafX2 on the PC: importing the sketches and converting formats for export.

KB: To be honest I think many of modern pixel artists are doing a great job. There are hundreds of active pixel artists right now, posting pixel art on a daily basis with no direct platform or set rules for limits in their work space, but they still set a limited palette and a certain pixel area for their work. I think it's an awesome homage to the old platforms, which lives on so vividly in these modern pixel art works even today.

Industry observers note that KB: Digital graphics had a big impact in my youth. As a kid I enjoyed playing video games, but as a young aspiring “artist” I also studied the graphics of the many games I tried (both Arcade and on my own C64). It took several years until a friend of mine demonstrated me his brand fresh Amiga 500 with Deluxe Paint – that was the moment I realised I might be able to create something like that myself.I took the first steps on a very long and interesting journey on finally becoming an art director. The Amiga was my first school that defined much of my professional life.

Sources indicate that KB: There are many techniques that more or less could be described as artistic knowledge, which I learned on the Amiga but aren't unique for this medium/platform. But there are some routines that could be blamed on my background with old-school pixel art:- The importance of setting a palette early on in the design process.- To keep full control of the pixels and resolution.

KB: The Amiga provides an interesting set of limitations to work with if you are into pixel art. Enforcing a specific resolution and a limited colour palette when creating pixel art is a very challenging and demanding practice, which forces the artist to be precise. With these clear restrictions in place, much more focus can be aimed at the actual creative work instead.

KB: I personally find it fascinating to take photos with a classic analogue camera, and see how the film can change with exposure settings. It's a special and rewarding experience to go through the processes by hand. You try and learn by mistakes, testing ideas, creating and discarding concepts, and finally finding a way to express your ideas. Digital tools can be a great help, working alongside you when sketching and trying out ideas. But there is a certain magic about when doing it by yourself, learning the craft.

KB: If you are into pixel art, don't hesitate to try out Deluxe Paint or Brilliance! These are the original software from which most modern pixel art tools has taken their UI concepts, as well as the early versions of Photoshop.If you are into creating music, try out some of the tracker software such as ProTracker, or AHX for unique chip sounds.For young people learning to code, AMOS is a fun and powerful language to start with. Something that could transition into C++ later on.Another nice tool was Dir Opus, file-handling made easy and logical. I wish Microsoft or Apple would have picked it up back in the days....

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian debuted Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

With substantial scholarships, exceptional facilities, accomplished faculty, and private studios, students pursuing an MFA in Studio Art and Design at the University of Louisville have the resources and creative freedom to develop their artistic practice within a dynamic, supportive community.

Industry observers note that the rigorous 60-credit MFA program encourages experimentation, critical inquiry, and interdisciplinary exploration. Students may pursue interdisciplinary practices or concentrate on individual media, including ceramics, drawing, glass, painting, photography, printmaking, sculpture, design, latest media, and installation.

According to recent reports, located in Louisville's Portland arts district, the MFA program occupies a dedicated, newly renovated warehouse featuring individual graduate studios, state-of-the-art production facilities, laboratories, a seminar room, and an exhibition gallery. This distinctive environment provides students with the space, resources, and opportunities to develop ambitious creative projects.

According to recent reports, the Hite Institute also offers a 31-credit-hour MA in Art History or Curatorial Studies. Combining critical theory, art historical research, contemporary art, and hands-on exhibition experience, the program prepares students for careers in museums, galleries, curatorial practice, arts administration, and art writing, as well as further academic study.

In a recent development, founded in 1946, the endowed Hite Institute of Art + Design has built a distinctive identity grounded in its avant-garde origins and oriented to creative experimentation and critical inquiry. Its accomplished faculty of practicing artists, designers, and scholars encourages students to expand their creative and intellectual horizons while engaging with contemporary cultural, social, and environmental challenges.

In a recent development, both graduate programs maintain small, selective cohorts, allowing for close faculty mentorship, individualized attention, and meaningful collaboration. Students benefit from the Hite Institute's extensive resources, including six galleries, outstanding glass and additive manufacturing facilities, partnerships with museums and cultural institutions, an active alumni network, and visiting lectures by internationally recognized artists, curators, and arts professionals.

In addition to guaranteed scholarships, graduate students may qualify for teaching assistantships, internships, and additional awards that provide valuable professional experience and support their creative and scholarly development.

Applications for Fall 2027 admission are due January 15, 2027.

To learn more, visit art.louisville.edu.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

What $10,000 grows to at different rates over 30 years — the rate difference matters more than you think.

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 6% annual return.

$10,000 invested for 30 years at 10% annual return.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Future value (FV) is the projected worth of an investment at a specific point in the future, based on an assumed rate of growth. It answers the most practical question in investing: "If I invest this money today, what will it be worth in 10, 20, or 30 years?".

Sources indicate that future value calculations rest on compound interest — the principle that your returns earn their own returns over time. Albert Einstein reportedly called compound interest "the eighth wonder of the world," and while the attribution is debatable, the math is not. The difference between simple interest (returns on your original investment only) and compound interest (returns on your investment plus accumulated returns) becomes enormous over long time horizons.

The basic future value formula for a lump sum investment is:.

For example, $10,000 invested at 8% for 20 years:.

FV = $10,000 x (1.08)^20 = $10,000 x 4.661 = $46,610.

Recent findings suggest that the table reveals two critical insights. First, small differences in return rates produce massive differences over long periods — $10,000 at 6% grows to $57,435 over 30 years, while the same amount at 10% grows to $174,494. That 4-percentage-point difference triples the outcome. Second, time is the dominant variable. At 8%, your money doubles roughly every 9 years — so 30 years gives you more than three doublings, turning $10,000 into over $100,000.

Most people do not invest a single lump sum and walk away. They invest regularly — monthly or per paycheck — over decades. The future value of a series of regular contributions uses a different formula called the future value of an annuity:.

FV = PMT x [((1 + r)^n - 1) / r].

Where PMT is the periodic contribution, r is the periodic rate, and n is the total number of periods.

In practice, you do not need to calculate this by hand. The insight that matters is this: regular contributions are far more powerful than most people realize because each contribution starts its own compounding clock. Your first $500 contribution compounds for the full 30 years, while your 360th contribution (at month 360) compounds for just one month — but together they build wealth that dwarfs a single lump sum.

A person investing $500 per month at 8% for 30 years accumulates $745,180 — from total contributions of only $180,000. That means $565,180, or 76% of the final balance, came from compound returns rather than your own deposits. This is the engine of wealth building.

Sources indicate that every future value calculation should be done twice — once in nominal terms and once in real (inflation-adjusted) terms. The nominal return is the raw number your investments earn. The real return subtracts inflation, showing you what your money will actually buy.

In a recent development, historically, the S&P 500 has returned roughly 10% nominally and 7% after inflation. The difference matters enormously over long periods:.

That $1.13 million in nominal terms has the purchasing power of roughly $610,000 in today's dollars — still excellent, but nearly half less than the headline number suggests. When planning for FI, always use real returns (6-7%) rather than nominal returns (9-10%) to avoid overestimating what your portfolio will actually support in retirement spending.

In a recent development, the Rule of 72 is the simplest and most useful mental math tool in investing. Divide 72 by your annual rate of return to estimate how many years it takes for your investment to double:.

This works in reverse too. If you want to know what rate of return you need to double your money in 15 years: 72 / 15 = 4.8%. The Rule of 72 is an approximation — it is most accurate for rates between 5% and 12% — but it is remarkably precise within that range and far faster than pulling out a calculator.

In a recent development, the FI community uses future value calculations as the backbone of retirement planning. The process works in three steps:.

The table reveals how starting balance and monthly contribution interact. Notice that increasing your monthly contribution from $1,500 to $2,500 (a $1,000 increase) with a $100,000 starting balance cuts 3.5 years off your time to $1 million. This is the savings rate lever in action — the amount you save each month matters more than any other variable you control.

Sources indicate that A common question is whether it is better to invest a lump sum now or spread contributions over time (dollar-cost averaging). The math is clear: lump sum investing wins approximately two-thirds of the time because markets trend upward over the long term. However, dollar-cost averaging reduces the psychological risk of investing a large amount right before a downturn and provides a behavioral advantage that keeps many investors on track. For most FI-seekers, the question is academic — you invest each paycheck as it arrives because you do not have a large lump sum sitting on the sidelines.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

When projecting your portfolio growth for retirement planning, use real (inflation-adjusted) returns of 6-7% rather than nominal returns of 9-10%. A $1 million nominal balance in 30 years has the purchasing power of roughly $550,000 in today's dollars at 2% average inflation. Planning with real returns ensures you are targeting a portfolio that can actually support your desired spending level.

Track your actual spending for 3 months and annualize it. Multiply by 25 to get your FI number using the 4% safe withdrawal rate. If you spend $60,000 per year, your FI number is $1,500,000.

Add up all retirement accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), taxable brokerage accounts, and savings. Exclude home equity and non-liquid assets. This is your starting balance for the future value calculation.

Recent findings suggest that subtract your monthly spending from your monthly after-tax income. Include employer 401(k) match and any other automatic savings. This is your periodic contribution amount for the future value formula.

Use the future value of a lump sum plus annuity formula, or a simple online calculator, to project when your current balance plus monthly contributions will reach your FI number. Use 7% real return (after inflation) for conservative planning.

Test what happens if you increase contributions by $200/month, $500/month, or $1,000/month. Seeing the concrete impact of a savings rate increase — often shaving 2-5 years off your FI timeline — makes the trade-offs tangible and motivating.

For long-term stock market projections, use 7% for inflation-adjusted (real) returns or 10% for nominal returns based on the S&P 500 historical average. For a more conservative estimate, use 6% real. For bond-heavy portfolios, use 3-4% real. Always specify whether you are using nominal or real returns — mixing them up is one of the most common planning mistakes.

According to recent reports, future value calculations show what WOULD happen if returns were constant every year. In reality, markets fluctuate — you might earn 25% one year and lose 15% the next. Over 20-30 year periods, average returns tend to converge toward historical norms, making future value projections reasonably useful for planning. Treat them as directional estimates, not guarantees.

Future value asks: "What will $10,000 today be worth in 20 years?" Present value asks the reverse: "What is $50,000 in 20 years worth in today's dollars?" They use the same variables but in opposite directions. Present value is useful for evaluating whether a future payout (like a pension or annuity) is worth the cost today.

Sources indicate that the Rule of 72 works for any compounding rate, including inflation. At 3% inflation, prices double every 24 years (72 / 3 = 24). This means $50,000 in annual spending today becomes $100,000 in 24 years in nominal terms — your purchasing power is halved if your income stays flat. This is why investing in assets that outpace inflation is essential.

Recent findings suggest that for FI planning, future value is more intuitive — it tells you what your portfolio will grow to. However, the most practical approach is to calculate future value using real (after-inflation) returns. This effectively gives you a future value stated in today's purchasing power, which is what you actually need to know for spending planning.

Industry observers note that in tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), your investments compound without tax drag, so the standard future value formula works directly. In taxable accounts, capital gains taxes, dividend taxes, and tax-loss harvesting all affect your real return. A rough adjustment is to reduce your assumed return by 0.5-1.0% for taxable accounts to account for ongoing tax drag.

In a recent development, future value calculations are the most practical tool in the FI planner's toolkit. They turn abstract concepts like compound growth and savings rate into concrete dollar amounts and specific timelines. The key takeaways are straightforward: use 7% real returns for conservative planning, always account for inflation by using real rather than nominal returns, and remember that your monthly contribution rate has a far larger impact on the outcome than chasing an extra point or two of return. The Rule of 72 gives you instant mental math for any investment decision — how long to double, what rate you need, and how inflation erodes purchasing power. Combined with a clear FI number and a disciplined savings rate, future value projections show you exactly when financial independence becomes reality. Run the numbers, test different scenarios, and let the math motivate you to increase that monthly contribution whenever you can.
